title: NIRJALA: Draining the Sea out of Gaussian Splatting with Three-Path Optics and Reversible Physics
comment: 21 pages, 11 figures
summary: Water does not just tint an underwater photograph; it rewrites it. Each pixel mixes attenuated scene radiance, backscattered light, and scene light scattered forward on its way to the camera, and many combinations of scene and water explain the same pixels. Most Gaussian-splatting methods for underwater scenes model only the first two effects and remove the water by dividing by a transmission that decays exponentially with range, so their inversion gain grows without bound. We present NIRJALA (Sanskrit for "without water"), a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that recovers water-free appearance and geometry together. TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model, adds a range-saturating forward-scattering term to direct transmission and backscatter; we prove that this keeps the inversion gain bounded at every range and bound how errors in the estimated backscatter and attenuation propagate into the recovered colours. PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor, ties a flexible neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model in both directions, so scene content cannot hide inside the water. SAMARASA collects the physics-informed objectives, including a range-binned colour prior. To score water removal against ground truth, we built SAJALA ("with water"), a 30-scene suite path-traced in Blender Cycles with water-free images, depth, and normals under controlled water colour and turbidity. On SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 while rendering at 44 FPS. We also discuss where appearance metrics and geometry disagree underwater, and the limits of our evaluation.

AI.tldr: NIRJALA is a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for underwater scenes that uses a three-path image formation model and a reversible physics anchor to jointly recover water-free appearance and geometry.
AI.motivation: Existing underwater Gaussian-splatting methods model only direct transmission and backscatter, dividing by an exponentially decaying transmission that causes inversion gain to grow without bound with range.
AI.method: The authors introduce TRIVENI, a three-path image formation model adding range-saturating forward scattering to keep inversion gain bounded; PRATIBIMBA, a reversible physics anchor tying a neural water model to a ten-parameter physical model; and SAMARASA, a set of physics-informed objectives including a range-binned colour prior.
AI.result: On the new 30-scene Blender Cycles benchmark SAJALA, NIRJALA raises PSNR from 24.34 to 24.76 dB and lowers depth AbsRel from 0.109 to 0.091 against the strongest baseline; on real SeaThru-NeRF scenes it lowers LPIPS from 0.194 to 0.175 at 44 FPS.
AI.conclusion: Modeling forward scattering and anchoring neural water representations to reversible physics enables bounded-gain underwater scene recovery with improved appearance and geometry.

title: GramStatTexNet: Efficient, Interpretable, and Neuro-Inspired Texture Analysis-by-Synthesis
summary: Deep networks achieve high realism in texture synthesis but often rely on opaque, over-parameterized representations that have limited direct connection to biological vision. Neuroscience-informed pyramid models are interpretable, compact, and biologically inspired, but rely on small, hand-curated statistics sets that are difficult to generalize or extend. We introduce GramStatTexNet, a hybrid analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines the multi-scale Gabor filter structure of classical models with the flexibility of Gramian-based correlations, organized into structured filter families. This structured representation enables analyses that are challenging for deep-feature methods: each statistic carries a named filter-family identity, allowing us to decompose synthesis fidelity into per-family contributions and to learn an interpretable, low-dimensional embedding that preserves perceptual texture content. We compare our framework to classical and deep texture-synthesis baselines across diverse texture categories, and on multiple perceptual metrics, highlighting the compactness and interpretability advantages of this hybrid representation, alongside competitive synthesis quality. This same framework extends naturally to peripheral textures via spatial pooling, and to dynamic textures using a spatiotemporal filter bank. GramStatTexNet provides a unified, interpretable framework for analyzing and modeling visual information with natural extensions across space, time, and eccentricity. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: GramStatTexNet is an interpretable, neuro-inspired texture analysis-by-synthesis framework that combines multi-scale Gabor filters with structured Gramian correlations.
AI.motivation: Deep texture synthesis networks use opaque, over-parameterized representations with limited biological grounding, while classical neuroscience-informed pyramid models rely on small, hand-curated statistics sets that are hard to generalize.
AI.method: GramStatTexNet organizes multi-scale Gabor filter responses and Gramian-based correlations into named filter families, enabling per-family decomposition of synthesis fidelity and a low-dimensional perceptual texture embedding, with natural extensions to peripheral textures via spatial pooling and dynamic textures via a spatiotemporal filter bank.
AI.result: Compared against classical and deep texture-synthesis baselines across diverse texture categories and multiple perceptual metrics, GramStatTexNet achieves competitive synthesis quality while offering higher compactness and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Hybridizing classical Gabor filter banks with structured Gramian statistics provides a unified, interpretable representation for visual texture modeling across space, time, and eccentricity.

title: Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate
comment: 32 pages, 12 figures
summary: Recent studies report that video diffusion models "know more than they show": physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model's own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM's layers add about 0.08 in $R^2$ (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1's clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

AI.tldr: Probing kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models along their sampling trajectories reveals that intermediate layers mostly do not hide physical knowledge beyond the model's own clean-sample estimate, except for jump fall rates early in denoising.
AI.motivation: Prior work suggests video diffusion models encode physical properties better in internal activations than in outputs, but comparing against outputs conflates hidden knowledge with readout ease because the clean-sample estimate is computed from those same activations.
AI.method: The authors record every layer along the sampling trajectories of two MDM checkpoints and MotionDiffuse on text-to-motion tasks, where exact physics of intermediate clean-sample estimates can be computed, and compare uniformly tuned readouts against the estimates.
AI.result: For balance and flight, adding a layer improves over the clean-sample estimate by at most 0.01; for jump fall rate, MDM layers add about 0.08 in R^2 (up to 0.11 in a refit) early in denoising before fading, while MotionDiffuse gains are small and not robust; aborting floating samples flagged by the estimate saves under a tenth of compute.
AI.conclusion: Motion diffusion models generally expose their physical state in their clean-sample estimates once readouts are matched, though early jump dynamics can briefly reside in intermediate layers.

title: A Differential Theory of Quality-Resource Trade-offs for AI Model Selection: The Multiresource Frontier and Its Minimax Price
comment: Under review
summary: Comparing AI models across resource budgets yields quality-resource frontiers relating error to latency, parameter count, training compute, and energy. Offset power laws summarize such frontiers, but their fitted parameters reveal neither the price-independent geometry nor the manner in which trade-offs extend across several resource channels. This paper addresses both gaps by developing a differential theory in which this structure is made explicit. Each frontier admits a price-independent plane-curve representation relating the effective number of active resource channels, $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = s^2/\kappa$ (squared slope over curvature), to the remaining log-error depth, $\Delta S = \ln(\varepsilon/\varepsilon_{\infty})$. This representation separates intrinsic shape from the scale and origin of the resource axis. Complete monotonicity and divisibility yield differential inequalities and frontier bounds. When each of $N$ resources contributes one active channel, the theory gives the parameter-free operating rule $N_{\mathrm{eff}} = 1$ in delivered units and derives minimax resource prices $\lambda^{\star}_i = \alpha_i/(N+1)$ with an exact worst-case regret of $\ln(N+1)$ nats. The results make it possible to interpret measured frontiers and compare resource costs without hand-chosen exchange rates. The theory is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and implemented in the open-source package nn-rank, which derives prices from measured quality and cost, ranks candidates, and reports supported choices and minimax regret: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper develops a differential theory of quality-resource frontiers that separates intrinsic trade-off shape from resource scale and derives parameter-free operating rules and minimax resource prices.
AI.motivation: Offset power laws summarize quality-resource frontiers across latency, parameters, compute, and energy, but their fitted parameters obscure price-independent geometry and how trade-offs extend across multiple resource channels.
AI.method: The authors represent each frontier as a price-independent plane curve relating the effective number of active resource channels N_eff = s^2 / kappa to remaining log-error depth Delta S = ln(epsilon / epsilon_infinity), using complete monotonicity and divisibility to derive differential inequalities, frontier bounds, and minimax prices lambda*_i = alpha_i / (N+1).
AI.result: When each of N resources contributes one active channel, the theory yields the operating rule N_eff = 1 and worst-case regret ln(N+1) nats; the framework is evaluated on 117 published frontiers and released in the open-source package nn-rank.
AI.conclusion: The differential formulation enables principled interpretation of measured frontiers and model selection across multiple resource budgets without hand-chosen exchange rates.

title: Bounded-Order Non-Identifiability in Latent Structure Block Models: The Fiber in Closed Form
comment: Submitted to AISTATS 2027
summary: A graphon is determined by all of its homomorphism densities, but motif-based methods use finitely many. We compute exactly what that truncation costs in a natural family: latent structure block models whose positions lie on $K$ rays, equivalently degree-corrected block models of rank two. For a given radial law, the configurations that agree on every graph with fewer than $2K-1$ vertices form a one-dimensional fiber, which we give in closed form with explicit endpoints; the friendship graph $F_{K-1}$ is its unique edge-minimal separator, so no fixed motif order serves every $K$. The separating signal is suppressed by a factor of at most $m_1^{2(K-1)}$, where $m_1$ is the mean squared slope, about $10^{-4}$ at $K=4$: detecting it from motif counts would take about $10^{15}$ nodes in a single graph, at any edge density. The information is nonetheless in the graph; the fiber belongs to the statistic, not the model. Common spectral pipelines, which count no motifs, still slide along the fiber by more than a third of its length at ordinary densities, with confidence regions that almost never contain the truth, while model-based fits of the same embedding do not. We give practitioners four checks: whether a fit is at risk, what to run instead, why a confidence interval will not warn, and how wide the remaining ambiguity is.

AI.tldr: The authors characterize in closed form the non-identifiability fiber of latent structure block models on K rays when observed only through motif counts of order below 2K-1, and show that spectral pipelines also suffer along this fiber.
AI.motivation: Motif-based graphon methods use finitely many homomorphism densities, but the exact information loss from truncating motif order in latent structure block models (equivalently rank-two degree-corrected block models) was unknown.
AI.method: For latent positions on K rays with a given radial law, the authors derive the closed-form one-dimensional fiber of configurations sharing all motif counts on fewer than 2K-1 vertices, identify the friendship graph F_{K-1} as the unique edge-minimal separator, and analyze spectral versus model-based fits.
AI.result: The separating signal is suppressed by at most m_1^{2(K-1)} (about 10^-4 at K=4, requiring ~10^15 nodes to detect from motif counts); common spectral pipelines slide along the fiber by over a third of its length with miscalibrated confidence regions, whereas model-based fits of the same embedding do not.
AI.conclusion: Truncated motif statistics and standard spectral pipelines suffer from severe non-identifiability on K-ray block models, for which the authors provide four practical diagnostic checks.

title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
comment: 58 pages, 5 figures, 6 tables
summary: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

AI.tldr: Applying gradient averaging to online sketched Newton methods eliminates the statistical efficiency loss caused by randomized sketching without extra oracle evaluations.
AI.motivation: Randomized sketching reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from O(d^3) to O(d^2), but the sketching randomness inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and averaged iterates.
AI.method: The authors replace the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step and analyze the resulting coupled two-timescale recursions for the iterate and gradient estimator, overcoming the loss of martingale difference structure in central limit theorem arguments.
AI.result: The last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging achieves limiting covariance no larger than without averaging, and the averaged iterate attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance of the exact Newton method, supported by numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression.
AI.conclusion: Proper gradient estimation via averaging allows sketched Newton methods to achieve O(d^2) per-step computation without sacrificing optimal asymptotic statistical efficiency.

title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
comment: To appear in NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight)
summary: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.

AI.tldr: Ellipsoid-regularized leverage score sampling improves query complexity for constrained active linear regression by adapting to anisotropic constraint geometry.
AI.motivation: Standard leverage score sampling ignores constraints or uses isotropic ridge regularization, leading to suboptimal query complexity when the constraint set C is anisotropic.
AI.method: The authors approximate the constraint set C by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to define ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores that bias sampling toward directions relevant under the constraint geometry.
AI.result: They prove O(d_eff(C) log d / epsilon^2) queries suffice for a (1+epsilon)-optimal solution, improving to 1/epsilon dependence for convex C, where d_eff(C) <= d is an anisotropic effective dimension; matching lower bounds are shown, and experiments on synthetic and parametric heat conduction problems show lower regression error than baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating outer-ellipsoid constraint geometry into leverage score sampling yields tighter query complexity and better empirical accuracy for constrained active linear regression.

title: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
summary: Stability under input perturbations is necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. Weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. However, existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are insufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. In this paper, we establish a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks under a split spectral norm product constraint. This theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as the network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed. We then propose a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still achieving the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, we establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and provide robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies show that the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to that of classical deep network methods.

AI.tldr: A penalized least squares estimator with a split spectral norm product constraint achieves optimal nonparametric regression rates while maintaining a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant.
AI.motivation: Bounding the Lipschitz constant of deep neural networks via weight norm constraints improves stability under input perturbations, but existing approximation results under fixed norm-product bounds cannot establish optimal statistical rates.
AI.method: The authors prove a sharp approximation theory showing deep ReLU networks can uniformly approximate smooth Holder functions under a fixed split spectral norm product constraint as depth grows, and propose a penalized least squares estimator based on this constraint.
AI.result: The estimator achieves the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor with a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, yielding optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning, adversarial robustness guarantees, and comparable accuracy with controlled sensitivity in numerical studies.
AI.conclusion: Split spectral norm product regularization resolves the tension between uniform Lipschitz stability and optimal statistical convergence in deep nonparametric regression.

title: ReliFlow: Reliability-Calibrated Residual Transport for Combinatorial Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
summary: Predicting the transcriptional response to combined perturbations requires distinguishing interactions between interventions from errors in their individual effect estimates. The latter become more pronounced when single-perturbation evidence is sparse or withheld. We introduce a conditional flow-matching model that estimates the reliability of single-gene effects from training-only cross-fitting and uses those estimates to calibrate the additive source distribution. The velocity is decomposed into a known correction of the additive reference and a learned residual transport field. On Norman genetic perturbations, reduces mean absolute error (MAE) from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld. On held-out ComboSciPlex drug combinations, MAE decreases from 0.191 to 0.176. Non-additive residual correlation improves from 0.574 to 0.638, and component ablations identify the contribution of reliability weighting. The results indicate that accounting for uncertain constituent effects improves generalization to unseen genetic and chemical combinations, with a moderate increase in training cost.

AI.tldr: ReliFlow is a conditional flow-matching model that calibrates single-gene perturbation reliability via cross-fitting to improve combinatorial single-cell perturbation prediction.
AI.motivation: Predicting transcriptional responses to combined perturbations is difficult because errors in sparse or withheld single-perturbation estimates can be confused with true non-additive interactions.
AI.method: ReliFlow estimates the reliability of single-gene effects using training-only cross-fitting to calibrate an additive source distribution, and decomposes the conditional flow-matching velocity into a known correction of the additive reference plus a learned residual transport field.
AI.result: On Norman genetic perturbations, ReliFlow reduces MAE from 0.142 to 0.131 for unseen combinations of observed singles and from 0.198 to 0.178 when constituent singles are withheld; on held-out ComboSciPlex drug combinations, MAE drops from 0.191 to 0.176 and non-additive residual correlation improves from 0.574 to 0.638.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling uncertainty in constituent single-perturbation effects improves generalization to unseen genetic and chemical combinations.

title: How Reward Gain Imbalance Shapes Ranking: Rethinking Rubric-Based Reward Aggregation
summary: Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formalize this heterogeneity as \emph{reward gain imbalance}: each criterion enters the aggregated reward with its own reward gain, the gap between its expected scores on satisfied and unsatisfied responses. Counterintuitively, our experiments show that removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy. To explain this, we derive an exact decomposition of the reward difference between any two candidates into a base satisfaction signal, a reward gain imbalance term, and a residual term, showing that reward gain imbalance can attenuate or amplify the base signal, and finding that misrankings usually concentrate on pairs where it attenuates. Guided by this analysis, we propose the adaptive \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{C}enter \textbf{C}lipping aggregation (DCC), which bounds each criterion's contribution to the reward difference instead of simply removing the imbalance. Using only the scores of the current candidate group, it determines a clipping interval that imposes a common upper bound on per-criterion score differences between candidates, limiting the excessive influence of extreme scores while preserving continuous judgment information....

AI.tldr: Analyzing reward gain imbalance in rubric-based LLM alignment reveals why removing it hurts ranking, and motivates adaptive Dual-Center Clipping (DCC) aggregation.
AI.motivation: Rubric-based RL equally aggregates continuous judge scores across criteria, but scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings in ways that are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors formalize reward gain imbalance, decompose pairwise reward differences into a base satisfaction signal, an imbalance term, and a residual term, and propose adaptive Dual-Center Clipping (DCC) to bound per-criterion score differences using only the current candidate group's scores.
AI.result: Experiments show that removing reward gain imbalance lowers ranking accuracy even with ground-truth labels, and that misrankings concentrate where imbalance attenuates the base signal; DCC limits extreme score influence while preserving continuous judgment information.
AI.conclusion: Bounding per-criterion contributions via DCC rather than eliminating reward gain imbalance improves rubric-based candidate ranking.

title: NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning
summary: Score-based structure learning estimates causal graphs by optimizing a data-dependent objective over structural equation models. We study how prior knowledge that selected pairs of variables are marginally independent can be incorporated into such causal discovery methods. Under faithfulness, marginally independent pairs cannot be connected by a trek, so the knowledge becomes a graphical no-trek constraint, which we call NOTREKS information. We introduce a power-series trek (PSTrek) penalty for gradient-based optimization and a trek constraint for order-based search, and we analyze why such information helps in finite samples and how it restricts the search space. Our numerical experiments illustrate to what extent NOTREKS information helps in causal discovery. In particular, using synthetic benchmarks with oracle NOTREKS information, we show that these constraints can improve both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.

AI.tldr: NOTREKS incorporates prior knowledge of marginal independence as no-trek constraints into score-based causal structure learning.
AI.motivation: Under faithfulness, marginally independent variable pairs cannot be connected by a trek in a causal graph, yet standard score-based structure learning methods do not exploit this constraint.
AI.method: The authors formalize marginal independence as NOTREKS (no-trek) constraints and introduce a power-series trek (PSTrek) penalty for gradient-based optimization alongside a trek constraint for order-based search, analyzing their finite-sample and search-space effects.
AI.result: In numerical experiments on synthetic benchmarks with oracle NOTREKS information, the proposed constraints improve both causal structure recovery and adjustment-based causal effect identification.
AI.conclusion: Encoding marginal independence as graphical no-trek constraints provides a principled way to improve score-based causal discovery.

title: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise
comment: NeurIPS 2026, to appear
summary: We revisit the classical problem of learning general Gaussian halfspaces in the presence of label noise, with particular focus on the large-bias regime, where information-computation gaps are conjectured in several standard label-noise models. Concretely, we present and analyze the rare-tail mean estimator, an extremely simple one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class. In the large-bias regime, classical Averaging (Servedio, 1999) and related global first-moment statistics are provably suboptimal, while the rare-tail mean estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (modulo log factors) under a broad class of label noise models, including probit noise and margin-dependent noise with very slow decay away from the boundary. Notably, our guarantees allow labels arbitrarily close to the decision boundary to be nearly random, while still giving strong directional recovery from a small number of samples. The estimator also cleanly interpolates between the noiseless and noisy regimes: without noise, it attains the same sample rate as classical separability-based methods for realizable halfspaces, and under low noise, or noise that decays away from the boundary, it keeps this rate even after linear separability has been destroyed. As an application, we consider a two-stage curriculum in which source samples, whose noise may be arbitrarily close to $1/2$ near the boundary and decay very slowly away from it, precede target samples, whose noise flips every label at the same rate, i.e., random classification noise (RCN). Since both stages share the same Bayes optimal halfspace, our estimator supplies the directional warm start needed by existing refinement routines, and together they learn the RCN target at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, up to log factors.

AI.tldr: The rare-tail mean estimator, which averages only the observed minority class, learns biased Gaussian halfspaces under broad label noise at the information-theoretic sample rate.
AI.motivation: In the large-bias regime of learning Gaussian halfspaces with label noise, classical global first-moment estimators like Averaging are provably suboptimal and information-computation gaps are conjectured.
AI.method: The authors analyze the one-shot rare-tail mean estimator (averaging only minority-class samples) and apply it as a directional warm start in a two-stage curriculum from margin-dependent source noise to random classification noise (RCN) target samples.
AI.result: The estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (up to log factors) under probit and slowly decaying margin-dependent noise, interpolates cleanly to the noiseless rate, and enables learning RCN targets at the information-theoretic rate in the large-bias regime.
AI.conclusion: Focusing solely on rare-tail minority samples overcomes the suboptimality of global averaging and achieves optimal directional recovery in biased noisy halfspace learning.

title: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation
summary: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification uses positive semidefinite kernels both to define reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and as covariance models for stochastic impulse responses. Sharp kernel conditions are known for RKHS stability, while almost-sure BIBO stability under Gaussian priors requires an even more restrictive covariance condition. These restrictions, however, need not persist beyond Gaussianity, where the covariance no longer determines the full probability law. We introduce the notion of a stability-compatible kernel, namely a covariance kernel admitting at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths. We show that stability-compatibility holds if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated RKHS, a condition strictly weaker than RKHS stability, and derive practical sufficient conditions, including a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. We then construct non-Gaussian priors that preserve a prescribed covariance while enforcing almost-sure stability. In particular, this yields a stable prior based on the stationary radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel, separating covariance structure from the mechanism enforcing stability. Numerical experiments show substantial estimation gains for several important classes of impulse responses, with particularly pronounced advantages when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.

AI.tldr: Stability-compatible kernels enable non-Gaussian priors for linear system identification that preserve a prescribed covariance while guaranteeing almost-sure BIBO stability.
AI.motivation: In kernel-based linear system identification, Gaussian priors require restrictive covariance conditions for almost-sure BIBO stability, excluding kernels like the stationary RBF kernel.
AI.method: The authors define stability-compatible kernels as covariance kernels whose associated RKHS contains a dense set of stable elements, derive a spectral criterion for stationary kernels, and construct non-Gaussian priors that enforce almost-sure absolute summability while preserving the target covariance.
AI.result: They obtain a stable prior based on the stationary RBF kernel and show in numerical experiments substantial impulse-response estimation gains, especially when dynamics occur at late lags or separated temporal regions.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling covariance structure from stability enforcement via non-Gaussian priors expands the class of usable kernels in system identification.

title: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes
comment: 25 pages, 16 figures
summary: While the notions of sphere packing and sphere covering underlie the most widely used criteria for space-filling design in computer experiments, namely, the maximin and minimax approaches, they suffer from major drawbacks in high dimensions. First, when the dimension $d$ is very large, deploying a space-filling design requires an extremely large number of design points, making the very notion of a space-filling design questionable. Second, these two design characteristics are highly sensitive to boundaries, particularly when the design domain is a hypercube (the case considered in this paper), and especially to its vertices. This sensitivity is particularly acute when the design size is less than $2^d$. Instead of considering the maximin or minimax criterion, we consider here the quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube. This error has three key advantages: it accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point $U$ to the design, is less sensitive to boundary effects than the maximin and minimax criteria, and, thanks to Zador's celebrated theorem, enables a smooth and natural transition to uniform designs as the design size tends to infinity. Building on recent results on the construction of optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772) we propose a method to generate random designs of a given target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error. The support of the resulting distribution is then used to construct designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$. We demonstrate that, for moderate $n$, designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well---and significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube. We also explain how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.

AI.tldr: Quantizing the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes yields sparse space-filling designs that avoid boundary sensitivity and outperform uniform designs for moderate sample sizes.
AI.motivation: Classical maximin and minimax space-filling designs suffer in high dimensions because they require huge sample sizes and are highly sensitive to hypercube boundaries and vertices when n < 2^d.
AI.method: Using the L_s-mean quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube and building on optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions, the authors construct random designs of target size n (and incremental designs up to n) and address lower-dimensional subspace projections.
AI.result: For moderate n, designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube achieve substantially lower quantization error than designs uniformly distributed over the full hypercube.
AI.conclusion: Quantization-based designs provide a boundary-robust, scalable alternative to maximin/minimax criteria for high-dimensional computer experiments.

title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
summary: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

AI.tldr: Likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampling with a pretrained diffusion model provably solves sparse recovery in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity.
AI.motivation: Pretrained diffusion models are widely used as priors for ill-posed inverse problems, but theoretical guarantees are often asymptotic or incur worst-case exponential computational costs.
AI.method: The authors analyze sparse recovery from linear measurements using a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler paired with a diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, followed by a final denoising step.
AI.result: They prove polynomial-time recovery with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices, and establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling when the signal is drawn from the prior.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion priors can support both statistically and computationally efficient inverse problem solvers under rigorous non-asymptotic guarantees.

title: A Generative Model for Higher-Order Network Dynamics
comment: 52 pages, 26 figures, 7 tables; includes appendices and references
summary: Conventional network representations inferred from multivariate time series describe statistical relationships between pairs of components, even when the underlying dynamics involve group interactions that cannot be represented by pairwise interactions alone. Several multivariate information-theoretic measures have been proposed to characterise dependence beyond pairs. However, due to a lack of systems with known generating mechanisms, these measures have not been carefully validated or compared for empirical use. To address this, we here introduce a generative model of stochastic network dynamics with pairwise and higher-order interactions specified by the user. The higher-order interactions are represented by directed hyperedges, and the model provides a controlled benchmark for evaluating information-theoretic measures. Removing only the higher-order term gives a pairwise-only reference. The experiments test whether a measure detects changes induced by the higher-order term relative to this reference and recovers the participating nodes and their source-target roles. A separate experiment tests discrimination between a product coupling and a specified nonlinear pairwise control, with equal root-mean-square coupling magnitude under the pairwise-only reference. Several measures detected sufficiently strong higher-order interactions across the tested network topologies and coupling functions. In the separate discrimination experiment, the measures also separated the product coupling from the specified nonlinear pairwise control. Recovery, however, became harder as the number of candidate interactions grew. The framework therefore provides a testbed where the link between higher-order signatures and mechanisms can be tested, rather than assumed, before measures are applied to empirical data.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a user-specified generative model of stochastic network dynamics with directed hyperedges as a controlled benchmark for validating higher-order information-theoretic measures.
AI.motivation: Multivariate information-theoretic measures aim to detect group interactions beyond pairwise links in time series, but lack controlled ground-truth systems with known generating mechanisms for validation.
AI.method: The authors construct a stochastic network dynamics model with user-defined pairwise and higher-order (directed hyperedge) couplings, using a pairwise-only reference (removing the higher-order term) and a matched-RMS nonlinear pairwise control to test measure sensitivity and role recovery.
AI.result: Across tested topologies and coupling functions, several measures detect sufficiently strong higher-order interactions and distinguish product couplings from the nonlinear pairwise control, though recovery degrades as the number of candidate interactions grows.
AI.conclusion: The generative benchmark enables systematic testing of whether higher-order information-theoretic signatures reflect true group mechanisms before empirical deployment.

title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
comment: NeurIPS 2026, 36 pages, 4 figures
summary: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.

AI.tldr: Decomposing SGD dynamics in two-layer neural networks shows that teacher-induced spectral spikes in the orthogonal complement of the teacher subspace inflate representation variance and degrade generalization.
AI.motivation: How first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect feature learning and generalization during SGD training on multi-index teacher models is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors decompose first-layer weights into a teacher-aligned signal component and an orthogonal complement, analyze their joint SGD dynamics with the second layer in the proportional limit, and introduce an analytically tractable surrogate called Decomposed Dynamics.
AI.result: Although orthogonal-complement updates are initially isotropic, training induces teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix that amplify variance and hurt generalization; in ReLU student simulations, freezing orthogonal-complement directions improves generalization, and the signal component rapidly aligns with second-layer weights.
AI.conclusion: Feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization through emergent anisotropy, explaining why constraining orthogonal directions can help.

title: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL
summary: While federated reinforcement learning (RL) has traditionally guaranteed high efficiency in homogeneous environments, collaboration is often hindered when agents possess distinct goals. In this paper, we flip this paradigm, framing reward heterogeneity not as a hurdle to consensus, but as a structural asset that catalyzes exploration. We first propose Personalized Federated Upper Confidence Bound Value Iteration (PF-UCBVI), which achieves optimal linear speedup by decoupling shared dynamics from personalized objectives. To eliminate the risks of explicit exploration, we then introduce Personalized Federated Exploration-Free Value Iteration (PF-EFVI), a purely greedy algorithm that leverages reward diversity to ensure state-action coverage. We prove that PF-EFVI attains logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses under sufficient reward diversity. Our results reveal that agent disagreement shifts the exploration burden from temporal complexity to spatial diversity, enabling efficient collective learning without explicit exploration.

AI.tldr: In personalized federated reinforcement learning, reward heterogeneity across agents can replace explicit exploration bonuses and enable logarithmic regret with a purely greedy algorithm.
AI.motivation: Federated RL typically assumes homogeneous rewards, viewing agent goal heterogeneity as an obstacle to consensus rather than a resource.
AI.method: The authors propose PF-UCBVI, which decouples shared dynamics from personalized objectives to achieve linear speedup, and PF-EFVI, a purely greedy exploration-free value iteration algorithm that exploits reward diversity across agents for state-action coverage.
AI.result: They prove that PF-EFVI attains logarithmic regret without explicit exploration bonuses when reward diversity is sufficient.
AI.conclusion: Agent reward disagreement shifts the exploration burden from temporal complexity to spatial diversity across agents, enabling efficient collective learning without explicit exploration.

title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
comment: Code available at this https URL
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

AI.tldr: Theoretical analysis of on-policy distillation (OPD) shows that sequence-level objectives suffer from a future agreement bias that reverses learning order, while divergence choice governs gradient optimization landscapes.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread use of OPD to train student language models on their own generations, there is little formal guidance on choosing between sequence-level vs. token-level objectives and among different divergences.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze token prioritization, learning order, and optimization landscapes across sequence-level and token-level OPD objectives and f-divergences.
AI.result: Sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias that matches later tokens first while favoring teacher-improbable early tokens, whereas myopic token-level objectives avoid this; forward KL yields a well-behaved landscape while reverse KL and other f-divergences can suffer vanishing gradients even when student and teacher are far apart.
AI.conclusion: Choosing the right OPD objective requires matching granularity and divergence to the student, teacher, and task to avoid reverse learning order and vanishing gradients.

title: When Does Subspace Direction Matter for LoRA? Regime Analysis of the Magnitude Principle in Few-Shot Adaptation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 43 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: We show that the importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction is regime-dependent, and we characterize this dependence in theory and experiment. This refines the recent view that spectral initializers help through update magnitude alone. Direction matters most when labeled data are scarce relative to the representation dimension and the activation subspace used for initialization captures supervised task structure. In this regime, the adapter's row span remains sensitive to its starting point, making task-aligned initialization especially useful. A spiked-covariance perturbation analysis characterizes the finite-sample stability of the estimated subspace. A first-step analysis of LoRA training explains why the subspace's alignment with the task matters and motivates an alignment coefficient $\rho$ that closely tracks gains across classification tasks. We test this account with PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training. In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA achieves the best average rank among 13 methods and improves over vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings, even though it starts from a smaller input-factor initialization norm. Additional classification experiments extend the evaluation to 7B and 8B Llama decoders. Classification gains diminish with more labeled data, consistent with the proposed regime dependence. A targeted extension to completion-only reasoning also shows improvements on GSM8K and StrategyQA. These findings identify conditions under which initialization direction matters, with subspace-task alignment offering a low-cost diagnostic before training for classification.

AI.tldr: The importance of a LoRA adapter's initial input-subspace direction depends on data scarcity, and task-aligned initialization via PivotLoRA improves few-shot adaptation.
AI.motivation: Recent work argued that spectral LoRA initializers help purely through update magnitude, leaving open when and why the initial subspace direction itself matters.
AI.method: Using spiked-covariance perturbation analysis and first-step training analysis, the authors derive a subspace-task alignment coefficient rho and propose PivotLoRA, which initializes adapters from activation PCA at prediction-relevant positions and applies one output-preserving orthogonal pivot early in training.
AI.result: In few-shot BERT-base classification, PivotLoRA ranks first among 13 methods and beats vanilla LoRA in 29 of 30 settings despite a smaller initial norm; gains extend to 7B/8B Llama decoders and GSM8K/StrategyQA reasoning, while diminishing as labeled data grows.
AI.conclusion: Subspace direction matters most in low-data regimes where the adapter's row span remains sensitive to initialization, and alignment rho provides a low-cost pre-training diagnostic.

title: The Spectral Distribution of Matrix Least Squares Solutions, and the Ellipsoid Fitting Problem
comment: 40 pages
summary: We study the spectral distribution of the least squares solution to a random linear system whose unknown is a symmetric matrix. In the normalized and isotropic setting, we derive a closed-form description of the support of the spectral distribution. As an application, we consider the ellipsoid fitting problem: given $n$ standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, does there exist a centered ellipsoid passing through all of them? It was recently shown that this problem has a sharp phase transition at $n \approx d^2/4$. On the satisfiability side, unlike earlier results, these sharp results do not rely on least squares candidates. We show that the least squares candidates considered in earlier works have a threshold of positive semi-definiteness at $n \approx d^2/10$, which was previously observed numerically and predicted non-rigorously using statistical physics methods. Moreover, we show that the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a threshold of positive definiteness at $n \approx 2d^2/5$. Our approach combines several matrix concentration tools. A key technical ingredient, which may be of independent interest, is showing that a certain kernel matrix is well-conditioned with high probability until $n \approx d^2/2$.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the closed-form spectral distribution support for symmetric matrix least squares solutions and establishes the exact positive-semidefiniteness thresholds for least squares candidates and dual certificates in ellipsoid fitting.
AI.motivation: While random Gaussian ellipsoid fitting has a sharp phase transition at n ≈ d^2/4, earlier least squares candidates appeared to fail much earlier (around n ≈ d^2/10) without rigorous proof.
AI.method: Using matrix concentration tools and proving a key kernel matrix is well-conditioned up to n ≈ d^2/2, the authors characterize the spectral support of normalized isotropic matrix least squares solutions.
AI.result: They prove that least squares candidates have a positive-semidefiniteness threshold at n ≈ d^2/10, and the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a positive-definiteness threshold at n ≈ 2d^2/5.
AI.conclusion: The results rigorously confirm statistical physics predictions for least squares ellipsoid fitting and explain the gap between least squares and optimal satisfiability thresholds.

title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations
comment: 78 pages. Comments welcome!
summary: Geometric convolutions on Riemannian manifolds depend on the geometry of the underlying domain, making stability under metric perturbations a fundamental question in geometric deep learning. This paper studies this question for parallel transport convolution through methods from differential geometry and analysis. On a fixed compact manifold, we establish that, for a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the convolution output depends continuously in $L^2$ on the Riemannian metric in the $C^2$-topology, under the specified localization and transport-path conventions. The analysis develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and uses these estimates to compare the transported kernels. A central difficulty is the cut locus, which obstructs uniform comparison of the transport construction over the entire manifold. We address this difficulty by combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume, while also controlling the change in the Riemannian volume measure. The resulting qualitative stability theorem connects perturbation theory for Riemannian geometric constructions with the analysis of spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.

AI.tldr: Parallel transport convolution on a compact Riemannian manifold depends continuously in L^2 on the Riemannian metric under C^2 perturbations.
AI.motivation: Geometric convolutions on manifolds depend on underlying domain geometry, making stability under metric perturbations a foundational question in geometric deep learning.
AI.method: The authors derive perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, exponential maps, and Riemannian volume measures, combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on small-volume neighborhoods of the cut locus.
AI.result: For a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the parallel transport convolution output is proven to be L^2-continuous with respect to C^2 metric perturbations.
AI.conclusion: This qualitative stability theorem links Riemannian perturbation theory to spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.

title: Efficient Variance-Aware Reinforcement Learning in Time-Inhomogeneous Linear MDPs
comment: 38 pages, 2 tables
summary: We study variance-dependent reinforcement learning in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with feature dimension $d$, horizon $H$, and $K$ episodes. While recent works have established variance-dependent regret with $\tilde{O}(1)$ deterministic-regime overhead for linear mixture MDPs (Zhao et al., 2023) and worst-case nearly minimax optimal regret $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K} + d^7 H^8)$ for linear MDPs (He et al., 2023),, existing variance-aware analyses for linear MDPs (Li and Sun, 2023; Huang et al., 2023) rely on a coarse concentration step whose resulting regret guarantees retain a polynomial $\tilde{O}(K^{1/4})$ additive term even in deterministic environments. We propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, a computationally efficient algorithm that achieves the variance-dependent regret bound $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H\min\{\mathrm{Var}_K^*,\mathrm{Var}_K^\pi\}}+d^5H^4)$, where $\mathrm{Var}_K^*$ and $\mathrm{Var}_K^\pi$ denote the cumulative conditional variances of the optimal value function and the played policies' value functions along the realized trajectory. Our result adapts to the minimum of the two realized trajectory variances, recovers the worst-case minimax optimal leading term $\tilde{O}(d\sqrt{H^3 K})$, and collapses to $\tilde{O}(d^5 H^4)$ in deterministic environments, free of polynomial-in-$K$ dependency. At the core of our analysis is a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for the optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value function estimators coupled with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments, which tightens the pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by a factor of $\tilde{O}(d H)$ and removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup.

AI.tldr: VA-LSVI-UCB++ achieves a variance-dependent regret bound in episodic time-inhomogeneous linear MDPs that adapts to the minimum of optimal and played-policy trajectory variances and collapses to O-tilde(d^5 H^4) in deterministic environments.
AI.motivation: Existing variance-aware algorithms for linear MDPs retain an undesirable O-tilde(K^{1/4}) additive regret term even in deterministic environments due to coarse concentration steps.
AI.method: The authors propose VA-LSVI-UCB++, combining a simultaneous three-way reference-advantage decomposition for optimistic, pessimistic, and squared value estimators with variance self-bounding and Freedman-type value-difference arguments.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves regret O-tilde(d sqrt(H min{Var_K*, Var_K^pi}) + d^5 H^4), tightening pessimistic and second-moment confidence radii by O-tilde(d H), recovering the worst-case minimax optimal leading term O-tilde(d sqrt(H^3 K)), and eliminating polynomial-in-K dependence in deterministic MDPs.
AI.conclusion: Simultaneous three-way decomposition removes the inverse-variance-floor blowup and yields sharp variance-adaptive regret in linear MDPs.

title: Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
summary: Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

AI.tldr: Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE) is a general generative framework for variable-length multimodal data on arbitrary state spaces using an insertion-based mechanism instead of padding.
AI.motivation: Most diffusion and flow-based models assume fixed-dimension data, requiring padding or ad-hoc length objectives for variable-length multimodal domains like layouts and molecules.
AI.method: VL-DE handles variable length through a principled insertion-based mechanism with a tractable training objective and leverages the additive form of its generator to build a higher-order sampler that accounts for time dependence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on layout generation and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of VL-DE.
AI.conclusion: Insertion-based generation provides a simple, unified alternative to padding for variable-length multimodal modeling on arbitrary state spaces.

title: Defining equations for two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties
comment: 22 pages
summary: We give a complete algebraic characterization of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties. We show that the determinantal equations arising from rank constraints imposed by the activation patterns generate the defining ideals, thereby proving a conjecture of Alexandr-Montúfar. The set-theoretic proof uses a characterization of orbit closures of matrix pencils in terms of the Kronecker canonical form.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the Alexandr-Montufar conjecture by showing that determinantal equations from activation-pattern rank constraints generate the defining ideals of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties.
AI.motivation: An algebraic characterization of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties was conjectured by Alexandr-Montufar but remained unproven.
AI.method: The authors give a set-theoretic proof using a characterization of orbit closures of matrix pencils in terms of the Kronecker canonical form.
AI.result: They prove that determinantal equations arising from rank constraints imposed by activation patterns generate the defining ideals of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties.
AI.conclusion: The result establishes a complete algebraic characterization of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties.

title: Infinity-Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Principal Component Analysis: Exact Reformulation, Finite-Sample Guarantee, and Efficient Algorithm
summary: Principal component analysis (PCA) is a fundamental and ubiquitous technique for dimension reduction and representation learning, yet its empirical formulation remains vulnerable to distributional uncertainty. While distributionally robust optimization (DRO) offers a natural remedy, existing order-2 Wasserstein models of PCA either preserve the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation. This paper demonstrates how the infinity-Wasserstein distance can reconcile these two desirable properties. For the resulting DRO model of PCA, we derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation and explicitly identify a worst-case distribution attaining the inner maximum. Crucially, the reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, revealing a mechanism through which distributional robustness can reshape the learned principal subspace. Under the mild assumption that the true distribution has a finite fourth moment, we further establish a uniform finite-sample performance guarantee for the proposed model. An iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm is also developed to solve the resulting nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization problem, with a rigorous analysis of its convergence properties. Numerical experiments substantiate the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm and the practical effectiveness of the infinity-Wasserstein model in downstream applications.

AI.tldr: Infinity-Wasserstein distributionally robust PCA admits an exact finite-dimensional reformulation, a finite-sample guarantee, and an iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm that reshapes the learned principal subspace.
AI.motivation: Existing order-2 Wasserstein DRO models for PCA either collapse to the nominal PCA subspace or lack an exact reformulation.
AI.method: Using the infinity-Wasserstein distance, the authors derive an exact finite-dimensional reformulation, identify the worst-case distribution, prove a uniform finite-sample guarantee under finite fourth moments, and develop an iteratively reweighted majorization-minimization algorithm with convergence analysis.
AI.result: The reformulated objective retains samplewise residual information beyond the empirical covariance matrix, and numerical experiments confirm the algorithm's efficiency and downstream effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Infinity-Wasserstein DRO reconciles exact reformulation with genuine subspace adaptation in robust PCA.

title: Risk-Controlled Correction for Frozen Multimodal Models under Missing Modalities
comment: Code: this https URL
summary: A deployed multimodal predictor may face missing modalities after its weights can no longer be changed. This raises a question that training-time repair does not answer: what part of the resulting error is still correctable from the information that remains? We show that this part is characterized by the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities. For cross-entropy and squared error, excess risk measures this gap in the geometry of the loss; ambiguity in the observed modalities cannot be removed. Thus, a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Estimating the Bayes prediction normally requires labels. However, when a model observing more modalities is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs conditional on the remaining modalities recovers this target without retrieval labels; with the same fixed blend and neighbors, it is no worse in expected cross-entropy or Brier risk than averaging hard labels. Some such assumption is unavoidable: otherwise the target is not identifiable from unlabeled data alone. GUARD (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment) leaves the deployed predictor unchanged. It estimates a candidate correction by retrieval, learns from deployment-matched labeled data when correction is likely to help, and calibrates a threshold on a held-out split by conformal risk control. Under exchangeability, the marginal probability that GUARD applies a correction whose loss increase exceeds a prescribed tolerance is bounded by a preset level, regardless of the learned score. In controlled experiments, correction gain follows headroom rather than raw error; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs spanning six domains, GUARD retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.

AI.tldr: GUARD is a retrieval-based, conformally calibrated correction method for frozen multimodal models under missing modalities that bounds the probability of harmful corrections.
AI.motivation: Deployed multimodal models with frozen weights often face missing modalities, yet it is unclear what portion of the resulting error is correctable from remaining modalities or how to correct it safely without labels at test time.
AI.method: The authors characterize correctable error via the Bayes gap and propose GUARD, which estimates candidate corrections by retrieval from a more-complete model, learns when correction helps from deployment-matched labeled data, and calibrates a gating threshold via conformal risk control.
AI.result: Under exchangeability, GUARD bounds the marginal probability of loss increases exceeding a tolerance; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs in six domains, it retains most of blanket correction's gains while respecting harm budgets that blanket correction often violates.
AI.conclusion: Conformal risk-controlled gating enables safe post-deployment correction of frozen multimodal predictors when modalities are missing.

title: A Capability Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Platforms in Regulated Enterprises
summary: Agentic AI platforms-systems in which LLM agents plan, invoke tools, retain memory and coordinate to change the state of enterprise systems-are being procured faster than they can be measured. Public agent benchmarks score models in fixed harnesses; enterprises buy integrated platforms whose orchestration, memory, governance and tooling layers dominate outcomes, and they buy them largely on the strength of vendor demonstrations. We report an industrial evaluation programme ("bakeoff") run by the innovation laboratory of a global bank in which ten platforms-spanning open-source frameworks, proprietary products and hyperscaler ecosystems-were assessed by a cross-functional panel on nine capability dimensions across three financial-services workloads: counterparty credit risk, retrieval-augmented generation and process automation. Scores separate the field into three tiers that are stable under alternative weightings, and surface workload-specific strengths that aggregates hide. A secondary analysis, however, finds Cronbach's alpha = 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions and rank correlations >= 0.93 with the total for eight of nine: a halo effect indicating that demonstration-based scoring measures presentation as much as capability. From these lessons we propose a gate-then-score evaluation protocol with four layers (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value), trace-level reliability metrics estimated over repeated runs, an autonomy-readiness scale and a reproducibility protocol. We state precisely what the present evidence supports, and what a controlled harness must add to turn enterprise platform evaluation from structured judgement into measurement.

AI.tldr: An industrial bakeoff of ten agentic AI platforms in a global bank reveals a severe halo effect in demonstration-based scoring and motivates a four-layer gate-then-score evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Enterprises procure agentic AI platforms largely from vendor demonstrations, while public benchmarks only test models in fixed harnesses rather than integrated orchestration, memory, governance, and tooling layers.
AI.method: A cross-functional panel evaluated ten platforms (open-source, proprietary, hyperscaler) across nine capability dimensions on three financial-services workloads (counterparty credit risk, RAG, process automation), followed by statistical reliability analysis.
AI.result: Scores separated platforms into three stable tiers and revealed workload-specific strengths, but Cronbach's alpha was 0.98 across nominally distinct dimensions with >= 0.93 rank correlation for eight of nine dimensions, indicating a strong presentation halo effect.
AI.conclusion: To move from structured judgement to measurement, the authors propose a four-layer gate-then-score protocol (capability, execution reliability, governance gates, business value) with repeated-run trace reliability metrics.

title: SoU-RHS: Bayesian Structured Sparsity for Compact Architecture Recovery in CNNs
summary: Highly parameterized convolutional neural networks often achieve strong predictive performance, but their memory, computation, and deployment costs motivate the search for methods that recover compact architectures from large reference models. We propose SoU-RHS, a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure that augments Regularized Horseshoe Shrinkage (RHS) with the so-called Sources of Uncertainty Sparse Global-Local mechanism (SoU-SGL). The resulting model sharpens the separation between active and inactive filters, providing an effective mechanism for architecture recovery. A key property of SoU-RHS is stability: across different overparameterized starting widths and under a reasonable range of pruning thresholds, it recovers compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation. This supports the interpretation that the procedure is identifying a compact structure adapted to the data, rather than merely compressing each initial model separately. Across standard image-classification benchmarks, SoU-RHS recovers substantially smaller architectures than deterministic structured-sparsity baselines, while maintaining competitive accuracy, achieving lower negative log-likelihood in every evaluated configuration and generally lower expected calibration error.

AI.tldr: SoU-RHS is a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure that recovers compact, stable CNN architectures across different starting widths and pruning thresholds.
AI.motivation: Recovering compact architectures from overparameterized CNNs is desirable for deployment, but deterministic pruning methods often yield unstable architectures sensitive to initialization width and thresholds.
AI.method: SoU-RHS augments Regularized Horseshoe Shrinkage (RHS) with the Sources of Uncertainty Sparse Global-Local (SoU-SGL) mechanism to sharpen separation between active and inactive filters.
AI.result: Across standard image-classification benchmarks, SoU-RHS recovers substantially smaller architectures than deterministic structured-sparsity baselines with competitive accuracy, lower negative log-likelihood in every configuration, and generally lower expected calibration error, while maintaining consistent total size and layer-wise allocation across widths and thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian global-local shrinkage identifies compact CNN structures adapted to the data rather than merely compressing individual initial models.

title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond
comment: 25 pages, 1 figure
summary: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate.
