Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes minimax optimal rates for sieve-based functional principal component analysis (FPCA) across the full spectrum from sparse to dense discrete observation designs.
AI.motivation: The minimax theory of FPCA for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observations has remained open for over two decades.
AI.method: Using a sieve-based FPCA framework over general bivariate function classes, the authors separate spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations to derive minimax rates for covariance estimation, individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices, and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimension.
AI.result: The optimal rates reveal two mechanisms—spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction—producing four or two sampling regimes from sparse to dense designs; applied to functional linear regression, the FPCA-based estimator attains minimax-optimal rates.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a precise characterization of discrete sampling effects in FPCA and offers a general tool for nonparametric spectral estimation.

title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
summary: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

AI.tldr: FedE2E is a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving that achieves strong closed-loop performance on Bench2Drive.
AI.motivation: Existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods focus mainly on perception.
AI.method: FedE2E combines multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous client models in a single round.
AI.result: On closed-loop Bench2Drive evaluation, FedE2E achieves a Driving Score of 55.85 in the one-shot setting (4.07 points above prior work) and reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, outperforming all compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining calibration, anchor alignment, and token-wise distillation enables effective one-shot and multi-round federated learning for end-to-end autonomous driving.

title: TRESS: A Fixed-Size History Representation for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
summary: A fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another. Earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable. We propose TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries), a forecasting model that retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows. Its query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon. A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods compared on all four benchmarks. Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12--2.60 across the four datasets. The code is at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TRESS is a fixed-size history representation for irregular time series forecasting that combines timestamped recent observations with full-history statistical summaries.
AI.motivation: Fixed-count recent observation windows span vastly different durations across variables, while older measurements remain needed to judge whether the latest value is unusual.
AI.method: TRESS retains 8 to 16 recent observations per variable at their original timestamps, uses a query-conditioned event lifting module to weight deviations by observation age and forecast horizon, and fuses these with historical statistics and a cross-variable summary in a channel-specific decoder.
AI.result: On four benchmarks, TRESS achieves the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among compared methods, and serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by 2.12x to 2.60x.
AI.conclusion: Combining a bounded recent event buffer with full-history statistics yields accurate, constant-size, and fast-serving irregular time series forecasting.

title: VAFL: A Vertical Analytic Federated Learning Mechanism for Efficient Crowdsourced Services via Closed-Form Solutions
summary: Intelligent services often rely on complementary information held by different organizations, motivating Vertical Federated Learning without centralized raw-data pooling. We propose VAFL, a Vertical Analytic Federated Learning framework that fits classification and regression heads on fixed local representations through regularized least squares. An agent-assisted protected-computation workflow supports two-party and multi-party collaboration. To reduce fitting overhead, we develop a full-dimensional equivalent solve that applies block factors directly to the target matrix, avoiding construction of the full inverse. We further study two width-reduction strategies: local spectral projection with coefficient lifting, and full-dimensional local fitting with low-rank cross-party correction. The first compresses the prediction space, whereas the second retains local components outside the collaboration subspace. We establish their algebraic properties and analyze their computational scope. Experiments on five benchmarks show the accuracy--cost tradeoffs of these strategies and compatibility with diverse frozen backbones. Predictive performance and training time identify useful operating points and the limits of compression.

AI.tldr: VAFL is a Vertical Analytic Federated Learning mechanism that fits closed-form regularized least squares heads on fixed local representations with agent-assisted protected computation.
AI.motivation: Vertical Federated Learning allows organizations with complementary features to collaborate without pooling raw data, but iterative training can incur high communication and fitting overhead.
AI.method: VAFL solves regularized least squares via a full-dimensional equivalent solve applying block factors directly to the target matrix, and explores two width-reduction strategies: local spectral projection with coefficient lifting, and full-dimensional local fitting with low-rank cross-party correction.
AI.result: Experiments on five benchmarks characterize the accuracy-cost tradeoffs of both compression strategies and demonstrate compatibility with diverse frozen backbones.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form analytic solving with structured width reduction provides an efficient, flexible mechanism for multi-party Vertical Federated Learning.

title: Latent Action Policies from Suboptimal Data
summary: Latent Action Models (LAMs) learn control representations from action-free video, but existing pipelines typically train latent policies with behavioral cloning, without an explicit policy improvement objective. Although offline RL offers a natural approach to policy improvement, standard methods do not transfer directly to learned latent action spaces. We find that the structure of learned latent actions makes naive offline RL unreliable: directly maximizing value over latent actions or fitting a unimodal policy can produce latent actions that cannot be realized by physical execution, while the latent representation can merge physical controls that receive different rewards. To understand when latent-space optimization remains valid, we derive conditions under which policy improvement transfers to decoded execution and under which latent and physical optima align. Building on these insights, we propose LAPIS for goal-conditioned latent policy improvement, grounding value-based policy improvement in observed state-latent transitions and using a conditional flow policy to capture their multimodal structure. LAPIS outperforms baselines on most tasks, with the clearest gains in visual manipulation, and remains effective even with only 1% action labels, where competing methods largely collapse.

AI.tldr: LAPIS enables goal-conditioned offline RL over learned latent action spaces by grounding value improvement in observed state-latent transitions and using a conditional flow policy.
AI.motivation: Standard offline RL fails when applied naively to Latent Action Models (LAMs) because maximizing value over latent actions can produce physically unrealizable actions, and latent spaces can merge controls with different rewards.
AI.method: The authors derive conditions for latent-to-physical policy improvement transfer and propose LAPIS, which grounds value-based policy improvement in observed state-latent transitions and models multimodal action distributions with a conditional flow policy.
AI.result: LAPIS outperforms baselines on most tasks, with the largest gains in visual manipulation, and remains effective with only 1% action labels where competing methods collapse.
AI.conclusion: Grounding value optimization in observed transitions and capturing multimodality with flow policies makes offline RL viable in learned latent action spaces.

title: The geometry of neural network decision boundaries
summary: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are built using well-understood mathematical operations, yet their complex nature poses significant challenges to intuitively understanding their decision-making processes. This work introduces a method for visualizing and measuring ANN decision boundary geometry directly in the high-dimensional input space, avoiding distortions found with traditional projection-based techniques. We analyze boundary curvatures and distances in diverse inputs, architectures, and training methods. Boundary distances grow smoothly and slowly with consistent curvature as the size of the subspace increases, suggesting that decision boundaries are close to input samples within large, continuous subspaces. We also quantify how much boundary distances and curvatures reduce near dataset samples after adversarial training. Training methodology has a significantly stronger impact on boundary distance and curvature than architecture or test-set accuracy. These findings are contextualized within prior work, supporting or refuting several previously proposed theories of boundary behavior. Our analytically and empirically supported methodology lays the foundation for future studies to improve network interpretability and understanding.

AI.tldr: Direct high-dimensional measurement of neural network decision boundaries reveals that training methodology shapes boundary distance and curvature far more than architecture or test accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional projection-based visualizations distort high-dimensional neural network decision boundaries, hindering accurate understanding of network geometry.
AI.method: The authors introduce a method to visualize and measure decision boundary curvatures and distances directly in high-dimensional input space across diverse inputs, architectures, and training methods.
AI.result: Boundary distances grow smoothly and slowly with consistent curvature as subspace size increases, adversarial training strongly reduces boundary distance and curvature near samples, and training methodology has a much stronger impact on geometry than architecture or test accuracy.
AI.conclusion: High-dimensional geometric measurement resolves distortions of projection methods and clarifies how training regimes govern decision boundary structure.

title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
summary: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.

AI.tldr: Adding the difference between alternative and factual world-model predictions to the observed outcome turns factual JEPA world models into zero-shot counterfactual predictors with O(h^2) error bounds.
AI.motivation: World models trained on factual transitions cannot by themselves answer counterfactual "what if" questions under hidden disturbances.
AI.method: Exploiting smooth dynamics where actions and disturbances interact at second order in time, the authors add the world model's predicted action-difference to the observed factual outcome, requiring no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining, and prove O(h^2) error bounds and a matching minimax lower bound.
AI.result: Tested with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and MAE encoders across four rendered simulators, counterfactual R^2 rises from 38-46% to 86-96% (and 90-94% on an underwater vehicle, matching 16x more factual data); four other frozen encoders give 81-95%, and hindsight planning reaches goals in 35-69% of events versus 14-23% for an oracle planner.
AI.conclusion: First-order outcome-anchored differencing unlocks accurate counterfactual reasoning and hindsight planning from existing factual world models.

title: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators
summary: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a general framework and Python package for equivariant modeling using minimal homogeneous generators of invariant and covariant polynomial features.
AI.motivation: Equivariant models between finite-dimensional semisimple real group representations have been developed separately across domains without a unified algebraic construction and automated software pipeline.
AI.method: The model expresses equivariant maps as linear combinations of minimal homogeneous covariant polynomial generators with coefficients given by learnable functions of minimal invariant polynomial generators, computed via explicit isotypic and Clebsch-Gordan decompositions.
AI.result: The feature computation algorithm achieves speedups over alternative computational algebra methods, and scientific modeling experiments yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters both end-to-end and within larger architectures.
AI.conclusion: Minimal homogeneous polynomial generators provide a unified, computationally efficient foundation for equivariant machine learning.

title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Under review at the EACL 2027 Industry Track
summary: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.

AI.tldr: Auditing a deployed human-in-the-loop CV priority sorter uncovered three measurement and UX pitfalls—length-based synthetic shortcuts, threshold-induced agreement drops, and counterproductive uncertainty sampling—and led to concrete product fixes.
AI.motivation: A deployed CV sorter using a frozen multilingual transformer and per-session linear model claimed 95% recall in half the reading pile on synthetic CVs, warranting a rigorous audit of its evaluation and active learning behavior.
AI.method: The authors audited the synthetic pool, the four-level agreement score, uncertainty-sampling next-CV suggestions, and cold-start embedding alternatives.
AI.result: The synthetic pool was sortable by length alone (though reading-depth gains held under a shared length budget); fixed-threshold agreement scores fell as labels accumulated; uncertainty sampling increased total reading load above the no-label baseline; and a hosted LLM embedding (or local cross-encoder) lifted zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80.
AI.conclusion: Auditing deployed human-in-the-loop ranking tools is essential to catch synthetic shortcuts, miscalibrated confidence displays, and active-learning strategies that increase user workload.

title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
summary: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

AI.tldr: Chorus shares a single set of n-gram embedding tables across all transformer layers with per-layer hidden-state rescaling and projection, matching prior methods with 87% smaller tables.
AI.motivation: Per-layer n-gram embedding tables in language models are memory-intensive and prevent cross-layer knowledge sharing, while naive table sharing degrades performance by forcing identical embeddings at every layer.
AI.method: Chorus maintains one shared set of n-gram embedding tables and lets each layer rescale the retrieved embedding using its current hidden state before applying a layer-specific projection.
AI.result: Across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters, Chorus outperforms Engram, TN-gram, and FactorEngram in every setting, achieving better text prediction at 1.2B table parameters than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram at 9.6B (87% smaller), and pairs with the Ember optimizer to save 99.2% of table-optimizer memory vs. AdamW.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise adaptation of shared n-gram tables enables memory-efficient scaling of n-gram capacity in language models.

title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
comment: Accepted to SoCalNLP 2026. 15 pages, 11 figures
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at this https URL

AI.tldr: Mechanistic interpretability of LLM reasoning traces in iterated games with incomplete information shows that models revise internal game beliefs across chain-of-thought steps and rarely recover from premature incorrect commitments.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread use of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in LLM agents, the relationship between externalized reasoning traces and internal computation during strategic decision-making is poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors apply mechanistic interpretability techniques to analyze how LLM agents form and update internal representations of iterated games with incomplete information throughout CoT traces, and release an interactive trace visualizer.
AI.result: Models iteratively form and revise internal game beliefs across the CoT, but once they prematurely commit to an incorrect belief, they rarely recover, with the failure visible in both literal traces and layer activations.
AI.conclusion: Tracking internal belief commitments across CoT traces enables targeted diagnosis of strategic reasoning errors in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Formal Adequacy Index (based on Polish-language material)
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 1 table
summary: Linguistic formality is one of the dimensions of stylistic variation in speech; however, simply measuring its level does not allow us to determine whether the chosen mode of communication is appropriate in a given situation. The aim of this article is to present the concept of a formal adequacy index (based on Polish-language material), which enables a quantitative assessment of how well the formality of a text matches the expectations arising from the communicative context. The proposed approach is based on the separate modelling of observed formality, determined on the basis of the linguistic features of the text, and expected formality, determined on the basis of the characteristics of the communicative situation. Adequacy is assessed by comparing these two measures, taking into account contextual tolerance thresholds, which may differ for a lack of formality and an excess of formality. The potential applications of the index are illustrated by an analysis of Polish-language emails containing apologies for being late, written by human language users or generated by a large language model. The implementation presented here is preliminary in nature and requires further calibration and empirical validation. The main contribution of this article is the proposal of a general methodological framework for the quantitative study of formal adequacy in various communicative contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a formal adequacy index to quantitatively assess how well a text's formality matches the expectations of its communicative context, illustrated on Polish-language apology emails.
AI.motivation: Simply measuring linguistic formality does not reveal whether the chosen level of formality is appropriate for a given communicative situation.
AI.method: The framework separately models observed formality from linguistic features of the text and expected formality from characteristics of the communicative situation, then compares them using contextual tolerance thresholds that may differ for insufficient versus excessive formality.
AI.result: The authors illustrate potential applications by analyzing Polish-language late-apology emails written by humans or generated by a large language model, noting that the current implementation is preliminary and requires further calibration and empirical validation.
AI.conclusion: The main contribution is a general methodological framework for quantitatively studying formal adequacy across diverse communicative contexts.

title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
comment: Published in Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves $.57$ micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a transformer-based time series model that forecasts the next proceeding outcome in criminal court cases, achieving 0.57 micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task.
AI.motivation: Prior machine learning approaches for criminal justice have focused on modeling single decisions such as recidivism, leaving the multi-step sequence of court proceedings underexplored for oversight and transparency.
AI.method: The authors model each court case as an event sequence and train transformer and GRU models on a newly constructed dataset from public court records of a mid-sized U.S. city, combining clerk note text with structured defendant, prior-charge, and courtroom features.
AI.result: On thousands of cases in a 20-class multi-label forecasting task, the transformer model achieves 0.57 micro-F1, significantly outperforming several baselines and matching a GRU trained on the same inputs.
AI.conclusion: Modeling court cases as event sequences can provide insights into judicial decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within a jurisdiction.

title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
comment: Published in EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 37 pages. Code and data: this https URL. Anthology: this https URL
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how factual prevalence affects LLM hallucinations in academic authorship attribution across 1.92 million papers, finding a strong inverse relationship between citation count and hallucination rate.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs frequently hallucinate in question answering, the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored.
AI.method: Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, the authors curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines stratified by citation level, evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs, and perform hidden-state probing on open-source models.
AI.result: Across all three models and eight disciplines, hallucination rates exceed 98% for rarely cited papers and fall below 37% for highly cited papers, while probing shows factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations and failures stem mainly from retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence.
AI.conclusion: The study provides convergent behavioral and mechanistic evidence that factual prevalence strongly governs LLM hallucinations via retrieval limitations.

title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. To examine this assumption, we introduce LUCID, a benchmark that evaluates whether models can infer latent market structures from event descriptions and historical financial observations. Models generate event-induced causal graphs representing inferred market structure and are evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework. Our evaluation of 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs shows that adding their generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, although a few metrics improve. These findings suggest that inferring informative, event-specific market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for the evaluated LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LUCID, a benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can infer latent causal market structures from financial events and historical observations, and finds that LLM-generated graphs generally degrade reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: LLMs are often evaluated on predictive accuracy under the implicit assumption that it reflects understanding of underlying mechanisms, even though accurate predictions can occur without recovering latent causal structures.
AI.method: In LUCID, models generate event-induced causal graphs from event descriptions and historical financial observations, which are then evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework across 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs.
AI.result: Adding the LLM-generated causal graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, though a few metrics improve.
AI.conclusion: Inferring informative, event-specific latent market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for current LLMs.

title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
summary: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that frontier LLMs routinely make unstudied research questions sound partly studied in ordinary answers, and proposes a two-step verification fix that raises clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95% on GPT-6-Astra.
AI.motivation: Researchers use LLMs to validate research questions, but models often overstate what related papers establish and obscure whether a question is genuinely unstudied.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 22 models including six frontier systems on 40 questions from newly accepted papers, then construct a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate full-text checks of cited papers, and also predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining multiple models' written ratings with a learned rule.
AI.result: On the 40 unstudied questions, GPT-6-Astra judges 98% to be unstudied when asked separately but states this plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers (with 30-90 percentage point reporting gaps across all six frontier systems); the verification fix raises Astra's clear reporting to 95% and improves all six systems, while novelty-grade prediction matches Think-Probe-Respond without needing weights or activations.
AI.conclusion: Separating full-text verification from answer generation corrects asymmetric reporting failures and enables weight-free novelty prediction for closed-weight frontier models.

title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
summary: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FutureBench, a renewable benchmark of 3,629 timestamped questions for evaluating knowledge-context conflict in LLMs, and shows that an Adversarial-Aware prompt restores 82.5-98.9% of answers displaced by verification prompts.
AI.motivation: Asking an LLM to check retrieved text can inadvertently bias which source it trusts when parametric knowledge conflicts with retrieved context.
AI.method: FutureBench uses timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes across 3,629 questions and six models, comparing Baseline, Verify (checking plus passage priority), and Adversarial-Aware (warning of misleading passages and prioritizing model knowledge) prompts.
AI.result: On pre-cutoff events, Verify increases false-answer adoption in all five tested models by displacing previously correct Baseline answers; on 902 post-cutoff questions, passage priority without checking raises adoption while Verify lowers it in all five models, and Adversarial-Aware restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point change in true-passage accuracy.
AI.conclusion: FutureBench provides a repeatable evaluation framework for knowledge-context conflict that can extend to new events as models evolve.

title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
comment: Accepted at the Trustworthy AI for Good (AI4GOOD) Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper extends RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, PII formats, and Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia transcripts, finding that LLM-based anonymizers achieve the best privacy-utility trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Text anonymizers used in public-sector and workplace LLM workflows may not transfer reliably to new linguistic, identifier, and cultural contexts.
AI.method: The authors extend RAT-Bench to Malaysian microdata, local PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, evaluating NER- and LLM-based anonymizers against an LLM attribute-inference attacker for re-identification risk and utility.
AI.result: Across both languages, the two LLM anonymizers reduce Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94, whereas non-LLM tools either leave high residual risk or severely over-redact, especially in Bahasa Malaysia.
AI.conclusion: Text anonymizers must be evaluated on deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in local AI pipelines.

title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LED, a post-training framework that adds insertion and deletion to diffusion language models via Levenshtein editing, improving average benchmark scores on LLaDA2.1-Mini Base from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing replacement-only editing in diffusion language models cannot efficiently handle sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens or widespread multi-position errors.
AI.method: LED reconstructs insertion and deletion supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning via longest-common-subsequence alignment and uses multi-stage training where each stage's output state becomes the next stage's input.
AI.result: Applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base across twelve benchmarks, LED raises the average score from 54.86 to 57.10 (and tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05) under confidence-guided decoding, from 27.52 to 47.19 under confidence-free decoding, and from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128, while also improving pass@k at large k.
AI.conclusion: Extending diffusion language models with Levenshtein-style insertion and deletion enables more robust self-correction and greater generation diversity.

title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
comment: 29 pages, 6 figures, 33 tables
summary: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that draft models in speculative decoding can use half or a quarter of the target model's hidden width while preserving acceptance, yielding up to 1.44x end-to-end speedup.
AI.motivation: Draft models that read target hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's full hidden width, which adds unnecessary computation.
AI.method: The authors narrow the draft model's entire residual stream to half or a quarter of the target width and, for DFlash, fold the trained output adapter into the target's vocabulary projection so logits remain unchanged up to floating-point rounding; they test DFlash and EAGLE-3 on Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4) in SGLang on B200 and DGX Spark (GB10) GPUs.
AI.result: At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft yields 1.06-1.12x end-to-end speedup on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10, and at larger batches from 32 up to maximum GPU capacity it reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs with no narrow draft slower than full width.
AI.conclusion: Matching the target's hidden width is unnecessary for speculative draft models, making narrower residual streams a simple and effective way to accelerate decoding.

title: Coverage Governs Accuracy: When to Expand the Lexicon and When to Fall Back in Low-Resource Manchu OCR
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables
summary: Character-level OCR for low-resource Manchu often produces near-miss spelling errors. Lexicon-constrained decoding can correct such errors with lexical knowledge, but a fixed dictionary cannot cover the many unseen word forms produced by agglutinative word formation. We study whether morphological expansion alleviates this limitation, and how the expansion size and confidence fallback affect recognition. We segment the training transcriptions with a dictionary-based stem list, extract roots and suffix chains from them, generate about 510k candidates, select the expansion size through frequency ranking on the validation set, and decompose accuracy under hard lexicon constraints into the product of coverage and in-lexicon precision. Across three CRNN training seeds, adding 250k candidates to a base dictionary of about 29k words raises the type accuracy on unseen combinations of seen roots from 63.6% to 86.3%, and overall token accuracy from 82.4% to 84.2%. Adding all candidates lowers overall token accuracy to 81.5%, showing that the coverage gain comes with a loss of in-lexicon precision. A further comparison shows that the base dictionary with confidence fallback performs best overall among the CRNN systems tested, reaching 76.1% type and 85.5% token accuracy and outperforming the expanded lexicon both with and without fallback. A Transformer recognizer shows similar trends. These results indicate that morphological expansion relieves the constraint of a fixed dictionary, but a larger lexicon does not guarantee better recognition; in the present low-resource Manchu OCR setting, a selective combination of reliable lexical constraints and open recognition is more effective.

AI.tldr: This paper studies morphological lexicon expansion and confidence fallback for low-resource Manchu OCR, finding that a base dictionary with confidence fallback outperforms expanded lexicons.
AI.motivation: Fixed-dictionary lexicon-constrained decoding in low-resource Manchu OCR cannot cover unseen agglutinative word forms, whereas expanding the lexicon may hurt precision.
AI.method: The authors segment training transcriptions with a stem list to extract roots and suffix chains, generate about 510k candidate words, select expansion sizes via validation frequency ranking, and decompose accuracy into coverage times in-lexicon precision across three CRNN seeds and a Transformer recognizer.
AI.result: Adding 250k candidates to a 29k-word base dictionary raises unseen-combination type accuracy from 63.6% to 86.3% and overall token accuracy from 82.4% to 84.2%, but adding all 510k drops token accuracy to 81.5%; overall, the base dictionary with confidence fallback performs best at 76.1% type and 85.5% token accuracy, with similar trends on the Transformer.
AI.conclusion: In low-resource Manchu OCR, combining a reliable base lexicon with confidence-based open-recognition fallback is more effective than large-scale morphological lexicon expansion.

title: ReflectRec: Cycle-Consistency Preference Verification for LLM-based Recommendation
comment: 15 pages. Published in the Proceedings of EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference)
summary: CoT-style LLM recommenders generate a natural-language preference note as a chain-of-thought prefix to ranking, but the note is trusted without verification, and the ranker never consults behaviorally similar users. We propose ReflectRec, organized around a preference-to-history round-trip verifier whose recall score serves as an operational signal of preference-to-history recoverability, enabling conditional regeneration for low-recoverability preferences and selection among regeneration attempts. Around this verifier, we wire a semantic Stage-1 prompt, conditional regeneration, and Forward-Look retrieval that injects future watches of behaviorally similar users as a collaborative hint. On MovieLens-100K and MovieLens-1M, the full pipeline outperforms CoT4Rec-ICL by +16.25 / +4.46 pp Hit@10, with positive gains across all ValScore buckets and three LLM backbones (Qwen3-30B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Llama-3.3-70B). We also observe a similar verifier-guided regeneration pattern on Amazon Electronics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReflectRec, a cycle-consistency preference verification and collaborative retrieval framework for LLM-based recommendation that outperforms CoT4Rec-ICL by +16.25 pp Hit@10 on MovieLens-100K and +4.46 pp on MovieLens-1M.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought LLM recommenders trust generated natural-language preference notes without verifying whether they faithfully recover user history and do not consult behaviorally similar users.
AI.method: ReflectRec pairs a semantic Stage-1 prompt with a preference-to-history round-trip verifier whose recall score triggers conditional regeneration and selection among attempts, alongside Forward-Look retrieval that injects future watches of behaviorally similar users as collaborative hints.
AI.result: On MovieLens-100K and MovieLens-1M across Qwen3-30B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Llama-3.3-70B, ReflectRec outperforms CoT4Rec-ICL by +16.25 and +4.46 percentage points in Hit@10 with gains across all ValScore buckets, and shows a similar verifier-guided regeneration pattern on Amazon Electronics.
AI.conclusion: Verifying preference-to-history recoverability and incorporating collaborative future-watch hints substantially improves LLM-based recommendation.

title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures
summary: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributions affect key token choices involving response structure, content selection, and factual values. We further show that role-consistent choices depend on sufficient role span support at these key decisions, while failing choices can be reversed when this support overcomes the deficit. These findings support a common mechanistic view of ICL and OOC hallucination: each functional role defines the pattern of output decisions over which role span contributions must remain effective, and differences in this organization account for the seemingly opposing outcomes.

AI.tldr: This paper unifies in-context learning (ICL) and out-of-context (OOC) hallucination through a mechanistic analysis of functional roles in dynamic context.
AI.motivation: Prior work has studied ICL and OOC hallucination separately, obscuring the shared mechanistic basis behind whether an LLM follows or violates provided context.
AI.method: The authors model functional roles in dynamic context, derive a first-order decomposition of the role effect, and perform causal analyses of role span contributions at key token decisions involving response structure, content selection, and factual values.
AI.result: They show that role information can be internally represented without constraining output, and that substantial role influence requires both sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation; failing choices can be reversed when role span support overcomes the deficit.
AI.conclusion: ICL and OOC hallucination share a common mechanism in which each functional role defines the output decision pattern over which role span contributions must remain effective.

title: Compression Effects on Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
comment: `Pilot study. 3 model families x 3 precisions x 6 directions on FLORES-200. Code and raw results: this https URL`
summary: We present a pilot study characterising the effect of post-training quantisation on multilingual machine translation quality and inference cost for three African languages - Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba - across three model families: a small general-purpose LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B), a larger multilingual instruction-tuned LLM (Aya-23-8B), and a dedicated multilingual MT model (NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B). Evaluating on the FLORES-200 devtest set (1,012 sentences per direction) under FP16, bitsandbytes INT8, and NF4 INT4 precisions on consumer-grade NVIDIA T4 GPUs, we find: (i) the specialised MT model outperforms both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on the Hausa and Swahili directions, and by 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba, despite being roughly a sixth the size of the 8B instruction-tuned LLM; (ii) post-training quantisation preserves aggregate translation quality within approximately 1 chrF across all model families and language directions, with a single worst case of 2.19 chrF; (iii) on consumer GPUs, INT8 and INT4 quantisation provide substantial memory savings (49-61% at INT4) but do not reduce inference latency relative to FP16 - in fact, latency increases by 1.3x to 5.3x; (iv) a clear performance gradient tracking training-resource availability is visible across languages (Swahili > Hausa > Yoruba). These findings motivate a research agenda focused on hardware-aware compression and error-type analysis beyond aggregate metrics for low-resource deployment.

AI.tldr: This pilot study evaluates post-training quantization on Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba translation, finding that INT8 and INT4 preserve quality within ~1 chrF and cut memory by 49-61% at INT4 but increase inference latency by 1.3x to 5.3x on consumer T4 GPUs.
AI.motivation: The trade-offs between translation quality, memory savings, and inference latency under post-training quantization remain poorly characterized for low-resource African languages on consumer hardware.
AI.method: The authors evaluate Qwen2.5-1.5B, Aya-23-8B, and NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B on the FLORES-200 devtest set (1,012 sentences per direction) for Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba under FP16, bitsandbytes INT8, and NF4 INT4 on NVIDIA T4 GPUs.
AI.result: NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B outperforms both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on Hausa and Swahili and 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba; quantization preserves quality within ~1 chrF (worst case 2.19 chrF) and saves 49-61% memory at INT4, but increases latency by 1.3x to 5.3x relative to FP16, with performance following resource availability (Swahili > Hausa > Yoruba).
AI.conclusion: Low-resource deployment requires hardware-aware compression and finer-grained error analysis beyond aggregate quality metrics.

title: A Hybrid RAG Framework for Deceptive Review Detection: Integrating RoBERTa-LoRA, FAISS-Based Retrieval, and LLM Reasoning
summary: The growth of deceptive online opinions poses a critical risk of misinformation and fraud. This paper proposes a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system to automatically distinguish spam reviews. The architecture integrates RoBERTa with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) classification, FAISS semantic vector retrieval, and a Large Language Model (LLM) for final reasoning. The system was evaluated across balanced and severely imbalanced real-world scenarios. Results demonstrate that five epochs of fine-tuning enable robust domain transfer, achieving an F1-score of 0.90 in cross-domain evaluation, outperforming baselines (OpenAI Detector,F1 = 0.82) and demonstrating competitive performance against specialized in-domain SOTA models (fakeRoBERTa,F1 = 0.97). The proposed architecture provides evidence-backed explainability and statistically significant precision gains while maintaining comparable overall detection performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid RAG framework combining RoBERTa-LoRA classification, FAISS semantic retrieval, and LLM reasoning for deceptive review detection, achieving 0.90 F1 in cross-domain evaluation.
AI.motivation: Automated detection of deceptive online reviews requires both strong cross-domain generalization and evidence-backed explainability under balanced and severely imbalanced scenarios.
AI.method: The system integrates a RoBERTa classifier fine-tuned with LoRA, FAISS-based semantic vector retrieval, and an LLM for final reasoning.
AI.result: Evaluated across balanced and severely imbalanced scenarios, five epochs of fine-tuning yield a cross-domain F1-score of 0.90, outperforming OpenAI Detector (0.82 F1) while remaining competitive with in-domain SOTA fakeRoBERTa (0.97 F1) and providing statistically significant precision gains and explainability.
AI.conclusion: Combining LoRA-adapted encoders, vector retrieval, and LLM reasoning offers an explainable and transferable approach to spam review detection.

title: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status
comment: 51 pages, 2 figures (plus 1 in the appendix). Submitted to Artificial Intelligence and Law. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Laws are increasingly turned into programs that decide cases, such as whether a firm was a small or medium enterprise (SME) on a given date, and large language models (LLMs) now write them. The programs are usually graded against answers written by someone who read the same law, so a program can score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than by getting the law right. LexTemporis grades them instead against records of what actually happened: 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Korean listed companies, with every version of the governing rules. An appendix adds comparison cases from US income tax and German hospital minimum volumes. The date changes outcomes mainly through provisions outside the main statutory text: one transitional provision raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%. The disclosures also test the author's reading of a contested provision, favouring it in 130 of 189 firm-years where readings diverge. Four LLMs wrote the rules, given different selections of the law. A pre-registered comparison finds no condition better across all four models. In exploratory analyses, supplying the right provisions looks better graded against the author's reading than against the records: the advantage shrinks for three models (for one, to between a quarter and three-fifths of its size), and per firm-year it is several times larger where the author's reading is wrong, partly by construction, since there reproducing that reading more faithfully must lose. Grading legal programs against the grader's own reading can overstate how well they work.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LexTemporis, a benchmark of 10,901 Korean firm-year SME status disclosures, showing that grading LLM-written legal programs against a human reader's interpretation can overstate accuracy compared to independent real-world records.
AI.motivation: Executable legal rules written by LLMs are typically graded against answers from someone who read the same statute, allowing programs to score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than getting the law right.
AI.method: LexTemporis grades legal programs against 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Korean listed companies alongside all versions of the governing rules, evaluating four LLMs given different statutory selections (with US tax and German hospital volume comparisons in an appendix).
AI.result: Transitional provisions outside the main text raise agreement with disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%, disclosures favor the author's reading in 130 of 189 contested firm-years, and supplying the right provisions looks better when graded against the author's reading than against actual records, shrinking for three models (to one-quarter to three-fifths of its size for one model).
AI.conclusion: Grading executable legal rules against independent empirical records rather than a grader's statutory reading avoids overstating model performance.

title: MIRAGE: A Framework for Multi-hop Reasoning under Dynamic Knowledge Injection
comment: Submitted to COLING 2027. 15 pages, 5 figures
summary: Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and synthesize multiple pieces of evidence into a coherent reasoning path, which is essential for complex tasks. However, prior work on knowledge updating for MQA has largely focused on simple fact edits, overlooking a more challenging and realistic setting---\emph{Knowledge Injection}---in which the model must simultaneously accommodate both conflicting updates and entirely novel information. Under this setting, a hop-level answer is often wrong simply because the model trusts the wrong knowledge source: it clings to outdated parametric memory when the injected knowledge conflicts with it (K2), and it cannot answer when the required fact is entirely new (K3). To investigate this, we introduce NEXUS, the first benchmark tailored for multi-hop reasoning under Knowledge Injection, which explicitly covers both conflicting (K2) and incremental (K3) knowledge. We further propose MIRAGE, an efficient, training-free framework whose core component, the Correlation-aware Dual-path Reasoner (CDR), resolves such per-hop source-trust errors via P(True)-based confidence routing, complemented by a lightweight template-guided corrector for residual structural deviations. Extensive experiments across four LLM families and two benchmarks demonstrate that MIRAGE consistently improves both final-answer accuracy and hop-level reasoning accuracy, establishing a new state of the art in this challenging setting.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the NEXUS benchmark and MIRAGE, a training-free framework for multi-hop reasoning under dynamic knowledge injection that improves both final-answer and hop-level accuracy across four LLM families.
AI.motivation: Prior knowledge-updating work for multi-hop QA focuses on simple fact edits and overlooks realistic Knowledge Injection, where models must handle both conflicting updates (K2) and entirely new facts (K3) without trusting the wrong source at each hop.
AI.method: The authors build NEXUS to cover both K2 and K3 knowledge and propose MIRAGE, which uses a Correlation-aware Dual-path Reasoner (CDR) with P(True)-based confidence routing and a lightweight template-guided corrector for structural deviations.
AI.result: Across four LLM families and two benchmarks, MIRAGE consistently improves both final-answer accuracy and hop-level reasoning accuracy, establishing a new state of the art.
AI.conclusion: Per-hop confidence routing between parametric and injected knowledge enables effective, training-free multi-hop reasoning under dynamic knowledge injection.

title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This large-scale study analyzes 62,873 LLM-generated children's bedtime stories across 16 models and 35 country settings, finding systematic gender stereotyping where son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion than daughter-directed stories.
AI.motivation: Because bedtime stories shape children's social role perceptions, it is important to understand whether LLMs alter narrative portrayals based on the intended child's gender.
AI.method: Using matched daughter/son prompts across 16 LLMs, 35 country settings, and 12 narrator roles, the authors analyze 62,873 stories via context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level probing.
AI.result: Son-directed stories consistently emphasize higher agency and lower communion than daughter-directed stories, with high sociability showing pronounced narrator-recipient interactions; human evaluations agree with these patterns, and hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information.
AI.conclusion: Persistent, context-dependent gender disparities exist in LLM-generated children's stories, motivating narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

title: CounselTraj: Synthesizing Process-Aware Psychological Counseling Dialogues via Dialogue-Act Trajectory Planning
comment: Accepted to EACL 2027 Main Conference
summary: The growing demand for psychological counseling has motivated the development of LLM-based systems that support human counselors, but training such systems requires large-scale, high-quality dialogue data. Authentic counseling transcripts are difficult to collect and share because of privacy concerns, making synthetic dialogues an important alternative. However, existing synthetic datasets, despite covering diverse scenarios and client profiles, often consist of brief exchanges and fail to capture session-level counseling processes. We propose CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for expanding brief synthetic dialogues into process-aware, session-level psychological counseling dialogues. CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from role-play counseling dialogues produced by human counselors, plans coordinated trajectories for clients and counselors, and uses them as flexible guidance for long-form dialogue generation. Experiments across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets show that CounselTraj produces more complete and coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than both direct expansion and expansion with randomly sampled trajectories. Based on CounselTraj, we construct CounselTrajD, a dataset containing over 10K process-guided Chinese psychological counseling dialogues, and use it to train CounselTrajLM for counseling response generation. Evaluations at both the response and session levels show that CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models in response quality, therapeutic understanding and intervention, and counseling-process coherence and progress. Our code and model are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CounselTraj, a dialogue-act trajectory planning framework for synthesizing process-aware psychological counseling dialogues, and uses it to build the 10K-dialogue CounselTrajD dataset and CounselTrajLM model.
AI.motivation: Existing synthetic counseling datasets consist mostly of brief exchanges and fail to capture long-form, session-level therapeutic processes, while authentic transcripts are scarce due to privacy concerns.
AI.method: CounselTraj learns dialogue-act patterns from human-counselor role-play dialogues, plans coordinated client-counselor trajectories as flexible generation guidance, and uses them to create CounselTrajD (>10K Chinese dialogues) to train CounselTrajLM.
AI.result: Across three Chinese synthetic counseling datasets, CounselTraj produces more complete, coherent sessions with higher-quality counselor interventions than direct or random-trajectory expansion, and CounselTrajLM outperforms publicly available Chinese counseling models at both response and session levels.
AI.conclusion: Explicit dialogue-act trajectory planning enables synthetic data generation and model training that better reflect session-level psychological counseling processes.

title: LipSpell: A Language-Independent Phonetic Scoring Framework for Spelling Correction Combining Distinctive-Feature Edit Distance, Keyboard Geometry, and Corpus Frequency
summary: Automatic spelling correction must handle both keyboard typographical slips and cognitive or phonetic misspellings where writers approximate a word's pronunciation. Conventional spell checkers rely either on orthographic edit distance and keyboard proximity--which struggle when phonetic errors diverge by multiple characters--or on English-centric phonetic hashes such as Soundex and Metaphone. We present LipSpell, a unified, language-independent phonetic scoring engine paired with swappable language-specific G2P frontends, keyboard maps, and lexicons integrating: (1) a precomputed |P|x|P| phone-distance matrix from universal IPA distinctive features, (2) physical keyboard geometry, and (3) corpus unigram frequency priors, accelerated by a two-stage symmetric-delete and seven-class phonetic-code index. Across six English benchmarks (including 1,000 L2 errors from TOEFL-Spell), LipSpell outperforms Norvig and Hunspell on every dataset and beats Aspell on Norvig1 (78.52% vs. 75.56%), Holbrook (32.00% vs. 26.67%), and TOEFL-Spell (77.30% vs. 72.80%). Evaluated across six languages spanning five branches (Germanic, Romance, Slavic, Semitic, Turkic), three families (Indo-European, Afro-Asiatic, Turkic), and three scripts, LipSpell achieves strong fixed-weight transfer on Brazilian Portuguese (73.00% Top-1 on n=500 Wikipedia without NFD tolerance and 75.80% with NFD vs. 66.40% Norvig, 64.20% Hunspell, 64.00% Aspell) and Russian Cyrillic (85.67% vs. 78.50% Norvig). On 50/50 clean non-word splits with lexicon cleaning and weak-character indels, tuning yields strong gains over Norvig in Portuguese (86.97% vs. 76.75%), Turkish (81.67% vs. 79.05%), Hebrew Abjad (74.59% vs. 62.30%), and French (74.53% vs. 67.92%), while fixed weights remain optimal for English (80.37%) and Russian (85.67%).

AI.tldr: This paper presents LipSpell, a language-independent phonetic spelling correction framework combining IPA distinctive-feature edit distance, keyboard geometry, and corpus unigram frequency, outperforming Norvig and Hunspell across six English benchmarks and transferring across six languages.
AI.motivation: Conventional spell checkers struggle either with multi-character phonetic misspellings when using orthographic distance or with non-English languages when relying on English-centric phonetic hashes like Soundex and Metaphone.
AI.method: LipSpell pairs swappable G2P frontends, keyboard maps, and lexicons with a precomputed phone-distance matrix from universal IPA distinctive features, physical keyboard geometry, and corpus unigram priors, accelerated by a two-stage symmetric-delete and seven-class phonetic-code index.
AI.result: LipSpell beats Norvig and Hunspell on all six English benchmarks and beats Aspell on Norvig1 (78.52% vs. 75.56%), Holbrook (32.00% vs. 26.67%), and TOEFL-Spell (77.30% vs. 72.80%); across six languages, it achieves strong fixed-weight transfer on Brazilian Portuguese (73.00% / 75.80% Top-1) and Russian Cyrillic (85.67% vs. 78.50% Norvig), and tuned gains on Portuguese (86.97%), Turkish (81.67%), Hebrew (74.59%), and French (74.53%).
AI.conclusion: Grounding phonetic edit distance in universal IPA distinctive features alongside keyboard geometry and frequency priors yields an accurate, language-independent spelling correction engine.

title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
