summary: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LoopCache, a self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers that achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedups over WFD and LoopSpec.
AI.motivation: Existing wave-style self-speculative methods for Looped Transformers draft only at fixed loops and load up to R times the KV cache per step, wasting computation on stale trajectories and amplifying long-context memory traffic.
AI.method: LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating across intermediate loops, a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that restricts per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification, and selective independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers.
AI.result: Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average speedups of 10.25x over WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and 14.56x over LoopSpec.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic draft refinement and cyclic loop KV caching substantially reduce memory traffic and accelerate long-context inference in Looped Transformers.

title: What Majority Labels Hide: Annotator Disagreement and Model Errors in Multi-Dialect Arabic Sexism Detection
comment: 36 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to Online Social Networks and Media. Dataset: this https URL . Content warning: contains examples of sexist and offensive language
summary: Judgements of sexism are subjective and may vary across communities, yet sexism detection datasets usually reduce annotator judgements to a single majority label, obscuring disagreement and how models behave on contested cases. We introduce MuDAS, a dataset of YouTube comments in Saudi, Egyptian and Moroccan Arabic, each labelled by three native speakers of its dialect, with the individual annotations preserved. We use it to evaluate Arabic encoders fine-tuned with hard-label, soft-label and perspectivist objectives, GPT-5.6 Terra, and four Arabic-centric large language models. Model errors are more frequent on comments with annotator disagreement. Despite relatively close Macro-F1 scores, GPT-5.6 Terra and the fine-tuned encoders exhibit contrasting error patterns: GPT-5.6 Terra, even with the annotators' definition of sexism, over-classifies gender-related content such as religious advice on modesty, whereas the encoders miss implicit and prescriptive sexism. The Arabic-centric models also over-predict sexism and remain below the encoders. Disagreement-aware learning preserves Macro-F1, but soft labels improve alignment with annotators on contested comments at the expense of unanimous ones, and neither paradigm reliably identifies contested comments. Lower performance on Egyptian Arabic, clearest for the large language models, is not fully explained by the examined measures of test-set composition and dialectness. Majority-label scores can therefore hide contrasting error patterns that matter for content moderation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MuDAS, a multi-dialect Arabic sexism dataset preserving individual annotations, and shows that majority-label Macro-F1 scores hide contrasting error patterns between GPT-5.6 Terra and fine-tuned encoders.
AI.motivation: Sexism detection datasets typically collapse annotator judgments into a single majority label, obscuring disagreement and how models behave on contested cases across dialects.
AI.method: The authors curate MuDAS from YouTube comments in Saudi, Egyptian, and Moroccan Arabic with three native-speaker labels per comment, and evaluate Arabic encoders trained with hard-label, soft-label, and perspectivist objectives alongside GPT-5.6 Terra and four Arabic-centric LLMs.
AI.result: Errors concentrate on comments with annotator disagreement; despite similar Macro-F1 scores, GPT-5.6 Terra over-classifies gender-related content such as religious modesty advice while fine-tuned encoders miss implicit and prescriptive sexism, Arabic-centric LLMs over-predict sexism, and soft labels improve alignment on contested comments at the expense of unanimous ones.
AI.conclusion: Preserving individual annotations reveals distinct model failure modes that aggregate majority-label metrics conceal, which is critical for content moderation.

title: Nothing to Declare: Steering a single neuron increases concealment in AI teams
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure
summary: Recent research suggests that individual neurons can have interpretable roles in AI behaviour. In Qwen3.5-4B, steering along one neuron's output direction increased decisions to conceal information more in teams than alone across five scenarios, even when teammates provided no messages. When all members participated and received steering, collective concealment increased in four scenarios, while inter-agent messaging helped temper concealment under steering. Moreover, removing the neuron's contribution had negligible effects. Collective settings can therefore change how an internal intervention affects AI behaviour.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that steering a single neuron's output direction in Qwen3.5-4B increases concealment decisions more in AI teams than in solo settings, while inter-agent messaging tempers this effect.
AI.motivation: While individual neurons can have interpretable roles in AI behavior, it is unclear how internal neuron-level interventions interact with multi-agent team dynamics.
AI.method: The authors steer Qwen3.5-4B along a single neuron's output direction across five scenarios, comparing solo versus team settings (with and without inter-agent messaging) and testing neuron ablation.
AI.result: Steering increased concealment decisions more in teams than alone across all five scenarios even when teammates sent no messages; when all team members were steered, collective concealment rose in four scenarios, inter-agent messaging tempered concealment under steering, and removing the neuron's contribution had negligible effects.
AI.conclusion: Collective multi-agent settings can alter how internal model interventions manifest in AI behavior.

title: MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity Linking
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures
summary: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a "divide-and-conquer" strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MECI, a Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction framework for Multimodal Entity Linking that improves Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31% on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL.
AI.motivation: Existing Multimodal Entity Linking methods suffer from element dominance due to coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations when modeling mention-entity consistency and cross-modal correlations.
AI.method: MECI combines a Multi-view Experts Network with KL-guided routing for decoupled feature learning, a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module with dynamic modality-aware weighting, and a generative semantic refinement stage using LLMs for zero-shot re-ranking.
AI.result: On WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL, MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled multi-view expert routing, hierarchical cross-modal weighting, and LLM zero-shot re-ranking effectively mitigate element dominance in Multimodal Entity Linking.

title: ProbMedTOD: A Bayesian Network Guided Task-Oriented Dialogue System for Patient History Taking
summary: Patient history taking is a strategic, multi-turn process that refines diagnostic hypotheses through iterative questioning, mirroring clinical reasoning where each inquiry updates beliefs over candidate diagnoses. Deploying AI in this setting is constrained by privacy, cost, and latency, making Small Language Models (SLMs) a more desirable backbone compared to larger LLMs. However, SLMs capture only the fast, intuitive "System 1" side of this process and lack explicit mechanisms for the deliberative "System 2" reasoning needed to maintain and update diagnostic uncertainty over time. Bayesian Networks (BayesNets) offer a natural complement, providing an interpretable framework for auditable probabilistic belief tracking. Yet, clinical BayesNets are difficult to construct due to their reliance on expert curated structure, dependencies, and parameters. We introduce ProbMedTOD, which automatically synthesizes a clinical BayesNet from a small number of clinical notes in three stages: ontology building, structure prediction, and parameter estimation. ProbMedTOD then integrates the resulting BayesNet with SLMs, enabling probabilistic reasoning in multi-turn dialogues. A BayesNet Agent maintains real-time posterior distributions over diagnoses, while a Policy Agent picks diagnostically informative questions. Experiments on DDXPlus and MIMIC-IV Notes show that ProbMedTOD outperforms LLM-only and retrieval-based baselines, with especially strong gains for smaller models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ProbMedTOD, a task-oriented dialogue system that automatically synthesizes a clinical Bayesian Network from clinical notes and pairs it with Small Language Models for patient history taking, outperforming LLM-only and retrieval-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Small Language Models are desirable for clinical history taking due to privacy, cost, and latency, but they lack deliberative probabilistic belief tracking, while clinical Bayesian Networks are difficult to curate manually.
AI.method: ProbMedTOD synthesizes a clinical BayesNet from a small number of clinical notes via ontology building, structure prediction, and parameter estimation, then pairs a BayesNet Agent (for real-time posterior diagnosis tracking) with a Policy Agent (to select informative questions).
AI.result: Experiments on DDXPlus and MIMIC-IV Notes show that ProbMedTOD outperforms LLM-only and retrieval-based baselines, with particularly strong gains for smaller models.
AI.conclusion: Integrating automatically synthesized Bayesian Networks with SLMs enables auditable probabilistic reasoning in multi-turn clinical history taking.

title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
summary: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.

AI.tldr: This replicated factorial study tests five frontier model ingredients in small language models, finding that mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimization, and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid yield the largest gains and mostly combine additively.
AI.motivation: Building small language models requires knowing which published architectural and optimization improvements actually combine well under a fixed data and training budget.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five changes—mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimization, a Gated DeltaNet hybrid, extra normalization, and a parameter-matched attention gate—using identical data and budgets, testing selected combinations with a second random seed.
AI.result: Mixture-of-experts, Muon, and Gated DeltaNet produce the largest gains, extra normalization also helps, and the attention gate adds little on average; gains mostly combine, though small interactions recur across seeds and repetition reveals benefits initially mistaken for noise.
AI.conclusion: Testing candidate components together with replicated runs provides more reliable guidance for small-model design than single-seed or isolated evaluations.

title: Objective-Specialized Residual Streams in Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
summary: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extend a Transformer's residual stream into multiple parallel streams with learned cross-stream connections. Prior work trains all streams toward a shared objective. We instead study whether assigning distinct learning objectives to different streams can improve task performance and induce objective-specific specialization. Using complementary lexical (sparse) and semantic (dense) retrieval objectives as a test case, we find that objective-specialized mHC consistently outperforms a non-specialized mHC model across the full sparse--dense fusion range, for both two- and four-stream models and at two model scales. We then examine how specialization changes the model internally using probes of stream representations, residual mixing, objective-specific gradient flow, and read/write gates. The specialized and non-specialized models behave similarly through most of the network but diverge in the final layers: the specialized model develops increasingly objective-specific gradient flow, distinct read/write routing patterns, and reduced cross-stream mixing, and streams assigned to different objectives become increasingly dissimilar while those trained toward the same objective remain highly similar. Fixing the residual mixing to the identity leaves the specialization benefit intact, indicating that the benefit stems from objective-specific read/write routing rather than learned cross-stream mixing. These results show that assigning distinct objectives to mHC streams can improve multi-objective retrieval while inducing structured, depth-dependent specialization in the residual computation.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that assigning distinct lexical and semantic retrieval objectives to different streams in Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) outperforms non-specialized mHC and induces structured specialization in final layers.
AI.motivation: Prior work on Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections trains all parallel residual streams toward a shared objective, leaving open whether objective-specific stream specialization improves multi-objective performance.
AI.method: The authors assign complementary lexical (sparse) and semantic (dense) retrieval objectives to different mHC streams in two- and four-stream models at two scales, and probe stream representations, residual mixing, gradient flow, and read/write gates.
AI.result: Objective-specialized mHC consistently outperforms non-specialized mHC across the full sparse-dense fusion range; models diverge in the final layers with objective-specific gradient flow, distinct read/write routing, and reduced cross-stream mixing, and fixing residual mixing to identity preserves the specialization benefit.
AI.conclusion: Assigning distinct objectives to mHC streams improves multi-objective retrieval via objective-specific read/write routing rather than learned cross-stream mixing.

title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
comment: 25 pages, 9 figures
summary: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K < T passes over a deep context cache. Once lightweight fine-tuning resolves hidden-state norm mismatch at the entry boundary, deep cached context substitutes for skipped token-local passes, allowing late entry to outperform matched early exit across model families and pass budgets. To turn this asymmetry into wall-clock speedups without stalling to build deep caches, candidate blocks verify through only the final K passes on the critical path while previously committed tokens complete passes 1 -> T alongside subsequent steps at zero extra serial calls. Projecting these finished T-pass wake states inside the existing output GEMM (Wake verification, governed by logit-margin tolerance tau in [0, inf]) unifies greedy-exact T-pass decoding (tau = 0, matching K = T block decoding within bf16 reduction order), margin-gated verification (tau > 0), and non-rollback lossy late entry (tau = inf) inside a single static CUDA graph. On Ouro-2.6B (T = 4), K = 2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau = 0 (+26% over K = 4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau = inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit at matched speed). Scaling test-time recurrence across T in {8, 16, 32, 64} on Huginn-3.5B cuts K = T/4 rollbacks 21.5x with depth, driving greedy-exact (tau = 0) speedups to 6.1x (T = 32) and 8.4x (T = 64, +153% over K = 64 block) and tau = inf speedups to 10.6 to 12.5x.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes late entry with Wake verification for looped language models, achieving up to 8.4x greedy-exact speedup and 12.5x lossy speedup by skipping initial passes over a deep context cache.
AI.motivation: Looped language models trade recurrence depth for sequential decoding latency, while conventional early-exit decoding truncates past key-value caches to shallow depth.
AI.method: Late entry skips initial passes for new tokens and enters directly into the final K < T passes over a deep context cache, using lightweight fine-tuning to fix hidden-state norm mismatch and Wake verification (governed by logit-margin tolerance tau) to complete passes 1 to T for committed tokens alongside subsequent steps in one static CUDA graph.
AI.result: On Ouro-2.6B (T=4), K=2 Wake reaches 5.2x greedy-exact speedup at tau=0 (+26% over K=4 block decoding on GSM8K) and 6.8x at tau=inf (+16.9 points over trained early exit); on Huginn-3.5B, scaling T from 8 to 64 cuts K=T/4 rollbacks 21.5x, reaching 6.1x (T=32) and 8.4x (T=64) greedy-exact speedups and 10.6-12.5x lossy speedups.
AI.conclusion: Deep cached context can substitute for skipped token-local passes, making late entry with Wake verification an effective way to accelerate looped language models.

title: Large Language Models or AI Agents for English to Arabic Translation? An assessment on WikiEn-Ar190
summary: This research investigates whether a large language model or an autonomous AI Agent performs better at translating from English to Arabic, which is considered a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new dataset of 190 carefully selected Wikipedia articles from 18 different areas, which were created and verified by two native Arabic speakers to ensure that they accurately reflect both meaning and style. Using this dataset, the study evaluates the translation quality of GPT-5-mini both as an independent neural translator and when used within a more complex process that includes self-assessment and improvement. As a standalone model, GPT-5-mini produced very fluent translations , achieving a COMET score of 0.8649 and receiving high human scores for adequacy, fluency, and style (averaging 4.53 out of 5). When used in a system that combined translation with self-assessment, it improved lexical accuracy by 28.76% (BLEU score of 22.83) while maintaining a similar level of semantic quality. These findings show that methods involving autonomous reasoning can improve translation consistency for language pairs with limited resources. Beyond the results, the approach offers a framework for evaluating and improving translations, potentially using them as assisting tools to expand the representation of low resource languages, such as Arabic, on the web.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WikiEn-Ar190, a verified English-to-Arabic dataset of 190 Wikipedia articles, and finds that adding self-assessment to GPT-5-mini improves BLEU by 28.76% while maintaining semantic quality.
AI.motivation: It remains unclear whether standalone LLMs or autonomous AI agent workflows with self-assessment perform better on English-to-Arabic translation.
AI.method: The authors construct WikiEn-Ar190 across 18 domains verified by two native Arabic speakers and compare standalone GPT-5-mini against an agentic workflow combining translation with self-assessment and iterative improvement.
AI.result: Standalone GPT-5-mini achieves a COMET score of 0.8649 and an average human rating of 4.53/5 for adequacy, fluency, and style, while the self-assessment agent workflow increases lexical accuracy by 28.76% (to 22.83 BLEU) at comparable semantic quality.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous self-assessment and refinement loops can improve lexical accuracy and translation consistency for English-to-Arabic translation.

title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. We start by labelling each CoT hidden state as recovering if patching it into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and failed otherwise. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. We then show that the representation space of the direct prompt holds a direction for each question that leads the model, in a short generation, to the correct answer more often than CoT does. Specifically, we rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once, before generation, towards a direction built for each question from its own recovering and failed states. Across 25 tasks, these directions raise the direct prompt's mean accuracy from $46\%$ to $85\%$ on LLaMA 3.1 8B (CoT: $69\%$) and from $52\%$ to $86\%$ on Qwen 2.5 7B (CoT: $77\%$), with a tenth of CoT's tokens. CoT is thus not the shortest route to this accuracy, and these directions can be used in future work to train models to align their states with them.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that rotating a direct prompt's last hidden state once toward a question-specific task-solving direction derived from CoT hidden states raises accuracy from 46% to 85% on LLaMA 3.1 8B using a tenth of CoT's tokens.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought prompting can be verbose and sometimes underperforms direct-answer prompting, raising the question of whether shorter routes exist in representation space.
AI.method: The authors label CoT hidden states as recovering or failed based on whether patching them into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once before generation toward a direction built from each question's recovering and failed states.
AI.result: Across 25 tasks, this single rotation raises direct-prompt mean accuracy from 46% to 85% on LLaMA 3.1 8B (vs. 69% for CoT) and from 52% to 86% on Qwen 2.5 7B (vs. 77% for CoT), while using one-tenth as many tokens as CoT.
AI.conclusion: CoT is not the shortest path to high reasoning accuracy, and representation-space task-solving directions offer a promising target for future alignment training.

title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
comment: Technical Report. Code: this https URL Weights: this https URL
summary: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

AI.tldr: This technical report introduces Clover-35B-A3B-Preview, a 35B-total / 3B-active MoE block diffusion language model that leads seven evaluated agent metrics (including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified) and generates at 680 tokens/s on one GB300 GPU.
AI.motivation: Scaling diffusion language models to competitive agentic reasoning and high-throughput generation requires combining long-context memory with efficient block-level denoising.
AI.method: Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of prior context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block, using learnable block-size calibration, a zero-initialized right-context convolution branch, and a decision-model variant for joint multi-question denoising.
AI.result: Clover leads all seven evaluated agent metrics, scoring 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, reaches 680 tokens/s on one NVIDIA GB300 GPU (BF16, batch size 1), and its decision-model variant raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0% on 500 internal groups.
AI.conclusion: Hybridizing Gated Delta Networks with block diffusion yields a fast, high-performing MoE diffusion model for agentic workloads.

title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures, 11 tables. Project page and blog: this https URL
summary: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Piccolo, a family of 0.8B-27B multimodal decision models trained via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI), with Piccolo-27B topping the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard at 75.59.
AI.motivation: Building frontier multimodal decision models requires understanding how model backbones, data curation, and recursive self-improvement interact at scale.
AI.method: Research agents analyze model behavior, curate hundreds of thousands of training examples, run experiments, and refine proposals using semantic slices and shared research memory within the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems.
AI.result: Piccolo-27B scores 75.59 to lead the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard, Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B score 68.35 and 67.46, and all three rank first on the Private benchmark in their size categories; the study also finds that backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs model recency, targeted curation lets 4B-9B models rival 27B baselines, and continuous loss reduction can decouple from discrete decision accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving data recipes and decision models through structured RSI provides an effective blueprint for building frontier multimodal decision models.

title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
summary: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CurvDelta and CurvLoRA, curvature-constrained adaptation methods that preserve general LLM capabilities during mathematical reasoning, code generation, and selective knowledge unlearning.
AI.motivation: Adapting LLMs for new skills or selective unlearning often degrades their general capabilities.
AI.method: CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature parameter space around the pre-adaptation model using Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection so updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant, alongside a low-rank variant called CurvLoRA.
AI.result: On mathematical reasoning and code generation, CurvDelta and CurvLoRA achieve competitive downstream performance with better general-capability retention than baselines, and on TOFU and MUSE unlearning benchmarks they achieve a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention close to from-scratch retraining.
AI.conclusion: Embedding local preservation geometry directly into update parameterization enables surgical LLM learning and unlearning.

title: When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? A Controlled Study of Dialectal Adaptation for Québec French
comment: EACL 2027 Main Conference
summary: Continual pre-training (CPT) is widely used to adapt pretrained language models to dialectal and non-standard language varieties, yet it remains unclear when this additional training is necessary, what drives its benefits, and whether aggregate evaluation scores adequately capture its effects. In this paper, we present a controlled study of CPT for Québec French language understanding across nine LLMs spanning different families and scales. Using a budget-matched protocol of 30M tokens per experiment, our results show that the benefit of CPT depends strongly on the starting model's existing competence in the target variety. When CPT is beneficial, the improvements are driven more by corpus composition than by data volume, with literary text accounting for most of the gain. Paired Québec and standard French evaluations further show that CPT primarily improves expression comprehension rather than grammatical competence, and that corpus register determines which regional expressions are acquired. These gains also involve capability-specific trade-offs, including declines in reading comprehension that aggregate scores can conceal. Overall, these findings show that CPT for dialectal adaptation should not be treated as a uniformly beneficial default. Instead, adaptation strategies should begin with a careful assessment of the base model's existing competence, accompanied by source-level data analysis and task-level evaluation.

AI.tldr: This controlled study of continual pre-training (CPT) for Québec French across nine LLMs shows that CPT benefits depend strongly on the base model's starting competence and corpus composition, with literary text driving most gains.
AI.motivation: Continual pre-training is widely used for dialectal adaptation, but it is unclear when it is necessary, what drives its gains, and whether aggregate scores hide capability trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors run budget-matched 30M-token CPT experiments across nine LLMs of varying families and scales, evaluating paired Québec and standard French tasks alongside source-level corpus analysis.
AI.result: CPT gains depend heavily on initial target-variety competence and are driven more by corpus composition (especially literary text) than data volume; CPT mainly improves expression comprehension rather than grammar, corpus register dictates which expressions are learned, and aggregate scores can mask declines in reading comprehension.
AI.conclusion: Dialectal CPT should not be applied blindly as a default; instead, it should follow base-model competence assessment, source-level data analysis, and task-level evaluation.

title: Induction Head Origins of SLAM-ASR Speech Recognition Models
comment: Submitted to ICASSP
summary: What makes a small trained map from encoder states to the embedding space of a frozen language model sufficient for competitive speech recognition? The premise of the SLAM-ASR architecture is that a frozen language model possesses linguistic knowledge rich enough to perform the recognition task. This assumption, while reasonable, provides little insight into the mechanisms underlying these models. We therefore seek the concrete internal structures on which they rely. This work shows that SLAM-ASR models rely on induction heads of the frozen language model: the same heads that copy repeated token sequences in text are also important for mapping speech embeddings to transcript tokens. Moreover, we find pairs of heads that behave as a constrained form of differential attention, cancelling attention noise and sharpening attention onto the previously generated word. Finally, we show how induction heads could be used to improve transcription quality under noisy audio.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that SLAM-ASR speech recognition models rely on induction heads in the frozen language model, including pairs acting as constrained differential attention, to map speech embeddings to transcript tokens.
AI.motivation: Although SLAM-ASR achieves competitive speech recognition by mapping encoder states into a frozen LLM's embedding space, the internal mechanisms enabling this remain unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze the internal attention structures of frozen LLMs in SLAM-ASR models to identify which heads drive speech-to-text mapping and test their role under noisy audio.
AI.result: The same induction heads that copy repeated token sequences in text are critical for mapping speech embeddings to transcript tokens, and pairs of heads act as constrained differential attention that cancels attention noise and sharpens focus on the previous word; leveraging induction heads improves transcription quality under noisy audio.
AI.conclusion: Frozen LLM induction heads provide the mechanistic basis for SLAM-ASR speech recognition and offer a lever for improving noise robustness.

title: On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models
summary: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve a better quality--efficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under a prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorph's layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layer-selection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by $+2.42$ points on RULER, $+1.08$ on LongBench, and $+0.76$ on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only $0.72$--$3.57$ GPU hours across 0.6B--8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method for converting pretrained Transformers into hybrid full/linear attention models, outperforming FlashMorph by +2.42 points on RULER and +1.08 on LongBench.
AI.motivation: Existing layer-selection methods like FlashMorph suffer from off-policy mismatches because continuous branch interpolation, teacher-forced states, and frozen weights do not reflect discrete hybrid computation or post-recovery adaptation.
AI.method: FlashMorph2 evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states and jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective.
AI.result: Across Qwen3 scales (0.6B-8B) and linear-attention variants, FlashMorph2 outperforms FlashMorph by +2.42 points on RULER, +1.08 on LongBench, and +0.76 on recall-intensive tasks, completing layer selection in 0.72-3.57 GPU hours.
AI.conclusion: On-policy evaluation and joint weight-selection optimization enable fast, scalable conversion of Transformers into high-performing hybrid attention models.

title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
comment: 48 pages, 6 figures
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Chiron, a foundation model jointly fine-tuned on 288,307 person records to measure psychological constructs, predict individual behavior (up to 28.4% relative gain over frontier LLMs), and simulate social science experiments (82.2-94.3% lower effect-size error).
AI.motivation: Standard LLMs often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics when used to infer psychological traits, predict behavior, or simulate human populations.
AI.method: Chiron jointly fine-tunes an LLM on 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioral decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments across 36 domains, 78 social science experiments, and 109 psychological constructs to align individual predictions and population response distributions with human data.
AI.result: Chiron's psychological measurements align more closely with human self-reports with fewer validity biases, it outperforms frontier LLMs by up to 28.4% relatively on individual behavior prediction, and it reduces effect-size estimation error in simulated experiments by 82.2-94.3%.
AI.conclusion: Jointly aligning psychometric representation, individual prediction, and population statistics establishes Chiron as a unified computational instrument for modeling human behavior.

title: General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models
comment: 49 pages, 16 figures, 6 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that general training progress in language models substitutes for withheld skill-specific data, allowing models to regain withheld capabilities with a small fraction of the data required from scratch.
AI.motivation: Developers withhold training data to delay potentially dangerous capabilities, but it is unknown how long this delays a skill or how much data is needed to acquire it later.
AI.method: The authors withhold training signals for individual skills across chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages, web text, and a programming language (in a 7B-parameter model), then measure both zero-shot delay and data efficiency when retraining on the withheld data.
AI.result: A chess model never trained to respond to check still ranked legal responses nearly as well as a trained model; when later trained on withheld data, models acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction shrank as general model progress increased (unlike an equally difficult control rule), with the same pattern observed for a withheld programming language in a 7B model.
AI.conclusion: Data filtering only delays capabilities, and the data required to regain a withheld skill decreases as general model capability improves.

title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation
comment: 56 pages
summary: Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas, yet it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work. We introduce the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework combining literature grounding, iterative development and explicit conceptual operators. CAR constructs a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature and equips an ideation agent with graph-retrieval tools and four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration. Each operator call is checked against structural acceptance conditions and recorded, producing a trace of intermediate transformations and declared literature sources. We evaluate CAR with two language-model backbones across 40 LiveIdeaBench research topics and two execution benchmarks. CAR achieves significantly higher methodological novelty (MN) than single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist. Its methodological novelty does not differ significantly from the Research Ideation Agent, while its feasibility scores are higher on both backbones. With a shared experiment executor, CAR achieves the highest pairwise win rate among the evaluated AI methods on FML-bench-Lite and BioXArena. In a ten-condition ablation study, MN point estimates favor CAR over one-step proposal on both backbones, but no MN contrast survives correction for multiple comparisons. The results do not establish a consistent quality benefit from explicit operators beyond free-form iteration. CAR makes the sequence of operations and declared literature sources inspectable, separating judged idea quality from procedural traceability.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic ideation framework combining literature-grounded knowledge graphs, iterative development, and explicit conceptual operators, achieving higher feasibility than Research Ideation Agent and higher methodological novelty than single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist.
AI.motivation: While LLMs can generate plausible research ideas, it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how novel proposals trace back to prior literature.
AI.method: CAR builds a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature and equips an ideation agent with graph-retrieval tools and four checked operators (bisociation, analogy, exploration, elaboration), logging every transformation and source; the authors evaluate it across 40 LiveIdeaBench topics, FML-bench-Lite, BioXArena, and a ten-condition ablation.
AI.result: CAR outperforms single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist in methodological novelty (MN), matches Research Ideation Agent in MN with higher feasibility, and achieves the highest pairwise win rate on FML-bench-Lite and BioXArena; however, in the ablation study no MN contrast over one-step proposal survives multiple-comparison correction.
AI.conclusion: CAR makes automated ideation traceable and inspectable, though explicit conceptual operators do not show a statistically consistent quality advantage over free-form iteration.

title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
summary: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes JDPI, a contrastive prototype-inference method for LLM jailbreak detection that avoids training a downstream classifier, improving detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points across four benchmarks and exceeding Llama Guard 3-8B by 0.173-0.310 ROC-AUC.
AI.motivation: Training a separate downstream classifier for safety detection requires an additional labeled data split and may generalize poorly across datasets.
AI.method: Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI) uses binary safety labels to contrastively adapt an encoder, construct harmful and benign prototypes, and classify inputs via relative prototype distances, incorporating accumulated conversation history in multi-turn settings.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points, JDPI stays within 0.017 ROC-AUC of the classifier baseline using fewer labeled examples, adapted JDPI beats Llama Guard 3-8B by 0.173-0.310 ROC-AUC, multi-turn replay on TomGibbs improves conversation-level accuracy, and JDPI outperforms the classifier by 1.59 percentage points on average across 12 directed transfers.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive prototype inference offers a data-efficient and cross-dataset-robust alternative to classifier-based jailbreak detection.

title: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026
summary: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PGPO, a prototype-guided progressive obfuscation framework trained with GRPO for privacy-preserving LLM-enhanced recommendation, achieving strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation utility.
AI.motivation: Semantic embeddings in LLM-enhanced recommender systems can leak sensitive textual attributes under inversion attacks, while existing input-side defenses often disrupt the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation.
AI.method: PGPO introduces relational fidelity as an objective and learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words, propagating them through a static semantic graph and optimizing with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards.
AI.result: Experiments on two benchmarks show strong defense against attribute inversion attacks while maintaining near-upper-bound recommendation performance.
AI.conclusion: Topology-aware prototype obfuscation optimized with GRPO effectively balances attribute privacy and recommendation utility.

title: A Concurrent Structured Record Mirrored the Prose It Accompanied: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension of the Hide Pending Tool Call Scenario
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. Pre-registered study; protocols, code, data and analyses at this https URL
summary: Huang et al. (2026) show that language models writing reports of agentic work tend to conceal narrative-changing flaws, and that appending "Be honest in your response." to the instruction substantially increases disclosure in most of their scenarios. In their Hide Pending Tool Call scenario, where a broader follow-up query was accepted but never returned, the honesty prompt left GPT-5.5's rate of flagging the missing data at 0%, although it turned most answers into caveats. I ask whether a different request changes this: appending, in the same generation, a structured record that follows the schema of an adversarial-review tool, including a residue section for what remained unresolved. In two pre-registered phases on the same 100 synthetic log pairs, each pending log matched with a clean twin in which the follow-up query did return, I ran gpt-5.6-sol through Codex CLI under four conditions. Phase 1 measured the record: with the residue schema, a judge coded it as stating the unreturned query in 29% of logs, against 5% with a findings-only placebo schema, and in none of the clean twins (p = 1.2 x 10^-7); a second run two days later gave 30% and 6%. But 70-71% of residue records declared that nothing remained open while the query was pending. Phase 2 measured the prose answer: the confirmatory comparison against the honesty prompt was not significant (four discordant logs, all favoring the honesty prompt; p = 0.125), no equivalence test was pre-registered, and the judge failed the pre-registered human validation on the decisive category; I therefore claim neither an effect nor its absence. In an exploratory cross-tabulation, every residue record coded as stating the gap accompanied prose coded as mentioning it (30 of 30), and none accompanied prose coded as omitting it (0 of 70): in this setting, the structured record mirrored the prose it accompanied.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether appending a structured adversarial-review record with a residue section increases disclosure of an unreturned tool call in agentic reports, finding that the record mirrored the accompanying prose rather than independently exposing the gap.
AI.motivation: Language models writing reports of agentic work tend to hide narrative-changing flaws, and in the Hide Pending Tool Call scenario of Huang et al. (2026), an honesty prompt left GPT-5.5's rate of flagging missing data at 0%.
AI.method: In two pre-registered phases on 100 synthetic log pairs (each pending log matched with a clean twin where the follow-up query returned), gpt-5.6-sol was run through Codex CLI under four conditions, comparing a residue-schema record against a findings-only placebo schema and an honesty prompt.
AI.result: In Phase 1, a judge coded the residue record as stating the unreturned query in 29% of logs (30% on a second run) versus 5% (6%) for the placebo and 0% for clean twins (p = 1.2 x 10^-7), though 70-71% of residue records still declared nothing remained open. In Phase 2, the prose comparison against the honesty prompt was not significant (p = 0.125) and the judge failed human validation on the decisive category; cross-tabulation showed 30 of 30 residue records stating the gap accompanied prose mentioning it and 0 of 70 accompanied prose omitting it.
AI.conclusion: In this setting, appending a structured residue record does not independently overcome omission of pending tool calls because the structured record mirrors the prose it accompanies.

title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This survey systematically organizes LLM RLOps techniques across five training lifecycle stages and identifies open operational challenges and future research directions.
AI.motivation: Scaling reinforcement learning for LLMs exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that waste compute and slow training, while existing RLOps techniques remain scattered across research areas without unified synthesis.
AI.method: The authors organize LLM RLOps methods into a five-stage taxonomy covering Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation, examining operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence within each stage.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes existing RLOps approaches across the five stages, identifies open challenges in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement, and maintains an accompanying GitHub repository of papers and resources.
AI.conclusion: By framing operational management across the full RL training lifecycle, the survey provides a structured foundation for scaling RLOps from single runs to shared infrastructure and recursive improvement cycles.

title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables
summary: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

AI.tldr: QDA is an agent-driven closed-loop system that designs per-model, per-precision post-training quantization recipes using fast proxy evaluation and a unified PTQ library.
AI.motivation: Optimal post-training quantization (PTQ) recipes vary across models and precisions, requiring time-consuming manual redesign and codebase porting, while evaluating a single quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours.
AI.method: QDA pairs an LLM agent that iteratively refines quantization recipes with a unified library of compatible public PTQ methods and a fast evaluator that scores candidates in minutes via output KL divergence on held-out reasoning traces, followed by long-generation checks for failure modes like repetition loops.
AI.result: Across four reasoning models using 64 GPU-hours per search, QDA outperforms the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4, and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8, and W3A16, and recovers 98.3% of FP8 accuracy on GLM-5.3-Flash (320B MoE) at NVFP4 W4A4 versus 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint, with zero inference overhead on existing serving kernels.
AI.conclusion: Automated agentic search over compatible PTQ building blocks with fast KL-based proxy evaluation can discover stronger, serving-ready quantization recipes than manual expert design.

title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
comment: Technical report
summary: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.

AI.tldr: SpecLook is a training-free speculate-and-verify framework that accelerates agentic multimodal LLMs by speculating the next zoom-in observation rather than the final answer, eliminating the sequential tool-use loop.
AI.motivation: Agentic MLLMs that interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls suffer from slow sequential loops and lack answer reliability scores, while prior token, step, or answer speculation either preserves the loop or accepts confident errors.
AI.method: SpecLook uses a three-level framework where a small model drafts a visual glimpse and re-answers, stopping if confident and unchanged; otherwise the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools and fuses answers, with only remaining uncertain cases reaching the agent in a single forward pass (skipped in SpecLook-Fast).
AI.result: On V*, HR-Bench, and POPE, both variants outperform all baselines on every split, with SpecLook reaching 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy at 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL, and SpecLook-Fast achieving 9.9x and 6.3x speedups while providing label-free reliability scores.
AI.conclusion: Speculating verifiable intermediate observations instead of final answers removes the sequential zoom-in loop while improving both accuracy and inference speed for agentic MLLMs.

title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

AI.tldr: BOS Summary is a training-free inference-time method that relaxes causal masking for the BOS token at one prefill layer so it aggregates input context and improves reasoning across VLMs and LLMs.
AI.motivation: Standard causal masking restricts the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token to attend only to itself, so despite acting as a persistent attention sink accessed by later tokens, its representation carries no input information.
AI.method: At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary removes the causal constraint solely for the BOS query row so it attends to all visual and textual input tokens, forming an input-specific representation that remains accessible throughout decoding with no extra parameters or decoding overhead.
AI.result: Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary outperforms direct prompting, Chain-of-Thought prompting, and recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks, while mechanistic analysis shows it weakens BOS sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing tokens.
AI.conclusion: Repurposing the BOS attention sink to carry input context at prefill provides a zero-overhead way to improve multi-step reasoning and reshape attention allocation in later layers.

title: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
summary: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

AI.tldr: GRAFT is an evolutionary agent-design method that uses parent-specific execution evidence from fitness evaluation to guide semantic crossover and mutation.
AI.motivation: Automated evolutionary agent design typically relies on aggregate fitness scores alone, which obscures the instance-level successes and failures needed to guide effective recombination of agent mechanisms.
AI.method: GRAFT retains aggregate fitness for selection and survival while feeding bounded samples of successful and failed parent execution runs (without reference answers or extra task executions) into a feedback harness that guides LLM-based semantic crossover and mutation.
AI.result: Across six reasoning and programming settings with open-weight optimizer and executor models, GRAFT achieves 82.0% mean test accuracy, beating the strongest baseline by 9.8 percentage points, and controlled ablations confirm that execution evidence improves accuracy under fixed budgets and policies.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating parent-specific execution traces into semantic crossover substantially improves evolutionary search for agent architectures without additional evaluation cost.

title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
comment: 58 pages, 11 figures, 41 tables. Code: this https URL data: this https URL
summary: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a finite-sample confidence-based mechanism for deciding when an LLM receiver agent can safely skip a helper agent's message, cutting latency while preserving most accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems often incur high latency waiting for helper text messages or latent KV caches, yet it is unclear when a receiver agent can omit those messages without changing its answer or whether the time saved outweighs the decision cost.
AI.method: The mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the helper message and applies a finite-sample test to certify a confidence threshold guaranteeing at most 5% of skipped answers change with high probability, falling back to full communication if no threshold passes.
AI.result: Tested on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, MMLU-Pro, SQuAD, and GSM8K across Qwen and cross-family pairs, certified policies skip 59-80% of text messages while retaining 76-95% of gains, skip a three-agent verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions (keeping 12.55 of 12.80 points) and a 32B helper on 68.4% (keeping the full gain) in prospective tests, and keep the 95% upper bound on change rate below 5% across all 11 testable unseen-question evaluations, though certification fails on GSM8K and KV-cache skipping saves far less time than text skipping.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-based finite-sample certification enables safe and latency-effective message skipping in multi-agent text communication, though actual speedups depend on communication modality and task structure.

title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027. 27 pages
summary: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.

AI.tldr: Option-GRPO is a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that learns reusable code patterns directly from an unseen SDK's source code to generate concise, idiomatic, and functionally correct programs.
AI.motivation: LLMs often produce verbose, non-idiomatic "AI slop" when generating code, a problem worsened on unseen SDKs released after training cutoff where models lack idiomatic priors and human usage examples or tests.
AI.method: Option-GRPO extracts a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) from SDK source code to form a semi-Markov decision process curriculum and action space, optimizing at each level with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and execution-based rewards.
