Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates six machine learning classifiers on a 58-patient Parkinson's disease dataset, finding high sensitivity for positive cases but poor separation of healthy controls.
AI.motivation: Accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) is challenging, motivating evaluation of standard machine learning classifiers on clinical data.
AI.method: SVM, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimization) were trained and evaluated on a 58-person PD dataset from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust.
AI.result: Decision Tree and Logistic Regression achieved the highest overall accuracy at 72-76% while MLP performed worst; all models showed high sensitivity on positive PD cases (up to 97.56% for SVM) but failed to meaningfully distinguish healthy controls from PD cases.
AI.conclusion: While standard classifiers detect positive PD cases with high sensitivity on this small cohort, larger datasets are needed to reliably separate healthy controls from patients.

title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

AI.tldr: This paper accelerates generative recommendation inference by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs using Tree Attention and pipeline optimizations without custom kernels.
AI.motivation: Generative recommendation features long shared prompts, wide beam search, and few output tokens, causing vLLM's independent-sequence batching and per-step host dispatch to incur redundant KV-cache reads and PagedAttention overhead.
AI.method: The authors concatenate beams along the sequence dimension with Tree Attention to share prompt KV caches, combined with pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV allocation, loop-unrolled dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding.
AI.result: Without custom kernels, the pipeline cuts end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs and matches a state-of-the-art custom-kernel solution.
AI.conclusion: Holistic pipeline and attention-layout optimization should precede custom kernel development for wide-beam generative recommendation serving.

title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
summary: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a continuous confidence-estimation framework combining domain rules and graph-structured learning to assess materials data quality.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous materials datasets often contain measurement errors, failed calculations, duplicates, and physicochemical violations that remain statistically plausible and evade binary outlier detection.
AI.method: Data quality is framed as continuous confidence estimation using a nine-dimensional feature-quality prior, duplicate-aware initialization calibrated with materials domain rules, sample-feature bipartite graph propagation, weakly supervised graph attention, and a Memory-GAT module for historical batch scoring.
AI.result: The generic module achieves 0.866 average AUC-ROC across 23 ODDS datasets; on mp_20 mixed-contamination experiments, rule calibration raises HistGradientBoostingRegressor test R^2 from 0.538+/-0.008 to 0.616+/-0.014 and graph refinement lifts average precision from 0.943+/-0.004 to 0.953+/-0.004, while MACE subset R^2 rises from 0.590+/-0.053 to 0.880+/-0.027.
AI.conclusion: Integrating physicochemical domain rules with graph-structured confidence propagation effectively filters subtle data corruption and improves downstream materials property prediction.

title: BiMa-ECGSR: reconstructing the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with bidirectional state-space models
summary: Wearables and monitors record few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads; most diagnostic tools assume 12 leads. BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder--decoder, as regression (BiMa-SR) or diffusion (DiBiMa-SR). Models were trained on PTB-XL for six input sets (I; II; I+II; I+II+V1; I+II+V2; I+II+V1+V4), see only the measured leads at inference, and were tested on the PTB-XL test fold (2,198 records) and two external cohorts (Georgia, 10,275 records; Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo, 43,559). From lead II alone, the pooled median Pearson correlation (PCC) over the 11 predicted leads was 0.914 on PTB-XL, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter (lead I: 0.906 against 0.789). As limb leads are exactly derivable from I and II, multi-lead inputs were compared on predicted chest leads: 0.939 against 0.849 for I+II and 0.979 against 0.962 for I+II+V1+V4. BiMa-SR exceeded the linear comparator in all 18 configuration--cohort pairs (by 0.012--0.136), a margin that shrank as chest leads were added. From lead II, regression was more accurate than diffusion (DiBiMa-SR: 0.903 one-step, 0.862 with six DDIM steps). A 12-lead classifier trained only on real ECGs reached a superclass macro AUROC of 0.912 on real PTB-XL ECGs, 0.843 on reconstructions from lead II and 0.908 from I+II+V1+V4; externally, reconstructions from three or four leads scored within 0.004 of real ECGs. BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU. Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

AI.tldr: BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs 12-lead ECGs from reduced lead sets using a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder-decoder, outperforming linear comparators across all 18 configuration-cohort pairs.
AI.motivation: Wearables and monitors record only a few ECG leads, whereas most diagnostic tools require 12 leads.
AI.method: The authors train bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder-decoder models on PTB-XL for six reduced-lead input sets, evaluating both regression (BiMa-SR) and diffusion (DiBiMa-SR) variants.
AI.result: Tested on PTB-XL (2,198 records), Georgia (10,275 records), and Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo (43,559 records), BiMa-SR achieves a pooled median PCC of 0.914 from lead II alone versus 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter, and 0.979 versus 0.962 on predicted chest leads from I+II+V1+V4. Regression outperforms diffusion from lead II (0.903 one-step, 0.862 six DDIM steps), a 12-lead classifier reaches 0.908 macro AUROC on I+II+V1+V4 reconstructions (versus 0.912 on real ECGs), and BiMa-SR (2.68M parameters) runs in 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional state-space reconstruction makes reduced-lead ECG recordings usable by 12-lead diagnostic tools, though it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
summary: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (this https URL).

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates binary BERT dependability under memory bit errors and proposes PIES, a permutation-invariance-enabled selective protection scheme that recovers most accuracy loss at low overhead.
AI.motivation: Approximate memory reduces power for binary Transformers but introduces bit errors, and existing research has not well studied model dependability against memory errors.
AI.method: The authors first evaluate binary BERT under bit error rates (BERs) up to 10%, then propose Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) protection, which exploits Transformer row and column permutation invariance to group critical weights and selectively protect them.
AI.result: Large accuracy loss occurs only at high BERs (5% or 10%), and simulations show PIES recovers most of the performance loss at BERs up to 10% with significantly lower overhead than traditional error correction schemes.
AI.conclusion: PIES demonstrates the feasibility of running binary Transformers on approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low-power edge devices.

title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

AI.tldr: TRACE-MAS diagnoses and repairs collaboration failures in LLM-based multi-agent systems by modeling normal interaction patterns, attributing root causes, and applying minimal interventions.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent system (MAS) safeguards rely on agent-level anomaly detection, which is insufficient when failures stem from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not reveal true sources.
AI.method: TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories, detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions, performs source-aware attribution, and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration.
AI.result: Across five MAS benchmarks, TRACE-MAS improves root-cause localization accuracy by 60.2% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.
AI.conclusion: Modeling interaction-level execution patterns enables more accurate root-cause diagnosis and effective repair of collaboration failures in multi-agent systems.

title: Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève Update
summary: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded-memory with state independent of the number of points processed. A forgetting factor lets the method track drifting distributions, and a sample-size-invariant embedding keeps outputs comparable across time. Experiments show agreement with Roseland to round-off on stationary data, and accuracy that exceeds equal-memory Roseland by an order of magnitude on long streams. On drifting data, we observe large gains from forgetting with a window matched to the drift.

AI.tldr: Incremental Roseland (iRoseland) computes landmark diffusion embeddings in a single bounded-memory pass over streaming data using a kernelized Sequential Karhunen-Loeve SVD update.
AI.motivation: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) reduces the cost of full diffusion maps, but it assumes all data are available at once and cannot process streaming data incrementally.
AI.method: iRoseland casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix updated via a kernelized Sequential Karhunen-Loeve (SKL) scheme, handles degree correction via a first-order expansion around a reference mean kernel row, and incorporates a forgetting factor and sample-size-invariant embedding for drifting distributions.
AI.result: iRoseland agrees with batch Roseland to round-off on stationary data, exceeds equal-memory Roseland accuracy by an order of magnitude on long streams, and achieves large gains on drifting data when the forgetting window matches the drift.
AI.conclusion: iRoseland enables scalable, single-pass spectral embedding on stationary and drifting data streams with bounded memory independent of stream length.

title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
summary: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.

AI.tldr: This paper shows a module-level double dissociation between declarative and procedural learning in Transformers and demonstrates that module stability does not mirror plasticity.
AI.motivation: Continual learning studies typically treat plasticity and stability at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, leading to divergent conclusions across settings.
AI.method: The authors study plasticity and stability across Transformer modules (QK, VO, MLPs) and task types (declarative memorization versus procedural tasks) in a controlled synthetic environment, followed by targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments and validation on a realistic model.
AI.result: QK and VO projections are most plastic on procedural tasks while MLPs are most plastic on declarative memorization; however, when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of stored declarative memory whereas updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths.
AI.conclusion: Plasticity tracks a module's suitability for primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways existing capabilities rely on that module, offering a task-dependent, module-level view of continual learning.

title: Conformally Calibrated Adaptive Computation in Neural Operators
comment: 27 pages, 7 figures
summary: Selecting less computation in a neural operator need not reduce inference time. We study this gap using conformal calibration to choose Fourier modes or channel width per input subject to a fixed error budget. A triangle-inequality envelope bounds all candidates simultaneously; a direct-score rule handles non-monotone candidate errors and, with an input-independent score, calibrates a static baseline under the same marginal guarantee. Under frozen-model and exchangeability assumptions, both rules bound the probability of issuing a prediction outside the budget and abstain when calibration is infeasible. On Burgers and Darcy flow across three training seeds, mode selection reduces active spectral support without a measurable latency reduction, because full-grid transforms and channel mixing dominate the cost. Narrowing channels does reduce Darcy forward cost, but reference-based selection must first compute the dense prediction. An input-only binary width selector avoids that pass and runs at 0.52-0.95 times dense latency; yet static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, and on a separately generated 1,000-example test set they generally achieve higher coverage, while the selector falls below its 90% target in more than half of the settings. Adaptive computation in neural operators should therefore be judged by achieved coverage and complete runtime against a matched static comparator.

AI.tldr: This paper uses conformal calibration to study adaptive Fourier-mode and channel-width selection in neural operators, finding that adaptive selectors often fail to outperform matched static baselines in runtime and coverage.
AI.motivation: Selecting less computation in a neural operator does not necessarily reduce inference time, creating a gap between theoreticalFLOP savings and actual latency under error budgets.
AI.method: The authors apply conformal calibration (using a triangle-inequality envelope for monotone errors and a direct-score rule for non-monotone errors) to select Fourier modes or channel widths per input on Burgers and Darcy flow across three seeds.
AI.result: Mode selection reduces active spectral support without measurable latency reduction; an input-only binary width selector on Darcy runs at 0.52-0.95x dense latency, but static widths calibrated under the same rule are often as fast or faster, achieve higher coverage on a 1,000-example test set, and avoid the selector's failure to meet its 90% target in over half the settings.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive computation in neural operators should be evaluated by achieved coverage and complete end-to-end runtime against a matched static comparator.

title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model generation by verifying multiple draft tokens in a single target-model pass. However, better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations do not necessarily produce faster generation. To examine this gap, we present FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training), an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions jointly affect acceptance and latency. Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, we first examine how training translates into accepted tokens. Backpropagating through predicted-feature rollouts with greater weight on early steps improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, yet average rollout proxy cross-entropy does not reliably rank drafters by acceptance. Beyond prediction quality, the placement of draft candidates also matters: with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, replacing static allocation with confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from $1.46\times$ to $2.02\times$ on HumanEval and from $1.31\times$ to $1.75\times$ on MT-Bench. This allocation benefit extends to an independently trained drafter, but stronger training does not consistently amplify it, showing that the two improvements do not necessarily reinforce each other. Even these speed gains depend on execution conditions: changing only host-thread settings can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance. Together, these findings show why training and allocation must be evaluated jointly using both acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.

AI.tldr: FACT is an experimental framework showing that drafter training, candidate allocation, and execution conditions must be evaluated jointly to realize end-to-end latency speedups in speculative decoding.
AI.motivation: Better draft predictions and longer accepted continuations in speculative decoding do not necessarily translate into faster generation.
AI.method: Using a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding, FACT evaluates cross-step rollout training with early-step weighting, confidence-guided candidate allocation under a fixed 256-node budget, and host-thread execution settings.
AI.result: Early-weighted rollout training improves acceptance by 15-24% over uniformly weighted detached training, confidence-guided allocation increases speedup over autoregressive decoding from 1.46x to 2.02x on HumanEval and 1.31x to 1.75x on MT-Bench, but stronger training does not consistently amplify allocation gains and host-thread changes can nearly eliminate speedup without changing acceptance.
AI.conclusion: Speculative decoding methods should be evaluated jointly on both token acceptance and end-to-end latency under controlled execution conditions.

title: AllotNet: an Interpretable Mixture-of-Experts Choice Model for Moral Judgement in Humanitarian Aid Allocation, Validated against a Planted Synthetic Population
comment: 83 pages, 16 figures, 36 tables. Public version: the elicitation instrument's scoring specification, the planted ground truth and per-criterion results are withheld under the study's pre-registration embargo (until 1 August 2030). A companion paper reports the designed-society simulation of allocation rules
summary: Official development assistance fell by 23.1 per cent in 2025, and the decision of who is helped first when there is not enough for everyone is moving into software. A leading published machine-learning targeting system excluded 53 per cent of eligible households as deployed. If the rule of distribution ends up in code, it should carry the judgement of many cultures, and the machine should execute while a person judges. AllotNet is an interpretable mixture-of-experts conditional logit for the allocation judgements elicited by Allot, a pre-registered six-language instrument: eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria, weighted by a gate over participant context, with a damped residual, an encoder for household intake, an outcome head and a budget-constrained planner that builds a review queue and never rejects anyone. A model of human judgement has no answer key on real data, so we wrote one first: a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions and 104 million responses (98 million usable choices), generated by the production code path from a ground truth hidden from the loss. All sixteen pre-specified checks passed: criterion ranking $\rho = 1.000$, hidden segments recovered (ARI 0.671), outcome head at 99 per cent of the noise ceiling, planner at 99.4 per cent of oracle. The caveats are reported with them: two checks are weaker than their titles, and a live-generation failure cost 260,712 seeds. The model has 23,550 parameters, is trained quantisation-aware for NVFP4 with its interpretable core in fp32 (welfare-rank parity $\rho = 0.9937$ at W4A16 on the shipped bundle; one parity threshold was relaxed post hoc), and ships as a 125 KB bundle with C11, Java, Rust and Python runtimes. Nothing has been trained on real data yet; at the study's real scale a hierarchical Bayesian mixed logit is the registered comparator.

AI.tldr: AllotNet is an interpretable 23,550-parameter mixture-of-experts conditional logit model for moral judgement in humanitarian aid allocation, validated on a 5.6-million-session planted synthetic population.
AI.motivation: Algorithmic targeting in humanitarian aid can exclude eligible households, so allocation rules encoded in software should reflect diverse cultural judgements while keeping humans in the loop.
AI.method: AllotNet combines eight linear taste experts over seven ethical criteria weighted by a participant-context gate, a damped residual, an intake encoder, an outcome head, and a budget-constrained planner, trained quantization-aware for NVFP4 as a 125 KB bundle.
AI.result: On a planted synthetic population of 5.6 million sessions (98 million usable choices), all 16 pre-specified checks passed, including criterion ranking rho=1.000, hidden segment recovery ARI=0.671, outcome head at 99% of noise ceiling, planner at 99.4% of oracle, and W4A16 welfare-rank parity rho=0.9937, though no real data has been trained yet.
AI.conclusion: AllotNet provides a compact, interpretable, and multi-runtime-ready architecture for modeling human allocation judgements, pending real-data evaluation against a hierarchical Bayesian mixed logit.

title: DuoCL: Dual-Path Online Continual Learning
comment: Technical Report
summary: Online continual learning (OCL) requires learning from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of model training speed. When training cannot keep pace, computationally expensive gradient-based methods update less frequently, limiting adaptation. Analytic methods reduce this overhead, but their frozen backbones cannot adapt representations to changing distributions. We propose DuoCL, a dual-path OCL framework whose fast analytic path accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch while its slow path periodically adapts the backbone. The slow path adjusts its sample count to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning. Feature alignment compensates for drift in the accumulated classifier statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline in each setting. DuoCL consistently outperforms analytic learning under distribution shifts, with gains of up to 4.00 percentage points on CIFAR-C, and achieves higher accuracy than prior methods across disjoint class-incremental, domain-incremental, and Si-Blurry settings.

AI.tldr: DuoCL is a dual-path online continual learning framework that pairs a fast analytic path with a slow budget-adaptive gradient path, outperforming gradient-based and analytic baselines.
AI.motivation: In online continual learning, gradient-based methods update too infrequently when data arrives faster than training, while analytic methods use frozen backbones that cannot adapt to distribution shifts.
AI.method: DuoCL accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch on a fast analytic path while a slow path periodically adapts the backbone within the available compute budget, using feature alignment to compensate for classifier statistic drift.
AI.result: Across four datasets and three compute budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gradient-based baseline, outperforms analytic learning by up to 4.00 percentage points on CIFAR-C under distribution shift, and leads across disjoint class-incremental, domain-incremental, and Si-Blurry settings.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling fast analytic accumulation from budget-aware backbone adaptation with feature alignment enables effective online continual learning under varying compute constraints.

title: Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients for Stable Feature Attribution
comment: 36 pages, 19 figures, 27 tables, including the appendix
summary: Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients (IG) are widely used to interpret neural networks, yet imperceptible input perturbations can drastically alter their attribution maps while leaving model predictions unchanged. We introduce Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients (ERIG), a path-based attribution method that intrinsically attenuates gradient irregularities along the integration path using maximum-entropy softmax weighting with temperature parameter $\tau$. We quantify the effect of the entropy-regularized weighting on attribution stability by using the Lipschitz properties of the model and its gradients. We decompose the attribution change under an input perturbation into a model-response term, whose bound is $\tau$-independent, and a weight-variation term, whose bound decreases at rate $\mathcal{O}(1/(2\tau))$. Their ratio $R(\tau)$ characterizes the trade-off between gradient information and attribution stability. We further add a new dimension to attribution evaluation by adapting classical noise estimators into two metrics, LINV-C and LINV-P, that quantify attribution noise. Across eleven CNN and Transformer backbones on ImageNet and Oxford-IIIT Pet datasets, our experiments show that, relative to the next-best method, ERIG remains comparable on ranking-based fidelity metrics while improving localization by approximately 24% and attribution stability by approximately 47-fold on average, reaching up to four orders of magnitude improvement over IG, all at negligible additional computational cost.

AI.tldr: Entropy-Regularized Integrated Gradients (ERIG) stabilizes path-based feature attribution using maximum-entropy softmax weighting, improving localization and stability at negligible extra cost.
AI.motivation: Path-based attribution methods such as Integrated Gradients (IG) suffer from drastic attribution map changes under imperceptible input perturbations that leave model predictions unchanged.
AI.method: ERIG attenuates gradient irregularities along the integration path via maximum-entropy softmax weighting with temperature tau, decomposes attribution change into model-response and O(1/(2*tau)) weight-variation terms, and introduces two noise metrics, LINV-C and LINV-P.
AI.result: Across 11 CNN and Transformer backbones on ImageNet and Oxford-IIIT Pet, ERIG matches next-best methods on ranking-based fidelity while improving localization by ~24% and attribution stability by ~47-fold on average (up to four orders of magnitude over IG) at negligible compute cost.
AI.conclusion: Maximum-entropy path weighting provides a principled, computationally cheap way to trade off gradient information and attribution stability in path-based explanations.

title: JEPA as a Transferable Optimizer: Learning and Understanding Black-Box Optimization from Reward-Agnostic Pretraining
summary: Black-box optimization evaluates candidates through simulations, rollouts, or experiments, often without gradients. Learned optimizers are usually judged by whether they outperform existing methods. We ask a complementary question: what information does a learned optimizer use from its search history? We introduce JEPA-PS (JEPA Policy Search), based on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It is pretrained on random rollouts using parameter vectors and scalar returns. Its latent-prediction objective predicts the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than its reward or gradient, allowing us to examine what was tried and how well it performed. At test time, JEPA-PS reads a short evaluation history and proposes a candidate in one forward pass, without task descriptions, reward shaping, or test-time gradients. We evaluate it on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, including evolutionary methods, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an LLM optimizer. JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines and outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost. It also transfers zero-shot to environments excluded from pretraining. Null-model comparisons and decoder-training ablations indicate that its latent representation carries information beyond simple history statistics; every trained decoder variant performs worse than the default frozen representation. Our main finding is that the history JEPA-PS uses depends on the task. On smooth landscapes it uses the full trajectory, whereas on rugged landscapes the best-seen point carries nearly all the signal. This memory requirement has a weak positive correlation with fitness-distance correlation (FDC; r=0.112, n=7), while an independent reward-ordering sensitivity probe does not corroborate the relationship (r=-0.024, n=7). Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: JEPA-PS is a reward-agnostic pretrained black-box optimizer that transfers zero-shot across control tasks and reveals that learned optimizers use full trajectories on smooth landscapes but mainly the best-seen point on rugged ones.
AI.motivation: Learned black-box optimizers are usually judged only by benchmark performance, leaving open what information they actually extract from search history.
AI.method: JEPA-PS uses a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture pretrained on random rollouts to predict the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than rewards or gradients, proposing candidates in one forward pass at test time.
AI.result: Evaluated on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines, beats an LLM optimizer by over 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost, and transfers zero-shot; ablations show it uses full history on smooth landscapes and mainly the best-seen point on rugged landscapes.
AI.conclusion: Reward-agnostic latent trajectory prediction yields a transferable black-box optimizer and exposes how landscape structure governs history utilization.

title: Label-Free Role-Aware Segmentation of Classroom Recordings: Recovering the Teacher from Transferable Structure
comment: Accepted at the AAAI track is IAAI (Innovative Applications of AI)
summary: How much the teacher talks and when are among the most informative and costly-to-measure signals of teaching. Yet, classroom audio is among the most sensitive data an AI system can process: recordings capture minors and fall under GDPR, preventing raw audio from leaving the recording device. We present a teacher-student segmentation pipeline designed to meet exactly this constraint: label-free at inference, running on a recording device, and requiring no per-session calibration. The pipeline chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compactly pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role based on session-relative structure rather than voice identity. We show that our structural cue transfers across classrooms, languages, and acoustic conditions. In leave-one-teacher-out cross-validation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers across English and German corpora, our pipeline achieves teacher F1 of 0.81 and 0.87, respectively, outperforming both enrollment-based baselines and a 30-second supervised enrollment ceiling. On a commodity smartphone, its performance matches pyannote, a strong neural diarization tool, while running 4.8x faster at comparable peak memory at a real-time factor of ~0.18. We also find that transcribing filtered audio only marginally increases teacher's word error rate from $0.26$ to 0.28. Residual failures concentrate where teacher and student voices are not acoustically separable. However, we show how to flag these sessions label-free at inference so that they can be routed to human review, enabling selective, privacy-preserving deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an on-device, label-free pipeline for teacher-student classroom audio segmentation that matches neural diarization accuracy while running 4.8x faster on a smartphone.
AI.motivation: Classroom audio is subject to strict privacy constraints such as GDPR that prevent raw audio from leaving the recording device, yet measuring teacher talk time is valuable for understanding teaching.
AI.method: The pipeline chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compactly pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role using session-relative structure rather than voice identity, plus label-free flagging of inseparable sessions.
AI.result: In leave-one-teacher-out cross-validation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers across English and German corpora, it achieves teacher F1 of 0.81 and 0.87, outperforming enrollment baselines, matching pyannote on a smartphone while running 4.8x faster (RTF ~0.18), and increasing transcription WER only from 0.26 to 0.28.
AI.conclusion: Session-relative structural cues enable accurate, privacy-preserving, and real-time teacher-student segmentation on commodity mobile devices.

title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
summary: Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincaré inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincaré constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

AI.tldr: This paper circumvents path-space analyses to show that reverse diffusion error accumulation is mitigated when the target distribution satisfies a Poincare inequality, nearly matching information-theoretic limits.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical analyses bound reverse diffusion sampling error via the entire path law, causing total variation error to accumulate polynomially with the horizon.
AI.method: The authors avoid path-space bounds and develop a framework that relaxes total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing statistics that do not witness multimodality, specializing to total variation when the target distribution satisfies a Poincare inequality.
AI.result: Under a bounded Poincare constant, the reverse diffusion sampler mitigates horizon error accumulation and nearly achieves the information-theoretic optimal total variation error given a learned score error bound.
AI.conclusion: Moving beyond path-space analyses explains why diffusion samplers remain accurate over long horizons and establishes their near-optimality under Poincare inequalities.

title: EEG2MCU: Sensing-to-Execution Co-Design for Wearable EEG Inference
comment: 7 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at DATE 2027
summary: Wearable EEG inference is constrained not only by model size, but also by the channel-dependent sensing front end that must process high-dimensional inputs before compact downstream computation. We present EEG2MCU, a sensing-to-execution co-design framework that treats electrode count as a hardware design variable through task-aware montage selection. EEG2MCU retains a compact time-frequency representation and generates only the INT8 regions required by each first-layer tile, avoiding full input materialization. Halo reuse and access-aware placement across Flash, SRAM, and tightly coupled memory further reduce redundant generation and data movement. On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x relative to the baseline, including a 1.71x reduction from the 62-to-19 electrode montage, while reducing latency by 2.57x and energy by 2.48x. It retains 94-96% of full-montage accuracy, demonstrating practical high-dimensional EEG inference under tight embedded-resource constraints.

AI.tldr: EEG2MCU is a sensing-to-execution co-design framework for wearable EEG inference that reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x, latency by 2.57x, and energy by 2.48x on a Cortex-M7 MCU.
AI.motivation: Wearable EEG inference on microcontrollers is bottlenecked not only by model size but also by high-dimensional channel-dependent sensing front ends and input materialization.
AI.method: EEG2MCU treats electrode count as a hardware design variable via task-aware montage selection, retains a compact time-frequency representation, generates only INT8 regions needed per first-layer tile, and uses halo reuse and access-aware memory placement across Flash, SRAM, and TCM.
AI.result: On a Cortex-M7 MCU, EEG2MCU reduces peak SRAM by 11.38x (including 1.71x from a 62-to-19 electrode montage), latency by 2.57x, and energy by 2.48x while retaining 94-96% of full-montage accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing electrode montage selection with tiled, memory-aware execution enables practical high-dimensional EEG inference on tightly constrained MCUs.

title: Agent Verifiers in Counterfactual Analysis: A Pilot Study Benchmarking Agentic Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development
summary: Agents can expand the covariate space of randomized experiments by retrieving fast-moving local context missed by slow-changing survey baseline covariates, helping characterize who benefits most from an intervention. Verifying such covariates is difficult: individual treatment effects are unobserved, retrieval leakage can pull post-treatment information into nominally pretreatment summaries, and encoder leakage can inject post-treatment pretraining knowledge into representations even after temporal filtering of inputs. Guided by a two-channel information bound separating summary provenance from encoder weights, we propose a three-layer benchmark protocol: (i) retrieval admissibility via pre-treatment date filtering; (ii) heterogeneity validation scored rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs); and (iii) encoder admissibility checked with chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, we compare session-isolated retrieval (sandboxed, bounded-budget agent runs per study) against a persistent workspace teammate (xAI's GrokBot) that builds one date-verified corpus per study while blinded to outcomes. The workspace teammate yields higher mean RATE ratios in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates. Even on fixed retrieved text, encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal. Chronologically vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, but single-record adapter perturbation analyses show that memorized future facts, once present, persist until injected noise degrades model output. Temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient: verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly examining source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a three-layer benchmark protocol to verify agent-generated covariates in counterfactual analysis against retrieval and encoder leakage across 11 datasets.
AI.motivation: Agents can enrich randomized experiments with fast-moving local context, but verifying such covariates is hard due to unobserved individual treatment effects, retrieval leakage of post-treatment data, and encoder pretraining leakage.
AI.method: Guided by a two-channel information bound, the authors propose a three-layer protocol checking retrieval admissibility (pre-treatment date filtering), heterogeneity validation via rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs), and encoder admissibility via chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations.
AI.result: Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, a persistent workspace teammate (GrokBot) yields higher mean RATE ratios than session-isolated retrieval in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7/11 for combined features without universal dominance, while encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal and memorized future facts persist under adapter perturbation until noise degrades output.
AI.conclusion: Temporal filtering of retrieval alone is insufficient; verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly auditing source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.

title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
summary: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an information-theoretic framework separating storage from expression to explain benign overfitting and provide a label-free model-selection criterion.
AI.motivation: Neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds based on label storage explain how overparameterized interpolators fit noisy labels yet generalize well.
AI.method: The authors distinguish storage (information retained about training labels, shown to be nH(Y|X) bits for every interpolator) from expression V (entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input), bounding excess risk via V and modal bias and estimating V from two disjoint halves for label-free model selection.
AI.result: Across 15 noisy datasets, V-based selection achieves 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost, matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost, and beats conditional mutual information selection at matched cost.
AI.conclusion: Vanishing expression characterizes benign overfitting across diverse interpolators and yields a practical, label-free model-selection criterion.

title: FairPGT: Partitioned Graph Transformers for Dual-Level Fair Graph Clustering
comment: Under review. 36 pages, 8 figures, 5 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Clustering on attributed graphs can produce demographically biased clusters, particularly when communities align with protected groups. Graph transformers can amplify this bias through same-group attention, while global attention limits scalability. We propose FairPGT, a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering. FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions and connects them through routing tokens, which divides the quadratic cost of attention by the number of partitions. A graph-aware self-training target guides clustering, with a provably bounded deviation from the standard DEC target. Fairness is imposed at two levels: a mutual-information term promotes demographic parity in cluster assignments, while a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) guides attention toward group neutrality through self-distillation. We prove that the nCGAR correction moves attention toward neutrality and establish a condition preventing overshooting. Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (Credit, Pokec-n, Pokec-z), with a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than DMoN, and is Pareto-dominated on only one dataset. On controlled stochastic block models, FairPGT attains 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide. These graphs further show that, under strong alignment, assignment-level fairness alone makes the attention group-heterophilous, whereas attention-level fairness alone improves neutrality without ensuring fair clusters. Code for reproducibility is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FairPGT is a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering that achieves state-of-the-art clustering and statistical parity on large attributed graphs.
AI.motivation: Attributed graph clustering can produce demographically biased clusters when communities align with protected groups, while global attention in graph transformers limits scalability.
AI.method: FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions connected via routing tokens to divide quadratic attention cost, uses a graph-aware self-training target, and enforces dual-level fairness via a mutual-information term on cluster assignments and a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) for attention neutrality.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on Credit, Pokec-n, and Pokec-z (with a statistical-parity gap ~10x lower than DMoN), and reaches 97% of the derived NMI upper bound on controlled stochastic block models.
AI.conclusion: Combining partitioned attention with dual-level assignment and attention fairness enables scalable, demographically fair graph clustering.

title: Toaster: Nonlinear Memory from Cascaded Linear Memories and Target Propagation
summary: Recurrent memories let language models process long sequences with a fixed-size state. Linear memories such as DeltaNet and KDA store one matrix and take one delta-rule step per token. The product of a chunk of such steps has an exact WY form, so they train fast. Deep memories such as TTT-MLP and Titans store a small MLP, which can hold maps that no matrix can, but their update has no WY form. Toaster bridges the two by building on a known fact: a gradient step on a linear layer is a delta-rule write. It builds a two-layer nonlinear memory from two linear memories with an activation between them. We use target propagation to give the hidden memory its values by projecting the output error back through the second memory. Given a chunk's cross-layer signals, approximated once per chunk, each layer can then run on an unmodified delta-rule kernel. Our default runs this kernel on the output layer and updates the hidden layer once per chunk. Running it on both layers gives a better model in our ablation. At matched backbones and training-token budgets, Toaster has lower loss than KDA at all five tested sizes (0.2B-1.6B non-embedding parameters) on both C4 and PG19. Its C4 perplexity also matches or slightly improves on the attention baseline at every size. At 1.2B it is also below Titans. In a 3:1 hybrid with global attention, the Toaster hybrid has the lowest perplexity of the four hybrids tested, and it is 0.18 (C4) and 0.44 (PG19) below the attention baseline. At the largest size, Toaster's mean three-shot accuracy on 13 tasks is 51.84%, compared with 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans. In length extrapolation, Toaster's loss stays below KDA's up to 20K tokens (5x the training length). On the 145M backbone, at a hidden width matched to Titans' memory, Toaster takes at most 1.33x KDA's training-step time and is 2.8-5.5x faster than the tested Titans configurations at 32K context.

AI.tldr: Toaster builds a two-layer nonlinear recurrent memory from cascaded linear memories and target propagation, outperforming KDA and Titans in perplexity, accuracy, and long-context speed.
AI.motivation: Linear recurrent memories like DeltaNet and KDA train fast via exact WY forms but lack expressivity, whereas deep memories like Titans and TTT-MLP are more expressive but lack WY forms and are slower.
AI.method: Toaster stacks two linear memories with an activation between them and uses target propagation to project output errors back to the hidden memory once per chunk, allowing both layers to run on unmodified delta-rule kernels.
AI.result: Across 0.2B-1.6B models on C4 and PG19, Toaster achieves lower loss than KDA, matches or beats attention on C4, outperforms Titans at 1.2B, reaches 51.84% 3-shot accuracy on 13 tasks (versus 50.52% for KDA and 50.04% for Titans), extrapolates to 20K tokens, and runs 2.8-5.5x faster than Titans at 32K context.
AI.conclusion: Cascading linear memories with chunk-level target propagation bridges the expressivity-efficiency gap between linear and deep recurrent memories.

title: Simpler Tiny Recursive Models
summary: Small models that execute deep looped computational graphs have shown great experimental results on puzzle-like problems like Sudoku, finding shortest paths through mazes, etc. The most well-known one is TRM (tiny recursive model), a simplification of HRM (hierarchical reasoning model). However, the underlying recursion is complicated and involves a high-level and a low-level state, a nested loop recursion, and the network calls with different input and output signatures depending on where we are in the loops. These mechanisms are needed to avoid memorization and overfitting. We propose STRM, a simplified design with a single state and a uniform update. STRM does not sacrifice generalization, improves training speed and final performance. Our key architectural choices that allow our simpler recursion to work are exponential moving updates on the states with varying rates that are jittered during training and readout of the solution on slow-updating channels only. We test STRM on Sudoku-Extreme, PPBench and Maze-Hard with the same data, parameters and compute as TRM: we improve over TRM by $3.8$ points on Sudoku-Extreme and $8.4$ points on PPBench and match it on Maze-Hard. On ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2, STRM improves over the published TRM results by $5.4$ and $0.5$ points. We will release our code upon acceptance of the paper.

AI.tldr: STRM simplifies Tiny Recursive Models (TRM) to a single state and uniform update using jittered exponential moving updates, improving speed and puzzle/ARC-AGI accuracy.
AI.motivation: TRM uses a complex nested-loop recursion with separate high-level and low-level states and varying call signatures to avoid memorization and overfitting.
AI.method: STRM replaces the nested recursion with a single state and uniform update, applying exponential moving updates with varying jittered rates during training and reading out solutions from slow-updating channels only.
AI.result: With matched data, parameters, and compute, STRM outperforms TRM by 3.8 points on Sudoku-Extreme and 8.4 points on PPBench, matches TRM on Maze-Hard, and improves over published TRM results by 5.4 and 0.5 points on ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2.
AI.conclusion: Jittered multi-rate exponential moving updates with slow-channel readout eliminate nested-loop complexity in recursive reasoning models while improving performance and training speed.

title: HypoLoop: Revising Weight-Editing Plans from Scientific Feedback
summary: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors. Effective updates depend on which parameters change and which errors drive the correction. We introduce HypoLoop, a family of native weight-editing methods that connects these choices to experimental feedback. Fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided policies produce editing plans; numerical solvers compute weight patches, and internal validation selects the deployed predictor. Successive observations and validation records support revisions to editable locations and fitting rules. Experiments cover 22 scientific tasks and both DeepSeek and Claude. On Burgers, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations. On DIODE, positive-residual weighting reduces absolute relative error (AbsRel) by 13.35% in internal cross-validation, with the same 33 editable coordinates. Revising the complete plan across rounds lowers final AbsRel by 10.59% relative to keeping the initial plan fixed. SpaceNet7 and Make3D connect accepted edits to improved spatial predictions. These results show how experimental evidence can shape the update problem itself. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: HypoLoop is a weight-editing framework that revises editable parameter locations and fitting rules from experimental feedback, reducing errors across 22 scientific tasks.
AI.motivation: Scientific experiments continually reveal prediction errors, and effective model updates depend on adapting which parameters are edited and which errors drive the correction.
AI.method: HypoLoop pairs fixed, numerically adaptive, and LLM-guided (DeepSeek, Claude) editing-plan policies with numerical weight-patch solvers and internal validation to iteratively revise editable locations and fitting rules across rounds.
AI.result: Across 22 scientific tasks, reallocating a matched parameter budget reduces Burgers error by 58.80% and 47.72% relative to fixed locations, positive-residual weighting cuts DIODE AbsRel by 13.35%, and multi-round plan revision lowers final AbsRel by 10.59%.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating experimental feedback to adaptively revise the weight-editing plan itself substantially improves scientific model updates.

title: Toward Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Neural AC Power Flow
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures. Accepted as an oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI Foundations for Power Grids: From Models to Deployment at Scale (AI4PowerGrids), Sydney, Australia
summary: Growing uncertainty in power system operations from renewables integration, extreme weather, and data center loads challenges the reliability of traditional power flow solvers at scale. Machine learning-based proxies are a potentially promising alternative, but the prohibitive cost of generating training data for large grids makes out-of-distribution generalization a key capability for deployment; currently, models trained on small grids lack that capability. In this work, we systematically evaluate how physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and perturbation-based data augmentation improve the zero-shot transfer of three graph neural network-based power flow models from smaller systems to a larger, unseen 500-bus system. We find that (1) physics-informed losses improve transfer relative to purely supervised objectives; (2) multi-grid training on smaller systems matches the best single grid but does not close the gap to target-grid training; (3) perturbation-based augmentation on edge attributes improves transfer by up to 54.6%; and (4) random line/generator dropout does not consistently improve performance.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, and data augmentation for zero-shot transfer of graph neural network AC power flow models to an unseen 500-bus grid.
AI.motivation: Generating training data for large power grids is prohibitively expensive, yet current ML power flow proxies trained on small grids fail to generalize out-of-distribution to larger systems.
AI.method: The authors evaluate three GNN-based power flow models trained on smaller systems and tested zero-shot on a 500-bus system, comparing purely supervised objectives, physics-informed losses, multi-grid training, edge-attribute perturbation augmentation, and random line/generator dropout.
AI.result: Physics-informed losses improve transfer over purely supervised objectives, multi-grid training on small systems matches the best single grid without closing the gap to target-grid training, edge-attribute perturbation improves transfer by up to 54.6%, and random line/generator dropout gives inconsistent results.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed objectives and edge-attribute perturbations are effective levers for zero-shot OOD transfer in neural AC power flow, though small-grid training alone still trails target-grid training.

title: Same Rank, Different Needs: Rethinking LoRA Redistribution in Federated Learning
summary: Federated low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables clients with different resource budgets to collaboratively fine-tune foundation models. To distribute an aggregated update within each client's rank budget, existing methods commonly retain its leading singular directions. However, directions that best reconstruct the update matrix need not best preserve its responses on a particular client's inputs: a lower-energy direction may matter more to that recipient. We formalize this mismatch and show that matrix-optimal truncation can incur arbitrarily larger response error than another readout of the same rank. Motivated by this result, we propose Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA), a plug-in framework for receiver-aware knowledge transfer. RASA uses compact diagonal input second moments to perform uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses. The resulting readout is globally optimal for the rank-constrained receiver objective and preserves at least as much response energy as spectral truncation under the diagonal metric. RASA also introduces spectral-reference aggregation, which removes the personalized initialization offset while retaining the locally learned increment. Experiments on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI demonstrate RASA's effectiveness across methods under resource, task, and data heterogeneity. In particular, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks with modest overhead.

AI.tldr: RASA is a receiver-aware subspace adaptation framework for federated LoRA that optimizes rank-constrained updates for each client's input distribution, outperforming spectral truncation.
AI.motivation: Existing federated LoRA methods distribute aggregated updates by retaining leading singular directions, which minimizes matrix reconstruction error but can incur arbitrarily large response errors on a specific client's inputs.
AI.method: Receiver-Aware Subspace Adaptation (RASA) uses compact diagonal input second moments to compute uncentered PCA of receiver-weighted update responses, combined with spectral-reference aggregation to remove personalized initialization offsets.
AI.result: Evaluated on DomainNet-100, NICO++, GLUE, and SuperNI, RASA improves DomainNet-100 accuracy by 3.23 percentage points with FlexLoRA and achieves gains of up to 8.33 ROUGE-L points on seen SuperNI tasks and 4.37 on unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: Aligning low-rank update truncation with each recipient client's input response geometry rather than global matrix norms improves federated LoRA under heterogeneity.

title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
comment: 5 pages total (ACM sigconf format). Companion code and trained models: this https URL
summary: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) across six seeds. DyGFormer shows corresponding training and history contrasts of 22.34 and 0.38 points across two seeds, despite greater exposure. Partial history permutations further separate nominal intervention strength, input changes, and aggregate accuracy. These comparisons turn a single permutation gap into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses, while leaving the internal mechanisms of temporal learning open.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a crossed diagnostic and input-exposure analysis to separate training-time and evaluation-history effects in timestamp-permutation tests for dynamic link prediction.
AI.motivation: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors use temporal information, but aggregate performance gaps conflate changes in training, evaluation history, and input exposure.
AI.method: The authors apply a crossed diagnostic separating training chronology from evaluation history and measure input exposure (whether altered histories change predictor inputs) on TCL and DyGFormer on MOOC.
AI.result: On MOOC, TCL gains ~8 pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history versus 0.03 points from changing history at fixed weights (68.37% unchanged inputs), with explicit time-encoding removal cutting the training contrast by 4.39 points; DyGFormer shows 22.34 training and 0.38 history contrasts.
AI.conclusion: Crossed diagnostics and input-exposure checks turn opaque timestamp-permutation gaps into interpretable statements about training conditions and model responses.

title: When Normal-Only Updates Are Not Enough: Test-Time Adaptation in Reconstruction-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practical TTA failures exhibit two distinct responses to this intervention, with 63 of 180 settings recovering a clear detection gain while 90 still show no clear detection gain; and (3) the updates reduce their immediate reconstruction objective across the evaluated settings, yet these reductions do not consistently lead to better anomaly ranking. Both failure patterns persist across alternative practical adaptation variants and modest perturbations of the benchmark labels. Together, these findings show that improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution to reconstruction-based TSAD TTA.

AI.tldr: A controlled study across nine benchmark families shows that restricting test-time adaptation updates to normal-labeled samples does not reliably improve reconstruction-based time-series anomaly detection.
AI.motivation: Online test-time adaptation (TTA) for time-series anomaly detection must filter out anomalies from incoming streams, raising the question of whether perfect normal-only sample selection is sufficient for reliable gains.
AI.method: The authors replace practical update selectors with an oracle rule using only benchmark-labeled normal samples while keeping the rest of online TTA unchanged across nine benchmark families, four optimizers, and five seeds.
AI.result: Using only normal-labeled samples does not reliably improve detection: 63 of 180 settings recover a clear gain while 90 still show no clear gain, and while updates reduce the immediate reconstruction objective, they do not consistently improve anomaly ranking.
AI.conclusion: Improving sample selection alone is not a complete solution for reconstruction-based time-series anomaly detection under test-time adaptation.

title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
comment: 57 pages, 17 figures, 7 tables. In the title, n-DAS denotes an optimizer of order n restricted to the dominant aligned subspace (DAS): 1-DAS for first-order and 2-DAS for second-order methods
summary: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), selected by gradient alignment rather than Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, and shows it matches full-space PINN training.
AI.motivation: Low-dimensional subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude fail to capture where neural network optimization moves because highest-curvature directions do not generally align with training steps.
AI.method: The authors construct DAS from a full Hessian eigendecomposition by selecting directions based on gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, testing DAS-restricted training with line search and Gauss-Newton on ill-conditioned PINN benchmarks (Poisson, heat, wave, viscous Burgers).
AI.result: DAS-restricted training with line search matches full-space training across all four benchmarks even when the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned.
AI.conclusion: Convergence in ill-conditioned landscapes depends on a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset of Hessian eigendirections rather than top curvature directions.

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
comment: 87 pages, 43 figures, including appendices and the NeurIPS paper checklist
summary: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TabBioMed is a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated biomedical tabular datasets evaluating 23 models, showing that optimal model choice depends strongly on data regime and compute budget.
AI.motivation: Evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, particularly for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance.
AI.method: TabBioMed unifies 94 public biomedical tabular datasets across eight domains (including EHR, drug discovery, and omics) with dataset-aware preprocessing and standardized evaluation across 23 classical, GBDT, neural, and tabular foundation models.
