AI.result: Tabular foundation models achieve the strongest family-level predictive performance overall, but their gains are regime-dependent, with tree-based models and tuned MLPs often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints.
AI.conclusion: TabBioMed provides a reproducible benchmark demonstrating that biomedical tabular model selection must account for data regime, task type, and computational budget.

title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
summary: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

AI.tldr: CAFE-AQI is a coverage-aware day-ahead AQI forecasting and warning framework that deduplicates trajectory records and uses conformal calibration, outperforming persistence in Bangladesh.
AI.motivation: Air quality forecasting often assumes city records are complete and independent, whereas an audit of Bangladesh data revealed a post-August 2022 coverage jump and 103 city labels mapping to only 61 unique AQI trajectories.
AI.method: CAFE-AQI weights identical trajectories, combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context, and adds a class-balanced warning head (AQI >= 151) with risk-conditional conformal calibration, evaluated chronologically (2022-2023 train, 2024 calibrate, 2025 test).
AI.result: On duplicate-balanced 2025 data, CAFE-AQI achieves 9.76 MAE (3.63 lower than persistence, 95% CI: 3.49-3.76), 15.04 RMSE, 0.910 R-squared, 0.908 F1 and 0.982 AUROC for unhealthy-air warnings, 92.09% coverage for nominal 90% intervals, and 10.66 MAE on an excluded spatial block.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for duplicate trajectories and coverage shifts enables accurate, well-calibrated day-ahead AQI forecasting and early warning.

title: Online State-Representation Adaptation under Synthetic Interaction-Cue Remapping
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Code and synthetic data are available at this https URL
summary: When cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned mapping may help an agent choose the appropriate action. We tested this in a one-step synthetic task by comparing a logistic state predictor that continued to learn from state labels with the same predictor frozen at transfer. We evaluated ten conditions in six held-out environments, with 1,296 paired runs per condition and 1,296,000 transfer records in total. Late action accuracy was 93.39% with online updates and 64.63% with frozen coefficients, a paired difference of 28.76 [8.73, 53.19] percentage points (95% environment-bootstrap interval). A direct policy reached 95.65% using the same predictions with a different action threshold. A contextual bandit reached 94.23% and earned more cumulative utility than the adaptive predictor. The bandit used the reward of its chosen action, which in this task reveals the true state when combined with that action. Weights based on development history lowered cumulative utility relative to neutral weights (difference -3.45 [-4.48, -2.43]). The adaptive predictor outperformed its frozen counterpart in late accuracy in each of the six test environments. The other comparisons show how the choice of action threshold and the information available in feedback affect what can be attributed to online adaptation.

AI.tldr: In a synthetic cue-remapping task across six held-out environments, online updates to a logistic state predictor raise late action accuracy from 64.63% to 93.39% over a frozen baseline.
AI.motivation: When interaction cues change what they predict, continuing to update a learned state mapping may help an agent act appropriately, but the effects of action thresholds and feedback structure need isolation.
AI.method: Across ten conditions in six held-out environments (1,296 paired runs per condition), the authors compare an online-updating logistic state predictor against a frozen predictor, a direct policy, and a contextual bandit.
AI.result: Online updates achieve 93.39% late action accuracy versus 64.63% for frozen coefficients (a 28.76 percentage-point difference), while a direct policy reaches 95.65% and a contextual bandit reaches 94.23% with higher cumulative utility; development-history weights lower utility by 3.45 relative to neutral weights.
AI.conclusion: Online state-representation adaptation consistently improves action accuracy under cue remapping, though action thresholds and reward feedback structure strongly influence overall utility.

title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
summary: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. Complete source removal increased reconstruction RMSE by 6.90% for electromyography-to-kinematics and 11.38% in the reverse direction. In contrast, cross-participant substitution increased RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67%, respectively, while the template reduced RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%. For POMA prediction, walking speed, age, and sex achieved an MAE of 3.693, compared with 4.229 and 4.427 after adding absolute and signed learned asymmetry, respectively. In all of the 20 repeated evaluations, all asymmetry representations performed worse than the covariate baseline. No localized learned feature remained significant after covariate adjustment and false-discovery-rate correction. The model mainly relied on shared gait-phase patterns, with no clear subject-specific coupling or added clinical value. Participant-level controls are therefore needed before reconstruction accuracy is treated as evidence of individualized physiology.

AI.tldr: Participant-level controls reveal that frozen bidirectional sEMG-kinematic models rely on shared gait-phase patterns rather than subject-specific neuromuscular coupling and fail to improve clinical POMA prediction.
AI.motivation: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction between sEMG and gait kinematics is often assumed to reflect subject-specific physiological coupling, but may instead reflect shared temporal patterns across participants.
AI.method: The authors test frozen bidirectional models on 82 able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants using complete source-modality removal, cross-participant source substitution, a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, and repeated nested cross-validation for POMA score prediction.
AI.result: Complete source removal increases RMSE by 6.90% (sEMG-to-kinematics) and 11.38% (reverse), whereas cross-participant substitution increases RMSE by only 1.68% and 1.67% and the template reduces RMSE by 2.89% and 0.55%; for POMA prediction, covariates alone achieve 3.693 MAE versus 4.229 and 4.427 with learned asymmetry.
AI.conclusion: Participant-level controls are essential before treating cross-modal reconstruction accuracy as evidence of individualized physiological coupling or clinical utility.

title: A Rank-One Bypass of Fixed Linear Erasure
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Child Safety in AI (poster). 10 pages, 3 figures
summary: Linear concept erasure can make a target unreadable to a specified family of linear classifiers applied to a model's current internal features. In an open-weight release, however, an attacker can modify the layers that produce those features. We study a fixed affine erasure layer whose upstream model is allowed to change. If the layer transmits even one direction visible to an allowed downstream classifier, the attacker can write a target score into that direction and carry it through the layer. We show that this condition is also necessary, and that for a nonconstant linear target score the required change is a rank-one affine update. Across six CIFAR-10 class-pair tasks, the route restores nearly all pre-erasure target performance and can leave a deployed benign linear head's scores unchanged to numerical tolerance. We then price the attack: with eight target labels and 2,000 unlabelled calibration examples, a 10% mean relative feature edit yields 79.8% test accuracy, which is 91.2% of the fitted score's gain over chance; tighter edit limits sharply reduce success. Linear guardedness therefore remains a valid guarantee about the current representation, but it is not by itself a tamper-resistance guarantee for an editable open-weight model.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a fixed linear concept-erasure layer in an open-weight model can be bypassed via a rank-one affine update to upstream features if any visible direction remains.
AI.motivation: Linear concept erasure makes a target unreadable to linear classifiers on current features, but open-weight attackers can modify upstream layers that produce those features.
AI.method: The authors analyze a fixed affine erasure layer with editable upstream weights, proving a necessary and sufficient condition for bypass via a rank-one affine update and pricing the attack under edit-norm budgets on CIFAR-10 class-pair tasks.
AI.result: Across six CIFAR-10 class-pair tasks, the rank-one update restores nearly all pre-erasure target performance while leaving benign linear head scores unchanged to numerical tolerance; with 2,000 unlabelled calibration examples and a 10% mean relative feature edit, it reaches 79.8% test accuracy (91.2% of fitted score gain over chance).
AI.conclusion: Linear guardedness guarantees protection only for the current representation and does not by itself provide tamper resistance for editable open-weight models.

title: Kernel Ridge Attention: Nonlinear Memory with Selective Forgetting
comment: 15 pages
summary: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.

AI.tldr: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a constant-state recurrent sequence mixer using recursive ridge regression and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck retention, outperforming attention and recurrent baselines in language modeling.
AI.motivation: Sequence models need nonlinear, adaptive memory that supports parallel training while maintaining a constant-size inference state independent of context length.
AI.method: KRA combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates via recursive ridge regression, uses a content-dependent Ornstein-Uhlenbeck transition for selective forgetting, and employs associative block maps and explicit adjoints for parallel training.
AI.result: In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput.
AI.conclusion: Recursive ridge regression with content-dependent retention provides a principled, scalable foundation for nonlinear recurrent sequence memory.

title: PGU-Decoder: Prior-Guided Unified Decoding for Industrial Road-Network Map Updating
comment: 11 pages. Accepted at KDD 2027, Applied Data Science (ADS) Track. This is the original submission version, prior to reviewer revisions
summary: Timely road-network map updates are essential to navigation and autonomous driving. Three key tasks are intra-intersection road network generation, merging/diverging detection, and drivable-area detection, covering topology, geometry, and attributes, respectively. Separate pipelines duplicate rule maintenance, quality assurance, and manual verification, increasing operational costs. We propose PGU-Decoder, a production-grade unified decoding framework for semantic prediction across these tasks. A Prior Query Module (PQM) constructs point-level prior queries from sampled locations on road-network geometries. Fixed reference points preserve positional priors throughout decoding, allowing the model to focus on surrounding context. Point-level representations are aggregated into instance-level representations, and a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT) captures inter-instance dependencies. Task-specific heads then generate predictions. We validate PGU-Decoder in large-scale automated road-network map updating across more than 360 cities in China, where it consistently outperforms seven baselines. Following deployment at AutoNavi Map, it achieves quality scores above 98% on all three tasks, reduces manual verification costs by 95%, and increases update frequency from weekly to hourly. These results demonstrate a practical and cost-effective industrial solution for road-network map updating.

AI.tldr: PGU-Decoder is a unified decoding framework for road-network map updating deployed at AutoNavi Map across 360+ cities, achieving >98% quality and cutting manual verification costs by 95%.
AI.motivation: Separate pipelines for intra-intersection road generation, merging/diverging detection, and drivable-area detection duplicate rule maintenance, quality assurance, and manual verification.
AI.method: PGU-Decoder uses a Prior Query Module (PQM) to build point-level prior queries from sampled road-network geometries with fixed reference points, aggregates them into instance representations, models inter-instance dependencies with a Relational Graph Attention Network (RGAT), and outputs predictions via task-specific heads.
AI.result: Across more than 360 cities in China, PGU-Decoder consistently outperforms seven baselines; deployed at AutoNavi Map, it achieves >98% quality scores on all three tasks, reduces manual verification costs by 95%, and increases update frequency from weekly to hourly.
AI.conclusion: Unifying topology, geometry, and attribute map-updating tasks around prior-guided relational decoding delivers major operational and quality gains at industrial scale.

title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
summary: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.

AI.tldr: OMNIS+ is a semantic RAN slicing and box-quantization framework for dynamic split neural networks in multi-cell edge computing, reducing QoS violation probability by up to 1.75.
AI.motivation: Existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models that cannot exploit dynamic semantic representations from modern split neural networks.
AI.method: OMNIS+ pairs dynamic neural compression with adaptive box quantization for bit-error resilience, solving interdependent mobile-device (branch/cell selection via causal contextual MAB under Lyapunov control) and edge-server (bandwidth, GPU frequency, MCS via block coordinate descent) optimization problems.
AI.result: Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy-violation trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing dynamic split neural compression, resilient quantization, and multi-cell RAN resource allocation improves edge inference reliability and accuracy.

title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book
comment: 65 pages (including appendix) , 2 figures, 20 tables
summary: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever new information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that asynchronous algorithmic market-making desks updating order distances via SGD-like rules with distinct lookback horizons induce power-law order-flow memory and rough volatility.
AI.motivation: Rough volatility can arise from near-unstable order flow with power-law memory decay, but it has been unclear how algorithmic market making generates such order flow.
AI.method: The authors model market makers as asynchronous desks using first-order gradient rules over distinct lookback horizons to adjust order distances toward oracle targets, taking a continuum limit to a conservative Dean-Kawasaki SPDE and validating on simulated agents and six months of Binance data (~790 million orders).
AI.result: The continuum limit yields power-law decaying order-flow memory and rough volatility via standard scaling arguments, and key predictions are confirmed on both agent simulations and Binance perpetual futures order books.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous, multi-horizon gradient-like quoting by algorithmic market makers provides a concrete microstructural mechanism for rough volatility.

title: From Data to Valves: A Self-Learning, Production-Grade Edge Stack for Sustainable HVAC Control
summary: Learned HVAC controllers rarely leave the simulator, and those that do are typically trained offline, frozen at deployment and retrained from the cloud. We present a production stack in which three learning components run on one NVIDIA Jetson Orin gateway per building, adapt continuously from the building's own data, and verify their own effect. (a) A compact transformer-encoder forecaster, one per equipment group with learned per-unit embeddings, predicts every air-side unit's next-cycle temperature and learns prequentially, one gradient step per five-minute cycle, behind five independent gates that bound the influence of any corrupt reading. (b) A distributional soft actor-critic agent, one shared policy across unit types, converts the measured state into a chilled-water valve position under a structural safety envelope that no learned component can soften; its second generation learns nightly on the device from recorded transitions alone, with a behaviour anchor and critic calibration terms, is scored by four model-free metrics and promoted by atomic hot-swap. (c) A change-point regression baseline held to ASHRAE Guideline 14 supplies the counterfactual against which savings are certified. On eighteen months of data from a hotel the forecaster converges from random weights within a week and reaches 0.37, 0.39 and 0.11 degree C MAE for air-handling, fresh-air and fan-coil units with no retraining event; on a different hotel the baseline reproduces a 46-day held-out period to within 0.07%. The RL agent has completed its in-simulator campaign and runs in shadow on 104 units; we report measured latency and memory of every service on a shared 15 GB device, the systems lessons of the campaign, and precisely what the evidence does and does not yet establish.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a self-learning edge stack running on a single 15 GB Jetson Orin per building for HVAC control, combining prequential temperature forecasting, offline-to-online RL, and ASHRAE counterfactuals.
AI.motivation: Learned HVAC controllers rarely leave simulation, and deployed ones are typically frozen offline models that require cloud retraining.
AI.method: The stack runs three components on a Jetson Orin: a gated prequential transformer-encoder forecaster updated every five minutes, a distributional soft actor-critic valve controller trained nightly on-device within a structural safety envelope, and an ASHRAE Guideline 14 change-point regression baseline.
AI.result: On 18 months of hotel data, the forecaster converges within a week to 0.37, 0.39, and 0.11 degree C MAE for air-handling, fresh-air, and fan-coil units; on a second hotel, the baseline reproduces a 46-day held-out period within 0.07%, and the RL agent runs in shadow on 104 units.
AI.conclusion: Continuous on-device learning with safety envelopes and counterfactual verification makes self-adapting HVAC control practical on resource-shared edge gateways.

title: Faster to the Wrong Answer: The Price of Local Updates in Federated Optimization
comment: 18 pages, 1 figure; includes supplementary proofs and reproduction code
summary: Local computation can improve the conditioning of federated updates but may also introduce bias, causing their fixed point to differ from the global minimizer. We characterize the minimum worst-case bias achievable under a prescribed conditioning bound. We consider strongly convex quadratic client objectives with Hessian eigenvalues in $[\mu,L]$ and local updates represented by a shared positive spectral filter. Client heterogeneity is measured by the root-mean-square gradient at the global minimizer. For a uniform surrogate condition number bounded by $\chi\in[1,L/\mu]$, we establish the exact worst-case bias per unit heterogeneity, $(L-\mu\chi)/(2\mu L\sqrt{\chi})$, and show that local gradient descent with sufficiently small step sizes and proximal updates attain this bound. Our analysis reduces populations of arbitrary dimension, including noncommuting Hessians, to distributions over scalar curvatures. This reduction provides optimality certificates and worst-case constructions involving at most three scalar clients. We further extend the sharp proximal bias bound to smooth strongly convex objectives beyond quadratics and quantify the error introduced by inexact local solves.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the exact worst-case bias of local updates in federated optimization under a prescribed conditioning bound, showing local GD and proximal updates attain it.
AI.motivation: Local updates improve conditioning in federated optimization but introduce bias that shifts the fixed point away from the global minimizer, and the optimal trade-off has not been sharply characterized.
AI.method: Analyzing strongly convex quadratic client objectives with Hessian eigenvalues in [mu, L] and local updates as a shared positive spectral filter, the authors reduce arbitrary-dimensional noncommuting populations to scalar curvature distributions and extend the proximal bound to smooth strongly convex objectives.
AI.result: For a surrogate condition number bounded by chi in [1, L/mu], the exact worst-case bias per unit heterogeneity is (L - mu*chi)/(2*mu*L*sqrt(chi)), attained by small-step local gradient descent and proximal updates, with worst-case constructions using at most three scalar clients.
AI.conclusion: This sharp characterization quantifies the fundamental conditioning-versus-bias trade-off of local updates in heterogeneous federated optimization.

title: Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts
summary: Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.

AI.tldr: Multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD) consolidates domain RL experts by replaying their logged training trajectories in order, beating on-policy distillation at roughly one-seventh of training compute.
AI.motivation: Consolidating domain RL experts via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) is expensive because the student must resample environments, query experts on every token, and suffer from final-expert drift.
AI.method: MRPD replays the experts' RL training logs in their original order, recomputing policy gradients on scored trajectories while distilling final experts' distributions at logged prefixes without environment sampling or reward-model calls.
AI.result: Across reasoning, search, and SQL agentic domains, MRPD produces the best student model, outperforming online RL baselines and surpassing MOPD at about one-seventh of expert training compute; ablations show log order matters more than data amount or rewards.
AI.conclusion: Expert RL training logs act as an effective curriculum, enabling cheap, quasi-on-policy multi-expert consolidation without environment interaction.

title: FDM+: A Framework for Constrained Control of the 2D Radiative Transport Equation
summary: Applying the frozen diffusion model (FDM) [29] to the constrained control of the 2D radiative transport equation presents several challenges. These include the dimensional difference between control variables and state functions, the resolution mismatch between traditional numerical solvers and deep learning models, and solution non-uniqueness. To address these obstacles, we propose a novel approach, FDM+, which includes three key improvements. Firstly, a decoupled prediction architecture is introduced to address the dimensional heterogeneity. Secondly, an efficient parameterization strategy resolves the resolution mismatch. Meanwhile, we derive a total error bound to analyze how the parameterization error and the model estimation error jointly affect the performance. Thirdly, the conditional distribution learned by the diffusion model is leveraged to perform design space exploration for multi-solution problems. A series of numerical experiments demonstrate that FDM+ outperforms existing methods in reconstruction accuracy and design flexibility.

AI.tldr: FDM+ adapts frozen diffusion models to constrained control of the 2D radiative transport equation via decoupled prediction, efficient parameterization, and conditional design-space exploration.
AI.motivation: Applying frozen diffusion models to 2D radiative transport equation control faces dimensional mismatch between controls and states, solver-model resolution mismatch, and solution non-uniqueness.
AI.method: FDM+ introduces a decoupled prediction architecture for dimensional heterogeneity, an efficient parameterization strategy with a derived total error bound, and conditional diffusion sampling to explore multiple solutions.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show that FDM+ outperforms existing methods in both reconstruction accuracy and design flexibility.
AI.conclusion: Decoupled architectures and resolution-aware parameterization make frozen diffusion models effective for constrained PDE control with non-unique solutions.

title: VESPA: Verifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to prevent agents from taking actions that are dangerous or destructive to their environment. This is especially important for safety-critical domains, such as robotics or autonomous driving. Formal verification can be used to prove agent safety through safety constraints. However, in practice, many policies do violate safety constraints, and thus are verified to be unsafe. Since the goal is to obtain a safe policy, we would need to retrain a new policy from scratch and then verify it again until a candidate happens to pass. Both training and verification are usually not cheap, which makes this process inefficient. We introduce VESPA ($\textbf{VE}$rifiable $\textbf{S}$ymbolic $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{A}$daptation), a framework for targeted fine-tuning of decision tree policies. We show that using counterexamples for policy adaptation can make existing unsafe policies safe, or at least make considerable progress towards safety. Targeted fine-tuning of the existing policy on those counterexamples enables it to learn how to avoid violating safety constraints. We thus use the result of a formal verification as a training signal for fine-tuning. On CartPole, VESPA raises the mean number of verified safe steps from 63.8 to at least 92.7, reaching after two iterations what the same loop without counterexamples reaches after ten. On MountainCarContinuous, VESPA turns an unsafe policy into a safe policy in 53 of 60 runs. We conclude that counterexamples from a verifier are an effective training signal, which can be utilized to systematically improve the safety of policies. Our implementation is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: VESPA uses counterexamples from formal verification to fine-tune unsafe decision-tree policies, turning unsafe policies safe on MountainCarContinuous and accelerating safe-step gains on CartPole.
AI.motivation: Formally verified RL policies often violate safety constraints, and retraining from scratch until a candidate passes verification is computationally expensive.
AI.method: VESPA (Verifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation) treats counterexamples produced by a formal verifier as a training signal for targeted fine-tuning of existing decision-tree policies.
AI.result: On CartPole, VESPA raises mean verified safe steps from 63.8 to at least 92.7, reaching in two iterations what retraining without counterexamples takes ten iterations to achieve; on MountainCarContinuous, it turns unsafe policies into safe ones in 53 of 60 runs.
AI.conclusion: Formal-verification counterexamples provide an efficient, targeted supervision signal for adapting unsafe symbolic policies toward provable safety.

title: UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations
summary: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.

AI.tldr: UCLIR learns independent unsupervised autoencoders over decomposed input parts with weight regularization, achieving competitive continual learning performance without replay.
AI.motivation: Regularization-based continual learning on a single shared representation suffers from interference across many tasks because dense connectivity distributes updates across the whole network.
AI.method: Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule, UCLIR decomposes inputs into components learned independently by separate autoencoders with unsupervised weight regularization, using a linear classifier at inference.
AI.result: On 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, and 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet, UCLIR achieves competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods.
AI.conclusion: Localizing parameter updates within independently learned representations reduces cross-task interference in unsupervised continual learning.

title: The 7th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2026): Summary and Results
summary: This report summarizes the seventh International Verification of Neural Networks Com- petition (VNN-COMP 2026), held as part of the Symposium on AI Verification (SAIV) co-located with the International Conference on Computer-Aided Verification (CAV) at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. The goal of the competition is to provide an objective comparison of the state-of-the-art methods in neural network verification, in terms of scal- ability and speed. Along this line, we used standard formats (ONNX for neural networks and VNNLIB for specifications), standard hardware (all tools are run by the organizers on AWS), and tool parameters provided by the tool authors. This report summarizes the rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned from this competition.

AI.tldr: This report summarizes the 7th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2026), held at SAIV co-located with CAV at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. It documents the competition rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned.
AI.motivation: The neural network verification community needs an objective, standardized comparison of state-of-the-art verification methods in terms of scalability and speed.
AI.method: Organizers ran all participating tools on standardized AWS hardware using ONNX for neural networks, VNNLIB for specifications, and tool parameters provided by the tool authors.
AI.result: The report presents the benchmark suite, participating verification tools, comparative performance results, and key lessons learned from VNN-COMP 2026.
AI.conclusion: VNN-COMP 2026 provides a standardized empirical baseline for assessing progress and remaining bottlenecks in neural network verification.

title: QuantAtlas-OM: Taming Neural Spectral Bias in Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Ocean Dynamics
summary: Autoregressive neural networks exhibit spectral bias in long-horizon spatiotemporal prediction. As rollouts progress, high-frequency details decay, blurring the predicted fields and destabilizing long-range forecasts. Ocean dynamics offer a particularly stringent test because kinetic energy is concentrated in mesoscale eddies and fronts spanning tens of kilometers. This degradation stems from coupling large-scale phase evolution and small-scale energy retention in a shared feature space. Evolution on a coarse grid smooths out high-wavenumber eddies, whereas evolution on a fine grid amplifies small-scale phase errors and triggers rollout instability. We introduce QuantAtlas-OM (QuantAtlas Ocean Model), a scale-spectral decoupling framework that confines deep temporal evolution to a low-wavenumber latent manifold for long-term stability while routing full-resolution eddy and front residuals through an outer bypass to the decoder. Across physical regimes, the evolution core pairs non-local attention with resolution-invariant dilated spatial gating. Across three western boundary currents, QuantAtlas-OM retains $43.7\%$ to $86.5\%$ of mesoscale spectral energy along the $k^{-3}$ cascade at Day $120$, sustains anomaly correlation coefficients of $0.81$ to $0.88$ at Day $60$, and reaches $0.66$ at Day $120$ in the Kuroshio ($2.5\times$ to $7.7\times$ the best baselines). Trained at $0.25^\circ$, QuantAtlas-OM transfers zero-shot to a global $0.125^\circ$ grid ($0.81$ Day-$10$ spatial correlation) and leads global $0.25^\circ$, $23$-level 3D ocean simulations ($120$ days) and coupled ocean-atmosphere forecasts ($60$ days), ranking first on $15$ of $16$ metrics and cutting $60$- to $120$-day salinity RMSE by $13\%$ to $27\%$ across global ocean basins.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces QuantAtlas-OM, a scale-spectral decoupling framework that mitigates spectral bias in long-horizon spatiotemporal ocean dynamics forecasting. It achieves strong 60- to 120-day forecast skill, zero-shot super-resolution transfer, and top rankings across 15 of 16 global ocean and coupled forecast metrics.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive neural networks suffer from spectral bias in long-horizon spatiotemporal prediction, where high-frequency mesoscale eddies and fronts decay or trigger rollout instability because large-scale phase evolution and small-scale energy retention are coupled in a shared feature space.
AI.method: QuantAtlas-OM confines deep temporal evolution to a low-wavenumber latent manifold for long-term stability while routing full-resolution eddy and front residuals through an outer bypass to the decoder, pairing non-local attention with resolution-invariant dilated spatial gating.
AI.result: Across three western boundary currents, QuantAtlas-OM retains 43.7% to 86.5% of mesoscale spectral energy along the k^-3 cascade at Day 120, sustains anomaly correlation coefficients of 0.81 to 0.88 at Day 60, and reaches 0.66 at Day 120 in the Kuroshio (2.5x to 7.7x the best baselines). Trained at 0.25 degrees, it transfers zero-shot to a 0.125-degree grid (0.81 Day-10 spatial correlation), ranks first on 15 of 16 metrics in 120-day global 3D ocean and 60-day coupled ocean-atmosphere forecasts, and cuts 60- to 120-day salinity RMSE by 13% to 27%.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling low-wavenumber temporal evolution from full-resolution residual pathways resolves spectral bias and enables stable, high-resolution long-horizon ocean and coupled climate forecasting.

title: Adaptive Action Horizon Selection via Flow-Field Uncertainty
comment: IEEE IROS 2026 Workshop
summary: Reliable uncertainty estimates are important for adaptive execution in vision-language-action (VLA) models. Existing approaches such as Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) estimate action entropy from multiple sampled action chunks, introducing additional inference cost and capturing both uncertainty within an action trajectory and diversity across alternative strategies. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC derives action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples. DUAC strongly correlates with AAC, while capturing distinct information: AAC measures global dispersion across sampled chunks, whereas DUAC measures local uncertainty around the trajectory selected for execution. Consequently, DUAC is less sensitive to diversity among distinct but valid action strategies. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably among the evaluated methods, combining strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency. These results establish the flow vector field as an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for robot decision making.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DUAC, a post-hoc method for extracting trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the flow vector field of a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model without multiple samples. It achieves strong task success with low uncertainty-estimation latency across robotic manipulation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Adaptive execution in VLA models requires reliable uncertainty estimates, but existing methods like Adaptive Action Chunking (AAC) sample multiple action chunks, incurring high inference cost and conflating trajectory uncertainty with diversity across valid strategies.
AI.method: Building on a closed-form flow-posterior covariance formulation, DUAC computes action-level uncertainty scores from a single generated chunk using Jacobian-vector products on the pretrained VLA vector field, without retraining or multiple endpoint samples.
AI.result: DUAC strongly correlates with AAC while capturing local uncertainty around the selected trajectory rather than global dispersion across strategies, making it less sensitive to multi-modal strategy diversity. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa, DUAC-based adaptive horizon selection performs favorably, combining strong task success with low latency.
AI.conclusion: The flow vector field of pretrained VLAs provides an efficient, trajectory-conditioned source of predictive uncertainty for adaptive robot decision making.

title: Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning
summary: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves conflicts between continual learning and machine unlearning by partitioning network weights at the individual synapse level. LwU matches or outperforms strong baselines across continual learning, machine unlearning, and dangerous content removal tasks.
AI.motivation: Integrating continual learning (acquiring new knowledge without forgetting) and machine unlearning (removing specific knowledge without harming the rest) in one system is difficult because both objectives modify the same weights and interfere with each other.
AI.method: LwU scores every weight against both retained and deleted data and partitions the network into four zones: retention-only weights are frozen, deletion-only weights are cleared and freed, contested weights take gradient-ascent steps projected orthogonally to the retention gradient, and remaining capacity learns new tasks via self-distillation from a privileged teacher without retraining.
AI.result: Across continual learning and machine unlearning benchmarks, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baselines, demonstrates practicality on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset, and outperforms the closest baseline in image generation and dangerous content removal.
AI.conclusion: Synaptic role partitioning enables simultaneous continual learning and post-hoc machine unlearning without retraining or destructive weight interference.

title: Continuous Noisy-Loop Models
comment: 51 pages, 7 figures
summary: Efficient learning and inference need not imply a compact probabilistic circuit. We quantify this distinction for continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with $d$ edges. With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is $\Theta(\min\{1,dN^{-2/3}\})$ from $N$ independent vectors, without a reliability lower bound. A spline estimator reaches this rate in polynomial arithmetic time given a fixed positive reliability bound; an exponential-size mixture removes that requirement. At fixed positive reliability, nonnegative decomposable circuits need $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt d))$ nodes for fixed total-variation error below one, even when each leaf uses at most $\alpha d$ coordinates, $0<\alpha<1$. Optimal Kullback--Leibler (KL) approximation error is $\Theta(d/\max\{\log d,\sqrt\ell\})$ in either direction with at most $d^r$ nodes and leaf scopes $\ell\leq\alpha d$, for fixed $r>1$ and $0<\alpha<2/3$. Node counts exclude leaf computation. For three fixed masks, optimal joint conditional KL has order $d/\log d$ when $\ell\leq(\log d)^2$. Local cycle identities relate joint divergence to identifiable channel products and separate weak-channel recovery from density estimation. Factorized evidence preserves a planar zero-field Ising model: given local integrals, exact queries cost $O(d^{3/2})$ arithmetic operations and one root extraction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies continuous noisy-loop models on a square grid, establishing minimax density estimation rates and proving exponential lower bounds on the size of nonnegative decomposable probabilistic circuits. It shows that efficient learning and inference do not guarantee compact circuit representations.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether problems that admit statistically and computationally efficient learning and inference also admit compact probabilistic circuit representations.
AI.method: The authors analyze continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with d edges, deriving minimax squared Hellinger risk rates, polynomial-time spline estimators, and lower bounds on nonnegative decomposable circuit size and Kullback-Leibler (KL) approximation error under bounded leaf scopes.
AI.result: With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is Theta(min{1, d N^(-2/3)}), achieved in polynomial arithmetic time by a spline estimator under a fixed positive reliability bound. However, nonnegative decomposable circuits require exp(Theta(sqrt(d))) nodes for fixed total-variation error below 1, and optimal KL error is Theta(d / max{log d, sqrt(ell)}) with at most d^r nodes and leaf scopes ell <= alpha d. Exact queries on factorized evidence cost O(d^(3/2)) arithmetic operations.
AI.conclusion: The results formally separate efficient statistical learning and exact inference from circuit compactness, showing that planar continuous noisy-loop models can be learned and queried efficiently despite requiring exponentially large decomposable circuits.

title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style tabular foundation models pretrained on synthetic data and evaluated on real-world datasets. It finds that synthetic and real-world scaling behaviors diverge and that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and compute.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models are pretrained on configurable synthetic data but evaluated on real-world datasets, raising the question of whether standard scaling laws reliably extrapolate and prescribe compute-optimal configurations across evaluation settings.
AI.method: Using the open-source nanoTabPFN training pipeline, the authors analyze scaling behavior across synthetic pretraining distributions, model sizes, compute budgets, and real-world evaluation sets.
AI.result: Synthetic and real-world scaling behaviors differ, and fitting a scaling law on too few evaluation datasets produces systematically over-optimistic prescriptions for unseen datasets. Expanding the maximum number of rows and features sampled during synthetic pretraining alongside model size and compute improves performance and yields more predictable scaling trends.
AI.conclusion: Reliable scaling prescriptions for tabular foundation models require diverse real-world evaluation suites and scaling synthetic pretraining dataset dimensions in tandem with model size and compute.

title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
comment: This paper is submitted to Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
summary: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GCN-SAGE-Residual) surrogate model for element-wise femoral stress prediction from finite element meshes. It outperforms 14 classical ML and baseline GNN models, achieving an R^2 of 0.8022 and MAE of 2.879 MPa.
AI.motivation: Finite element analysis (FEA) for biomechanical assessment of femoral strength is clinically limited by high computational cost, while conventional ML surrogates fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes.
AI.method: The authors propose GCN-SAGE-Residual, a hybrid GNN architecture combining graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across graph-structured finite element mesh elements.
AI.result: Evaluated across 14 models spanning classical ML and baseline GNNs plus an architectural ablation, GCN-SAGE-Residual achieves the strongest performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and a mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating mesh topology via hybrid GNNs provides a scalable and accurate surrogate for FEA-based orthopedic stress analysis and hip fracture risk assessment.

title: Supervised Hebbian Class Networks: Learning Without Backpropagation
summary: This paper introduces Supervised Hebbian Class Networks as a method for training multi- layer perceptrons and convolutional networks without gradient calculations or backpropa- gation. Each neuron in a learned layer is assigned a class, while connections follow the usual fully connected or convolutional pattern. The method combines a class-based supervision rule shared across layers with a Lion optimizer adapted to Hebbian activity products. All layers train together throughout the run, and their activities provide class predictions di- rectly, without a separately trained classifier. The experiments test the method on MNIST with a multilayer perceptron and on CIFAR-10 with a convolutional networ

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Supervised Hebbian Class Networks, a method for training multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks without gradient calculations or backpropagation. It evaluates the approach on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: Standard deep learning relies on backpropagation and gradient computation, motivating exploration of biologically inspired, gradient-free local learning rules.
AI.method: Each neuron in a learned layer is assigned a class within standard fully connected or convolutional topologies, and all layers train jointly using a shared class-based supervision rule combined with a Lion optimizer adapted to Hebbian activity products, with layer activities directly providing class predictions.
AI.result: The method is evaluated experimentally on MNIST using a multilayer perceptron and on CIFAR-10 using a convolutional network.
AI.conclusion: Supervised Hebbian Class Networks demonstrate that multilayer neural networks can be trained end-to-end for classification without backpropagation or separate classifier heads.

title: Structure-Preserving Neural Approximation of Convex, Semiconvex, and Quasiconvex Functions
summary: Input convex neural networks provide a natural way to enforce convexity globally through architectural constraints. We study how this structure-preserving approximation framework extends to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions. For $C^{1,1}$ convex functions on compact convex domains, we establish the sharp $W^{1,p}$ minimax rate $m^{-1/d}$ under max-affine approximation with $m$ affine pieces, and show that every max-affine function admits an exact bounded-width ICNN representation with complexity linear in $m$. The same $W^{1,p}$ approximation rate extends to semiconvex functions through quadratic lifting and to convex transformable functions through monotone composition. For general Lipschitz quasiconvex functions, we develop a quantitative finite-probe approximation theory based on monotone responses to affine projections and obtain a structure-preserving IqCNN with an $L^\infty$ approximation guarantee. We further show that these approximation results extend to ReLU-transferable smooth activations, including Softplus and ELU. Numerical experiments on PDE-based approximation problems compare the proposed architectures with parameter-matched MLPs and validation-tuned shape penalties, demonstrating global structural validity without penalty tuning while maintaining competitive approximation accuracy. Overall, the results identify recoverable convex latent structure as the key mechanism enabling gradient-level structure-preserving approximation beyond convexity.

AI.tldr: This paper extends structure-preserving neural approximation theory from convex functions to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions using Input Convex Neural Networks (ICNNs) and a new IqCNN architecture. It establishes sharp approximation rates and demonstrates global structural validity without penalty tuning on PDE-based problems.
AI.motivation: ICNNs enforce convexity globally via architectural constraints, but it has been unclear how to extend structure-preserving approximation guarantees to broader classes such as semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions.
AI.method: The authors establish sharp W^(1,p) minimax rates for max-affine and bounded-width ICNN representations of C^(1,1) convex functions, extend them to semiconvex functions via quadratic lifting and convex transformable functions via monotone composition, and introduce a structure-preserving IqCNN with L^infinity guarantees for Lipschitz quasiconvex functions, including ReLU-transferable smooth activations (Softplus, ELU).
AI.result: On PDE-based approximation problems, the proposed architectures achieve global structural validity without validation-tuned shape penalties while maintaining competitive approximation accuracy against parameter-matched MLPs and penalty-regularized baselines.
AI.conclusion: Recoverable convex latent structure is the key mechanism enabling gradient-level, structure-preserving neural approximation beyond strict convexity.

title: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification for Weather Forecasting: Conformal Prediction Under Spatiotemporal Dependence
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage and has begun to be applied to gridded weather forecasts. Marginal coverage concerns the long-run fraction of covered points at a location, not how coverage behaves jointly across space and time on a given day. I benchmark eight interval-construction procedures (Gaussian, pooled and per-cell split conformal, per-season, adaptive conformal inference and rolling windows) for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts at eight lead times from 6 hours to 10 days, using ERA5 at 5.625 degree resolution, a deliberately modest convolutional forecaster and ECMWF's operational HRES, with calibration in 2017-2018 and testing in 2019-2021. Alongside coverage, width and interval score, I report dependence diagnostics: a spatial overdispersion index, quantiles of daily spatial coverage and miss persistence relative to a shuffled-days null. Per-cell methods reach near-nominal marginal coverage, yet the day-to-day variance of the fraction of cells covered is roughly 3 to 10 times what independent cells would give, and misses cluster in time; both effects grow with lead time for the CNN, also appear for HRES, and are shared by all methods. An oracle that divides each day's normalised errors by that day's mean removes 81 to 92 percent of the excess dispersion for the CNN and 93 to 98 percent for HRES, so days of large errors across much of the grid account for most of it. A day-scale predicted from seasonal terms and already-verified errors lowers the overdispersion index without widening intervals but improves interval score by at most 0.6 percent; on HRES from 12 hours to 3 days it has the lowest overdispersion index while ACI or season-conditional calibration has the best interval score, so no method is best on both. The study covers one variable, one coarse grid, a reanalysis target and two forecasters.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks eight conformal and Gaussian uncertainty quantification methods for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts on ERA5 and ECMWF HRES, introducing spatiotemporal dependence diagnostics. It finds that per-cell methods achieve nominal marginal coverage but exhibit 3x to 10x excess daily spatial variance and temporal miss clustering.
AI.motivation: Conformal prediction guarantees long-run marginal coverage at individual locations, but its joint behavior across space and time on a given day in gridded weather forecasts is poorly understood.
AI.method: The author benchmarks eight interval-construction methods (Gaussian, pooled and per-cell split conformal, per-season, adaptive conformal inference, and rolling windows) on 6-hour to 10-day 2 m temperature forecasts (ERA5 at 5.625 degrees, a CNN, and ECMWF HRES; calibrated 2017-2018, tested 2019-2021) using spatial overdispersion, daily spatial coverage quantiles, and miss persistence.
AI.result: Per-cell methods reach near-nominal marginal coverage, but daily covered-cell variance is 3 to 10 times higher than under spatial independence, and misses cluster in time. An oracle daily-error scaling removes 81-92% (CNN) and 93-98% (HRES) of excess dispersion, while a causal day-scale predictor lowers overdispersion without widening intervals and improves interval score by at most 0.6%.
AI.conclusion: No single conformal method optimizes both interval score and spatial overdispersion, highlighting the need for spatiotemporal dependence-aware calibration in operational weather forecasting.

title: OpenGNS: An Open Dataset of the Gradient Noise Scale across Vision, Language, and Diffusion Models
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at AutoML 2026 (Oral)
summary: The Gradient Noise Scale (GNS) metric measures the signal-to-noise ratio of gradients in stochastic gradient descent and, as shown by McCandlish et al. (2018), can be used to approximate the Critical Batch Size (CBS) during neural network training. Despite its appearance in technical reports of frontier models, no open dataset of GNS measurements across modern architectures exists, limiting systematic study of the metric. We close this gap by releasing OpenGNS, a dataset of more than 400 GNS measurement trajectories spanning three domains: image classification with ResNets, autoregressive language modeling with Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs), and image synthesis with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), covering models from 11M to 1B parameters trained under Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) with dense batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. Building on this dataset, we study how the GNS depends on hyperparameters, scale, and training progress, and how it relates to the CBS. We find that the GNS behaves as a consistent "temperature of training", remaining stable across model sizes under muP at equivalent loss, and our results suggest task-dependent biases in its relation to the CBS: a tendency to overestimate the CBS for classification and to underestimate it for generative tasks, consistent in direction across common CBS definitions. The dataset is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper releases OpenGNS, an open dataset of over 400 Gradient Noise Scale (GNS) trajectories across ResNets, GPTs, and Diffusion Transformers (11M to 1B parameters). Analyzing the dataset reveals that GNS acts as a consistent training temperature under muP and exhibits task-dependent biases when estimating Critical Batch Size (CBS).
AI.motivation: Although GNS is used to approximate Critical Batch Size in frontier model training, no open dataset of GNS measurements across modern architectures existed to enable systematic study.
AI.method: The authors release OpenGNS, containing over 400 GNS trajectories across image classification (ResNets), autoregressive language modeling (GPTs), and image synthesis (DiTs) from 11M to 1B parameters trained under Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) with dense batch-size and learning-rate sweeps.
AI.result: Under muP, GNS remains stable across model sizes at equivalent loss, behaving as a consistent temperature of training. Compared to CBS, GNS systematically overestimates CBS for classification tasks and underestimates CBS for generative tasks across common CBS definitions.
AI.conclusion: OpenGNS provides a foundational empirical resource for studying gradient noise dynamics and exposes task-dependent biases in GNS-based batch-size scaling laws.

title: Tell Me How Sure You Are: Communicating Uncertainty in Auxiliary Evidence to Foundation Models
comment: 28 pages, 8 figures
summary: In many queries, the context information provided to generative foundation models, such as LLMs and VLMs, is inherently uncertain, including its representations of the physical world. While conventional prompting discards the associated uncertainty, this paper, for the first time in the literature, systematically demonstrates that communicating such uncertainty in context provides useful additional cues for downstream decisions and yields improvements across a wide range of settings. We formulate the decision-making problem as a zero-shot foundation model-assisted image classification task supported by auxiliary text-based characteristics. We choose this due to the availability of well-defined auxiliary properties, associated uncertainty, and unambiguous task correctness. Using five downstream foundation models across three datasets, we extensively evaluate uncertainty arising from both humans and learned models when observing or predicting auxiliary evidence. Across all settings, we find that communicating uncertainty substantially improves downstream LLM classification performance: macro-F1 improves up to $26.18$ percentage points compared to when the uncertainty information is not communicated. We further observe how the foundation models process such uncertainty information and find that auxiliary uncertainty contains predictive information about the correctness of downstream decisions. Together, these results establish uncertainty as useful contextual information and motivate more systematic consideration of uncertainty communication in future foundation-model inference pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically demonstrates that communicating uncertainty in auxiliary text-based evidence to foundation models (LLMs and VLMs) substantially improves zero-shot downstream classification. Macro-F1 improves by up to 26.18 percentage points across five models and three datasets.
AI.motivation: Context information provided to generative foundation models often carries inherent uncertainty from human observers or learned models, yet conventional prompting discards this uncertainty.
AI.method: The authors formulate a zero-shot foundation model-assisted image classification task with auxiliary text-based characteristics and associated uncertainty, evaluating five foundation models across three datasets with uncertainty originating from both humans and learned models.
AI.result: Communicating auxiliary uncertainty in context improves downstream LLM classification macro-F1 by up to 26.18 percentage points compared to omitting uncertainty, and the auxiliary uncertainty contains predictive signal about downstream decision correctness.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly communicating uncertainty in auxiliary evidence provides valuable contextual cues that significantly enhance foundation-model decision making.

title: LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization: Fusing Expert Knowledge with Numerical Data
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables
summary: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate. However, when HF data are scarce, the LF-HF discrepancy is difficult to learn from numerical data alone, especially when physics omitted in the LF model makes it design-dependent. Yet even without sufficient data, domain experts often know which physics the LF model omits and under which conditions its effect grows. Existing multi-fidelity (MF) models cannot use such qualitative knowledge directly, but large language models (LLMs) can interpret it and compare designs accordingly. The proposed LLM-Assisted MFBO adds a knowledge basis to the conventional MF model: from an expert description of the omitted physics, an LLM judges which of two designs requires the larger signed residual correction, and a pairwise Gaussian process converts these judgments into the basis. HF data calibrate its contribution and sign, so the knowledge is not trusted blindly. On a lithium-ion battery design problem, the proposed method reduced the regret area under the curve of conventional MFBO by 61%. Knowledge quality, rather than the choice of LLM, determined whether the search was accelerated, as shown by a controlled study that varied the two independently. A knowledge-level ablation further quantified the contribution of each knowledge statement. These results show that LLM-interpreted expert knowledge can complement numerical data as an information source in MFBO.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization (MFBO), which uses an LLM to convert qualitative expert knowledge about omitted physics into a pairwise Gaussian process basis. On a lithium-ion battery design problem, it reduces regret area under the curve by 61% compared to conventional MFBO.
AI.motivation: When high-fidelity (HF) data are scarce, the discrepancy between low-fidelity (LF) and HF models is hard to learn from numerical data alone, yet existing multi-fidelity models cannot directly incorporate qualitative expert knowledge about omitted physics.
AI.method: Given an expert description of physics omitted in the LF model, an LLM judges which of two designs requires a larger signed residual correction; a pairwise Gaussian process converts these judgments into a knowledge basis added to the MF model, with HF data calibrating its contribution and sign.
AI.result: On a lithium-ion battery design problem, LLM-Assisted MFBO reduced the regret area under the curve of conventional MFBO by 61%. A controlled study showed that knowledge quality, rather than LLM choice, determined search acceleration, and ablations quantified individual knowledge statements.
AI.conclusion: LLM-interpreted expert knowledge serves as an effective complementary information source to numerical data in data-scarce multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization.

title: How to Turn an Attention Neural Network into an Interpretable Hard-Logic Predicate Circuit: Truth-Table Predicate Extraction and State-Machine Merging under Ship-of-Theseus Replacement
summary: We convert a trained attention network as a whole, attention included, into a hard-logic predicate circuit that runs in its place. Every unit of the circuit is a 0/1 predicate on tokens, and every map between predicates is a minimised truth table. Short tables, such as the product of a query code and a key code, are minimised exactly, and wide feature-to-feature transitions become implication rules by noise-tolerant minimisation. Blocks are replaced one at a time from the output down, in the manner of the Ship of Theseus, and after each replacement the remaining soft part re-adapts to the frozen circuit. Attention selection takes two forms, a row-wise comparison of integer scores (order selection) and a learned rule (rule selection). Both are fitted on the ordinary training set alone, and only on the examples that the teacher classifies correctly, so that the circuit imitates the teacher where the teacher is right. On TweetEval-emotion, the complete circuit of DistilGPT2 reaches a test gold accuracy of 66.5 $\pm$ 1.3% with order selection and 57.4 $\pm$ 2.5% with rule selection over three seeds, against 74.7% for the teacher and 64.0% for a bag of word pieces fitted on the same tweets, and that of BERT-base reaches 70.0 $\pm$ 0.5% with order selection and 63.7 $\pm$ 1.2% with rule selection against 77.8%. The circuit needs no multiplier and no weight traffic, and its exported hardware description reproduces it bit for bit. By a synthesis-based estimate it classifies one tweet in about 1-2 $\mu$s (DistilGPT2) and 3-5 $\mu$s (BERT) on an FPGA card and in 5-9 $\mu$s on a palm-sized board whose module draws 7.5-15 W, two to three orders of magnitude faster than the network on a GPU at batch 1 (measured, 0.9-2.6 ms for DistilGPT2 including an optimised CUDA-graph baseline), at a cost of 8.5 (DistilGPT2) and 8.6 (BERT) points of gold accuracy for the synthesised seed-0 circuits.

AI.tldr: This paper converts entire trained attention networks into interpretable hard-logic predicate circuits via truth-table extraction and Ship-of-Theseus block replacement. Exported to FPGA hardware, the circuits classify tweets 2 to 3 orders of magnitude faster than GPU baselines with an 8.5-8.6 point accuracy trade-off.
AI.motivation: Attention-based neural networks are opaque and computationally expensive, motivating methods to convert them into fully interpretable, multiplier-free logic circuits.
AI.method: Each unit is converted into a 0/1 token predicate with minimized truth tables for short maps and noise-tolerant implication rules for wide transitions, replacing blocks from output to input (Ship of Theseus) while re-adapting remaining soft layers, and fitting attention via order or rule selection on correctly classified training examples.
