AI.result: On TweetEval-emotion, complete circuits achieve 66.5% +/- 1.3% (DistilGPT2, order selection) and 70.0% +/- 0.5% (BERT-base, order selection) test gold accuracy versus 74.7% and 77.8% for teachers. Synthesis estimates show 1-2 us (DistilGPT2) and 3-5 us (BERT) per tweet on an FPGA card (5-9 us on a 7.5-15 W palm-sized board), 2 to 3 orders of magnitude faster than 0.9-2.6 ms GPU batch-1 inference, at a cost of 8.5-8.6 accuracy points for seed-0 circuits.
AI.conclusion: Whole-network conversion into hard-logic predicate circuits enables bit-exact, multiplier-free hardware deployment of attention models with massive latency gains.

title: Temporal Rank in Recurrent Neural Networks
summary: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a natural framework for temporal modelling, yet are often dismissed due to their sequential, non-parallelisable computation and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies, typically attributed to vanishing and exploding gradients. We identify a distinct and under-explored limitation: an information bottleneck induced by rank-constrained hidden state dynamics, which limits the number of independent input directions that can be preserved over time, as reflected in the rank of the input-to-state mapping. We show that this constraint restricts temporal capacity independently of gradient stability. To address this, we introduce structured high-dimensional state dynamics that preserve temporal separability and prevent saturation of the input-to-state Jacobian over time. On controlled sequence tasks, the resulting model exhibits rapid learning despite remaining strictly within a standard RNN formulation. Our results demonstrate that RNN performance is governed by the evolution and preservation of temporal rank, and suggest that mitigating gradient pathologies alone is insufficient without explicitly maintaining temporal capacity.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies temporal rank—the rank of the input-to-state mapping—as a fundamental bottleneck in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) independent of gradient stability. Introducing structured high-dimensional state dynamics that preserve temporal rank enables rapid learning on controlled sequence tasks within a standard RNN formulation.
AI.motivation: RNN difficulties in capturing long-range dependencies are typically attributed to vanishing or exploding gradients, overlooking rank-constrained hidden state dynamics that limit how many independent input directions can be preserved over time.
AI.method: The authors analyze the evolution of the input-to-state Jacobian rank and introduce structured high-dimensional state dynamics that preserve temporal separability and prevent Jacobian saturation over time while remaining strictly within a standard RNN formulation.
AI.result: On controlled sequence tasks, the resulting temporal-rank-preserving RNN exhibits rapid learning, demonstrating that temporal capacity is governed by temporal rank preservation rather than gradient stability alone.
AI.conclusion: Mitigating gradient pathologies is insufficient for long-range sequence modeling in RNNs without explicitly preserving temporal rank.

title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
comment: 22 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 production-scale training and inference optimization tasks across up to 32 NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Across evaluated results, 66.2% exceed 1.10x validated end-to-end speedup, though consistent end-to-end gains remain challenging.
AI.motivation: Existing agent-driven optimization benchmarks focus on isolated layers like kernels, leaving unclear whether AI agents can optimize their own training and inference infrastructure end-to-end at production scale.
AI.method: RSIBench-Infra comprises 20 training and inference tasks across diverse model families and modalities on up to 32 accelerators, where agents modify engine, kernel, and instruction layers from official runnable baselines and submit OCI image layers for independent end-to-end evaluation under quality constraints.
AI.result: Across all task results, 66.2% exceed 1.10x validated end-to-end speedup, demonstrating that agents can achieve meaningful production-scale infrastructure improvements, though reliably translating local optimizations into end-to-end gains remains difficult.
AI.conclusion: RSIBench-Infra establishes a reproducible testbed for evaluating recursive self-improvement of AI training and inference infrastructure at production scale.

title: MINT: Meeting-time Indicators for Truncation in Multi-Step Off-Policy RL
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 81 pages, 40 figures, including appendices. Code: this https URL
summary: Many multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods handle policy mismatch through products of per-step trace coefficients, leading to a trade-off between variance control and long-horizon signal. The maximum trace length consequently becomes a sensitive hyperparameter. We propose MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation), which replaces these products with a binary stopping indicator: one until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet, zero thereafter. At the true value function, the indicator's idempotence yields a variance bound governed by meeting-time survival. For practical implementation, a single sampled action provides a model-free surrogate for the stopping rule, requiring no transition model or mixing-time estimate. We derive separate sufficient conditions for contraction of the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control tasks, MINT outperforms the reported multi-step baselines; the main MuJoCo comparison uses a common cap without per-task cap-length tuning. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of MINT on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench experiments; MINT adapts the backup horizon to reduce target variability relative to long fixed-horizon backups across tasks and dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MINT, a multi-step off-policy RL method that replaces products of trace coefficients with a binary stopping indicator based on coupled trajectory meeting times. MINT outperforms multi-step baselines on MuJoCo and DeepMind Control and adapts backup horizons across Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench.
AI.motivation: Multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods use products of per-step trace coefficients, creating a trade-off between variance and long-horizon signal and making maximum trace length a sensitive hyperparameter.
AI.method: MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation) uses a binary stopping indicator that is 1 until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet and 0 thereafter, with a single sampled action serving as a model-free surrogate without requiring a transition model or mixing-time estimate.
AI.result: The authors prove contraction conditions for both the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control, MINT outperforms multi-step baselines without per-task cap-length tuning, and adapts backup horizons to reduce target variability on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench.
AI.conclusion: Meeting-time truncation indicators provide a principled, model-free mechanism to adaptively balance variance and horizon length in multi-step off-policy RL.

title: Predicting Process-Level Behavior: A Benchmarking Study
comment: Accepted as main track paper at International Conference on Process Mining (ICPM) 2027
summary: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks statistical, ML, foundation model, business process simulation, and aggregated trace-level predictive process monitoring (PPM) methods on two process-level prediction tasks. It finds that aggregating trace-level predictions compounds errors, establishing process-level prediction as a distinct research problem.
AI.motivation: Predictive process monitoring typically forecasts individual process traces, whereas process managers make decisions at the process level (such as staffing and KPIs), and it is unclear how well existing methods support process-level forecasting.
AI.method: The authors conduct a benchmarking study on concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction across synthetic and real-life event logs, comparing statistical, ML, foundation models, business process simulation, and aggregated trace-level PPM approaches.
AI.result: Performance varies substantially across modeling paradigms, and aggregating trace-level PPM predictions to the process level causes errors to compound, reducing overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Process-level behavior prediction is a distinct predictive task that cannot be reliably solved by aggregating trace-level PPM models and warrants dedicated research.

title: DyNA-Mixer: Decoupling Time and Topology for Scalable Dynamic Node Affinity Prediction
comment: Includes appendices
summary: Continuous-time dynamic graphs preserve the ordering, timing, and evolving strength of interactions that static snapshots discard, making dynamic graph mining essential for evolving systems such as recommender systems, trade networks, and transaction platforms. Research in this area has centered on dynamic link prediction, which forecasts only whether a future interaction will occur, whereas many applications also need its intensity. The dynamic node affinity prediction (DNAP) problem generalizes this task to continuous targets and full-candidate ranking, making it more broadly applicable but substantially harder. This raises two coupled difficulties: ranking requires a predictor expressive enough to capture both multi-scale temporal evolution and graph-wide collaborative patterns, yet running such a predictor over every source--destination pair is computationally prohibitive. We propose DyNA-Mixer, which decouples temporal forecasting from collaborative structure modeling. It adopts a multi-scale temporal predictor for pair-specific affinity evolution, constructs a Virtual Collaborative Graph that infers query-time relationships and aggregates trends from related interactions, and fuses the two through a gated residual mechanism. A sparsity-aware evaluation strategy further restricts expensive forecasting to pairs with recent non-zero affinities. Experiments on four Temporal Graph Benchmark datasets for the DNAP problem show that DyNA-Mixer achieves new state-of-the-art NDCG@10 on every dataset, including a 17.8\% relative test improvement over the strongest baseline on tgbn-token, the largest dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DyNA-Mixer, a scalable framework for dynamic node affinity prediction (DNAP) that decouples temporal forecasting from collaborative structure modeling. It achieves state-of-the-art NDCG@10 on all four Temporal Graph Benchmark datasets, including a 17.8% relative improvement on tgbn-token.
AI.motivation: Dynamic node affinity prediction requires forecasting continuous interaction intensities and ranking all candidates, which is computationally prohibitive when running expressive temporal-collaborative predictors over every source-destination pair.
AI.method: DyNA-Mixer decouples a multi-scale temporal predictor for pair-specific affinity evolution from a Virtual Collaborative Graph that aggregates trends from related interactions, fusing them via a gated residual mechanism and using sparsity-aware evaluation to restrict expensive forecasting to pairs with recent non-zero affinities.
AI.result: On four Temporal Graph Benchmark datasets for DNAP, DyNA-Mixer sets new state-of-the-art NDCG@10 on every dataset, achieving a 17.8% relative test improvement over the strongest baseline on tgbn-token.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling temporal evolution from collaborative structure with sparsity-aware evaluation enables both high accuracy and scalability in continuous-time dynamic node affinity prediction.

title: ICICLE: In-Context Inference for Curve-Learning Extrapolation
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures. Accepted at the AXIOM Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Code and pretrained model: this https URL
summary: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization allocates training budget by predicting how partially observed learning curves will continue. LC-PFN first applied prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) to learning-curve extrapolation, and FT-PFN extended this approach to configuration-aware freeze-thaw optimization with a ten-slot hyperparameter encoder. We introduce In-Context Inference for Curve-Learning Extrapolation (ICICLE), an in-context surrogate that accepts a variable number of hyperparameters through a shared set encoder and is trained on a synthetic prior covering typed hyperparameters, heavy-tailed noise, quantization, and divergence. ICICLE has 1.28 million parameters (8.7% of FT-PFN's count) and produces similar mean-regret trajectories to FT-PFN on LCBench, PD1, and TaskSet. On the 86-task Meta-Album benchmark with 33 hyperparameters, ICICLE reaches lower mean normalized regret than Quick-Tune overall and on extended, with no clear difference on mini or micro. It does so without pre-training or meta-training on Meta-Album tasks, whereas Quick-Tune is meta-trained on related Meta-Album tasks. Our release samples synthetic training tasks on the fly and provides a freeze-thaw scheduler for Ray Tune and an ONNX model for inference without JAX or PyTorch.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ICICLE, a 1.28M-parameter in-context surrogate for learning-curve extrapolation in freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization that handles variable numbers of hyperparameters. It matches FT-PFN with 8.7% of its parameters and outperforms Quick-Tune on Meta-Album without meta-training on Meta-Album tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing prior-data fitted networks for configuration-aware freeze-thaw optimization, such as FT-PFN, use fixed-slot hyperparameter encoders and large parameter counts.
AI.method: ICICLE uses a shared set encoder to accept a variable number of hyperparameters and is trained on a synthetic prior covering typed hyperparameters, heavy-tailed noise, quantization, and divergence, with an ONNX release and Ray Tune scheduler.
AI.result: With 1.28M parameters (8.7% of FT-PFN), ICICLE achieves similar mean-regret trajectories to FT-PFN on LCBench, PD1, and TaskSet. On the 86-task Meta-Album benchmark (33 hyperparameters), it achieves lower mean normalized regret than Quick-Tune overall and on extended without meta-training on Meta-Album tasks.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic-prior in-context surrogates with set encoders provide lightweight, generalizable learning-curve extrapolation across arbitrary hyperparameter spaces.

title: From Activity Recognition to Shift Detection: Variational Wi-Fi Sensing with Evidential Uncertainty
comment: 17 pages,8 figures, 8 tables
summary: Human motion perturbs wireless channels, making commodity Wi-Fi devices a practical platform for device-free activity recognition. Yet Channel State Information (CSI) also depends strongly on the person, receiver position, recording session, and surrounding environment, so a classifier can continue producing activity labels after its deployment conditions have moved away from those seen during training. We propose Wi-HAR, a multi-antenna architecture in which four Variational Auto-Encoders learn compact distributions from raw Wi-Fi 6 CSI magnitudes and a delayed-fusion classifier combines their means and log-variances. On twelve activities from a public benchmark, Wi-HAR reaches 96.6% median recognition accuracy, compared with 70.8-81.5% for independently optimized single-antenna models, showing that the antennas provide complementary views of the same activity. We then use the same latent backbone to detect deployment shifts without using shifted samples for model selection or calibration. A class-conditional uncertainty score derived from Evidential Deep Learning achieves a macro-average ROC-AUC of 0.897 across eleven datasets that change receiver position, participant, recording session, or room, and detects 82.5% of shifted samples at a realized 5.2% in-distribution rejection rate. Detection performance nevertheless varies substantially across receiver positions, showing that the same physical change does not induce a uniform uncertainty response. The compact representation also supports shallow decision-tree analysis using variables from several antennas.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Wi-HAR, a multi-antenna VAE architecture with evidential uncertainty for Wi-Fi 6 activity recognition and deployment shift detection. It achieves 96.6% median recognition accuracy on 12 activities and 0.897 macro-average ROC-AUC for shift detection across 11 shifted datasets.
AI.motivation: Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) varies strongly with person, receiver position, session, and environment, causing classifiers to make overconfident predictions under deployment shifts.
AI.method: Wi-HAR trains four Variational Auto-Encoders on raw Wi-Fi 6 CSI magnitudes from separate antennas and combines their means and log-variances in a delayed-fusion classifier, then derives a class-conditional Evidential Deep Learning uncertainty score on the latent backbone without using shifted samples for calibration.
AI.result: On 12 activities, Wi-HAR reaches 96.6% median accuracy versus 70.8-81.5% for single-antenna models. Across 11 shifted datasets (varying receiver position, participant, session, or room), it achieves 0.897 macro-average ROC-AUC and detects 82.5% of shifted samples at a 5.2% in-distribution rejection rate, though performance varies across receiver positions.
AI.conclusion: Multi-antenna variational representations paired with evidential uncertainty enable accurate Wi-Fi activity recognition and unsupervised deployment-shift detection.

title: Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA) for Plant Spectroscopy
summary: Plant reflectance spectroscopy across the visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared domain encodes foliar biochemical and anatomical traits into contiguous spectral signatures with locally differentiable structure; however, extreme inter-band collinearity and unfavorable sample-to-feature ratios challenge predictive modeling. Conventional dimensionality reduction methods routinely adopted in spectroscopy, are column-permutation invariant: they treat adjacent wavelengths as unordered tabular columns and discard the sequential differential geometry of absorption features. Here, we propose Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA), a supervised dimensionality reduction operator that projects contiguous spectra into a compact morpho-spectral subspace through three complementary blocks: (i) additive continuum-removed absorption depth, area, and red-edge inflection kinematics; (ii) local multi-order singular eigenmodes (0th, 1st, and 2nd derivatives) partitioned across contiguous radiative sub-windows; and (iii) global Fisher-weighted canonical subspaces regularized via trace-normalized isotropic covariance shrinkage. We validated MSPA across 8,963 spectra spanning five plant systems, coupled with six classical machine learning classifiers and four Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabDPT v1.2, and TabFM). Despite compressing the 1,580-band spectrum by 96%, MSPA outperformed the full spectrum in 92.0% of all benchmarks and conventional reducers in 90.0% of all model-crop evaluations, raising the global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 (full spectrum) to 0.8520, accelerating in-context inference by up to 126.5x. Designed as a self-contained spectral projection operator, the MSPA method can be directly integrated into spectroscopy workflows via the open-source code available at GitHub: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA), a supervised dimensionality reduction operator for plant reflectance spectroscopy that preserves sequential absorption geometry. Compressing 1,580 bands by 96%, MSPA improves global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 to 0.8520 and accelerates in-context inference by up to 126.5x.
AI.motivation: Conventional dimensionality reduction methods in spectroscopy are column-permutation invariant, discarding the sequential differential geometry of contiguous absorption features and struggling with inter-band collinearity and unfavorable sample-to-feature ratios.
AI.method: MSPA projects spectra into a compact morpho-spectral subspace combining continuum-removed absorption depth, area, and red-edge kinematics; local multi-order singular eigenmodes (0th-2nd derivatives) across radiative sub-windows; and global Fisher-weighted canonical subspaces regularized via trace-normalized isotropic covariance shrinkage.
AI.result: Validated across 8,963 spectra from five plant systems with six classical classifiers and four Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabDPT v1.2, TabFM), MSPA compresses 1,580 bands by 96%, outperforms the full spectrum in 92.0% of benchmarks and conventional reducers in 90.0% of evaluations, raises mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 to 0.8520, and speeds up in-context inference up to 126.5x.
AI.conclusion: Encoding sequential spectral morphology into supervised projections substantially boosts both predictive accuracy and inference efficiency for classical and foundation-model spectroscopy pipelines.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Location Encoding Methods for Species Distribution Modelling
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning
summary: Understanding the spatial distribution of species is a key question in ecology. A variety of solutions, from statistical, traditional machine learning, through to deep learning-based methods have been proposed. These methods take sparse observations for a species of interest as input and aim to generate dense spatial outputs indicating the spatial range of the species. Orthogonal to the choice of statistical model used is the question of what input features are most informative. Thanks to recent developments, the number of options has greatly expanded, with choices spanning different climate variables, learning-based encodings, earth embedding models, or raw transformed geographic coordinates. In this work, we introduce a standardized evaluation framework and quantify the effectiveness of different location encodings in the context of species range estimation, both at the local and global scale.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a standardized evaluation framework to quantify the effectiveness of different location encoding methods for species distribution modelling at local and global scales.
AI.motivation: Species distribution modelling uses diverse input features—including climate variables, learned encodings, earth embeddings, and transformed coordinates—yet lacks a standardized comparison of location encoding effectiveness.
AI.method: The authors establish a standardized evaluation framework comparing climate variables, learning-based encodings, earth embedding models, and raw transformed geographic coordinates for species range estimation from sparse observations.
AI.result: The framework quantifies the effectiveness of each location encoding family across both local and global spatial scales.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a unified benchmark to guide feature and location-encoding selection in ecological species distribution modelling.

title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight bridge for multimodal materials language models that adaptively combines representations from multiple structural encoders. TCAF outperforms MatterChat with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, fewer parameters, and half the training time.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal materials models like MatterChat rely on large bridge modules and separate contrastive alignment stages, and single-encoder final-layer features miss complementary information distributed across depths and encoders.
AI.method: TCAF uses task-conditioned latent queries in a lightweight attention bridge to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 (and optionally UMA-S) representations, trained directly on downstream tasks without separate contrastive pretraining.
AI.result: Across materials classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat with up to 47.8% lower RMSE while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving training time; a three-encoder configuration (with UMA-S) achieves 89.61% macro-average classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Task-aware attention fusion over multi-depth, multi-encoder structural representations eliminates the need for separate contrastive alignment while improving accuracy and efficiency.

title: Equal Steps, Unequal Curvature: Where Muon's Update Goes Wrong
summary: Muon updates each hidden weight matrix along the polar factor of its momentum, the steepest-descent direction under the spectral norm. That choice fixes two allocations without consulting the loss: every singular direction of the momentum receives the same step, and in a non-square matrix each neuron's step is set by its leverage score. Whether they are good is a question about curvature, which steepest-descent arguments do not answer; we measure it. Using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products, we decompose Muon's step by singular-value band and by neuron group and compute each group's second-order optimal multiplier. In a 124M-parameter decoder trained on FineWeb-Edu, the multipliers rise monotonically from the top singular directions to the tail: Muon over-steps the high-curvature top of its spectrum. We prove in Lean when such a diagnostic licenses an intervention at Muon's own update norm. On the measured curvature, the criterion predicts, and held-out losses confirm, that moving step length off the top helps mid-training and early in the cooldown, but not at its end. We then test interventions under per-step norm matching, tuned baselines and paired seeds. Orthogonalizing Q, K and V separately rather than as one fused matrix lowers the loss by 0.0250 nats and accounts for all of the gain of block-wise variants. A matmul-only, rotation-equivariant spectral tilt $\sigma^{-1/4}$ applied in the cooldown lowers the loss of this stronger baseline by a further 0.0120 nats, additively with NorMuon (0.0158 nats together, three seeds; the baseline needs about 4.3% more tokens to match), and by 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters (three seeds). Energy-matched Schatten-1 weight decay adds a further 0.0052 nats. Geometrically principled changes that do not act on the measured miscalibration, namely exact polar factors, steepest-descent input whitening and top-heavy decay, do not help.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses curvature miscalibration in the Muon optimizer, showing it over-steps high-curvature top singular directions, and proposes rotation-equivariant spectral tilting and separate Q/K/V orthogonalization. These interventions lower language model loss by up to 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters.
AI.motivation: Muon updates weight matrices along the polar factor of momentum, assigning equal step sizes across singular directions without consulting loss curvature, and it is unclear whether this allocation is optimal.
AI.method: Using held-out gradients and Hessian-vector products on a 124M-parameter FineWeb-Edu decoder, the authors decompose Muon's step by singular-value band and neuron group, prove in Lean when curvature diagnostics license norm-matched interventions, and test separate Q/K/V orthogonalization, a matmul-only spectral tilt sigma^(-1/4) during cooldown, and energy-matched Schatten-1 weight decay.
AI.result: Optimal multipliers rise monotonically toward the tail, confirming Muon over-steps top singular directions. Separate Q/K/V orthogonalization lowers loss by 0.0250 nats; adding the sigma^(-1/4) cooldown tilt lowers loss by a further 0.0120 nats (0.0158 nats with NorMuon, saving ~4.3% tokens) and 0.0188 nats at 355M parameters; Schatten-1 decay adds 0.0052 nats. Exact polar factors, input whitening, and top-heavy decay do not help.
AI.conclusion: Aligning Muon's spectral step-size allocation with measured loss curvature yields consistent, additive gains in language model pretraining.

title: Zonotopic Analysis of Quantization Error in Neural Networks
summary: Quantized neural networks achieve computational efficiency by reducing precision, but bounding their quantization error remains a challenge due to discrete rounding and clamping operations. We present a zonotope-based abstract interpretation framework for quantized ReLU feed-forward network verification, introducing a unified round-clamp abstract transformer that jointly handles both operations. We extend this framework to constrained zonotopes, which add linear constraints to tighten bounds, and derive sound quantization error representations. We establish soundness and affine-strip optimality of the round-clamp abstract transformer, as well as convex-hull optimality of its complete constrained formulation. On the ACAS Xu benchmarks, our constrained zonotope method reduces average error-bound widths by approximately 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% compared to QEBVerif's symbolic DRA propagation at the two smallest tested perturbation radii (r=3 and r=6). These improvements are not uniform across bitwidths, and symbolic DRA achieves tighter bounds at larger radii. Our plain zonotope method delivers competitive sound bounds nearly 300 times faster on average.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a zonotope and constrained-zonotope abstract interpretation framework for bounding quantization error in quantized ReLU feed-forward networks. On ACAS Xu, it reduces error-bound widths by 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% at small perturbation radii compared to QEBVerif.
AI.motivation: Bounding quantization error in quantized neural networks is challenging due to discrete rounding and clamping operations.
AI.method: The authors introduce a unified round-clamp abstract transformer for zonotopes and extend it to constrained zonotopes with linear constraints, proving soundness, affine-strip optimality, and convex-hull optimality of the constrained formulation.
AI.result: On ACAS Xu benchmarks at small perturbation radii (r=3 and r=6), constrained zonotopes reduce average error-bound widths by 70-85% and runtimes by 65-80% compared to QEBVerif's symbolic DRA propagation (though symbolic DRA is tighter at larger radii and improvements vary by bitwidth), while plain zonotopes run nearly 300x faster on average.
AI.conclusion: Zonotopic abstract interpretation with unified round-clamp transformers provides sound, tight, and fast quantization error verification, particularly at small perturbation radii.

title: Stealing Exact Training Data from Other Clients during Federated Learning
comment: Preprint. 22 pages, 21 figures
summary: Malicious adversaries can employ gradient inversion attacks to reverse-engineer private data using the model updates of a round in Federated Learning. While there have been developments in gradient inversion for text, exact text recovery by a malicious client has so far remained infeasible, as FedAvg entangles the gradient contributions of many clients and obscures the signal of any individual sentence. We introduce a novel attack pipeline that unwinds this entanglement progressively through an iterative loop, in which the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round are subtracted from the aggregate, exposing the remaining sentences for recovery in the next iteration. We show, for the first time, exact sentence recovery, with 100% precision, and on aggregates containing up to $4\times$ more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, we recover up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly, a regime where existing attacks recover none exactly.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an iterative gradient-inversion attack that recovers exact client training sentences from aggregated FedAvg updates in Federated Learning. It achieves 100% precision and recovers up to 80.2% of client sentences exactly where prior attacks recover none.
AI.motivation: Exact text recovery from FedAvg updates by a malicious client has been considered infeasible because aggregating gradients across many clients entangles and obscures individual sentence signals.
AI.method: The attack pipeline progressively unwinds gradient entanglement in an iterative loop by subtracting the gradient contributions of sentences recovered exactly in one round from the aggregate, exposing remaining sentences for recovery in subsequent iterations.
AI.result: The method achieves exact sentence recovery with 100% precision for the first time, recovering up to 80.2% of client sentences on aggregates containing up to 4x more tokens than the model's hidden dimension, a regime where existing attacks recover zero sentences exactly.
AI.conclusion: Iterative gradient-subtraction attacks break the privacy protection of multi-client FedAvg aggregation for text, enabling high-rate exact sentence reconstruction.

title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning
comment: 15 pages (9 main + references + appendix), 5 figures, 10 tables. Accepted at the Northern Lights Deep Learning Conference (NLDL 2027); to appear in PMLR vol. 352
summary: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $\mu$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Meta-LSQ, a few-shot meta-learner that fits tasks via a closed-form regularized least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis while meta-learning only three scalars. It outperforms first-order MAML by 5.5x on 10-shot sinusoid regression while training 36x faster, though it struggles on non-smooth targets.
AI.motivation: Gradient-based meta-learners like MAML require differentiating through an inner gradient-descent loop and meta-learning all network weights, incurring high computational cost.
AI.method: Meta-LSQ solves each task in closed form via regularized least squares over a fixed random Fourier basis—supporting exact derivative observations and closed-form derivatives—while meta-learning only three scalars: bandwidth, ridge, and derivative weight.
AI.result: On 10-shot sinusoid regression, Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s (36x faster than first-order MAML) with 5.5x lower error. On simulated DESY ARES beam tuning, it achieves a 7.3 um median error versus 14.4 um for an RL agent across full targets (though RL leads on small targets). On real sensor calibration, it beats MAML on two of four targets but trails exact Gaussian processes and ALPaCA-style models and breaks down on non-smooth targets.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form Sobolev least-squares over random Fourier features offers fast, accurate meta-learning for smooth physical control tasks, while exposing limitations on non-smooth targets.

title: How Generative Models Generate: A Concise Guide to the Generative AI Landscape
summary: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

AI.tldr: This article presents a concise, generation-centered technical guide to the generative AI landscape, organizing methods into three generation routes and their underlying modeling and learning principles.
AI.motivation: The rapid proliferation of generative AI architectures, objectives, and sampling procedures makes it difficult for readers to form a coherent, unified understanding of the field.
AI.method: The authors develop a two-level conceptual framework: first categorizing methods into three generation routes (direct transformation/decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating/transport), and second examining their underlying modeling principles, learning objectives, sampling procedures, and cross-method connections.
AI.result: The guide synthesizes representative generative approaches within a compact framework that highlights how different architectures and mechanisms overlap or combine.
AI.conclusion: This generation-centered taxonomy helps practitioners and researchers understand unfamiliar generative models and navigate connections across the generative AI landscape.

title: Approximate Dynamic Programming with Basis Function Learning
summary: This work presents a novel approach for approximating the value function in Markov decision processes (MDPs). Our approach is grounded in the approximate linear programming (ALP) framework, wherein basis functions (BFs) play an important role. Traditionally, BFs have been pre-defined, randomly generated, or restricted to specific structures, which both limits the accuracy that can be achieved and leaves no mechanism for improving a given approximation. We instead learn BFs from the model itself, by repeatedly applying the Bellman operator to the current value estimate. We introduce the Bellman operator basis function (BOBF) learning method, and prove that each learned BF improves the approximation by a quantifiable amount and that the method converges to the optimal value function. Its shrunken counterpart (SBOBF) retains this guarantee while capping the number of BFs, and therefore the computational effort per iteration. For large-scale problems, where the number of constraints is prohibitive, we develop hybrid variants (HBOBF and SHBOBF) that combine constraint sampling with BF learning, and we show that the improvement and finite-termination guarantees are preserved under explicitly stated conditions. Numerical experiments on (continuous) perishable inventory and queueing control problems demonstrate that our BF learning techniques significantly outperform existing methods in the literature.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Bellman Operator Basis Function (BOBF) learning and its bounded-size and constraint-sampled variants (SBOBF, HBOBF, SHBOBF) for approximate linear programming in MDPs. It proves convergence to the optimal value function and outperforms existing methods on perishable inventory and queueing control.
AI.motivation: Approximate linear programming (ALP) for Markov decision processes traditionally relies on pre-defined, random, or structurally restricted basis functions, limiting accuracy and offering no mechanism to iteratively improve the approximation.
AI.method: BOBF learns basis functions directly from the MDP model by repeatedly applying the Bellman operator to the current value estimate; SBOBF caps the number of basis functions per iteration, while HBOBF and SHBOBF combine constraint sampling with basis function learning for large-scale problems.
AI.result: The authors prove quantifiable per-step improvement and convergence to the optimal value function for BOBF and SBOBF, and preserve improvement and finite-termination guarantees for HBOBF and SHBOBF. On continuous perishable inventory and queueing control problems, the methods significantly outperform existing literature baselines.
AI.conclusion: Iteratively learning basis functions via the Bellman operator provides provably convergent and scalable value-function approximations within the ALP framework.

title: Uneven gains in protein-RNA affinity and mutation-effect prediction
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables. Supplementary material included as an ancillary file
summary: Accurate matched affinities determine mutation effects, but gains in aggregate affinity prediction may transfer unevenly to average effects, ordering and local accuracy. We evaluated eleven method families using method-specific matched populations. Controlled CoPRA reduced absolute-affinity mean absolute error from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd. Across 220 mutation pairs from 20 families, it generated stronger responses and improved mean-effect accuracy, with uncertain ranking gains and no decrease in mean centered local error. In an independent external test (24 quantitative pairs from three source-matched families), absolute and ordinary mutation-effect errors fell in all three families. Mean centered local error fell from 0.4198 to 0.3761 pKd, with improvements in two families and higher error in one. Error decomposition localized gains in landscape means. PRA-Pred feature tracing, fixed-weight M2-PRNet input controls and matched supervision interventions identified specific restrictions on mutation response. These results establish the need to evaluate average effects, ordering and quantitative local variation jointly.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates eleven protein-RNA affinity prediction method families on matched populations and mutation pairs, finding that gains in aggregate affinity accuracy transfer unevenly to mutation-effect ranking and local variation.
AI.motivation: Accurate matched affinities are needed to predict mutation effects, but it is unclear whether improvements in aggregate affinity prediction translate to better average mutation effects, ordering, and local accuracy.
AI.method: The authors evaluate eleven method families using method-specific matched populations, including 220 mutation pairs from 20 families and an external test of 24 quantitative pairs from 3 families, alongside error decomposition, PRA-Pred feature tracing, and M2-PRNet input controls.
AI.result: Controlled CoPRA reduced absolute-affinity MAE from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd and improved mean-effect accuracy across 220 pairs, but showed uncertain ranking gains and no reduction in mean centered local error. On the external 24-pair test, mean centered local error fell from 0.4198 to 0.3761 pKd (improving in two families, worsening in one), with error decomposition localizing gains to landscape means.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating protein-RNA affinity models requires jointly assessing average effects, ordering, and quantitative local variation rather than relying on aggregate affinity metrics alone.

title: Variance-Optimal Counterfactual Policy Design for Sample-Efficient Online A/B Testing
summary: Online A/B testing is the standard approach for evaluating changes to user-facing systems, such as a new recommendation or ranking policy, before deployment. While the difference-in-means estimator of a standard A/B test is unbiased, it often suffers from high variance. When the treatment and production policies choose the same actions with similar probabilities, the resulting observations can add noise while providing little information about the difference between the policies. Consequently, A/B tests can require large amounts of traffic and long durations to detect small treatment effects. Existing variance-reduction methods mainly improve the estimator after the data-collection scheme has been fixed, and recent overlap-aware designs only optimize a single traffic split between the two policies; thereby, they cannot direct traffic to the actions on which the policies disagree. In this paper, we jointly optimize how actions are sampled and how the resulting observations are used to estimate the treatment effect. Our contributions are two-fold. First, building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, we derive the variance-optimal action-level logging policy for estimating the average treatment effect between two policies, which has a closed-form solution for any fixed control variate. Second, we use historical logs to jointly optimize the logging policy and a control variate to further reduce variance. Our experimental results in simulated policy A/B tests show that our designs estimate the average treatment effect more accurately than existing variance reduction methods on every evaluated setting, while generally improving statistical power and reducing how often the worse policy is selected. As a result, our designs enable practitioners to reach reliable deployment decisions with considerably less online traffic.

AI.tldr: This paper jointly optimizes action-level logging policies and control variates for online A/B testing of recommendation and ranking policies. In simulated A/B tests, the approach estimates treatment effects more accurately than existing variance-reduction methods, improving statistical power with less online traffic.
AI.motivation: Standard A/B testing suffers from high variance when treatment and production policies often choose similar actions, while existing variance-reduction methods either post-process fixed data or only optimize a global traffic split without directing traffic to actions where policies disagree.
AI.method: Building on pairwise off-policy evaluation, the authors derive a closed-form variance-optimal action-level logging policy for any fixed control variate, and use historical logs to jointly optimize both the logging policy and the control variate.
AI.result: Across all evaluated simulated policy A/B testing settings, the joint design estimates average treatment effects more accurately than existing variance-reduction baselines, generally improves statistical power, and reduces the rate of selecting the worse policy.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimizing action-level counterfactual logging and control variates enables reliable deployment decisions with substantially less online A/B testing traffic.

title: Elysium: Simulation-Free Unbalanced Schrödinger Bridges
comment: 44 pages, 9 figures
summary: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from snapshots is challenging because the destructive nature of single-cell measurements makes tracking the same cells over time impossible. Cellular dynamics are inherently stochastic and involve changes in population size through proliferation and apoptosis. Growth-based methods represent population change as a rate on the density, which does not assign exits and entries to individual cells. Unbalanced Schrödinger bridges model individual events, but neural solvers for killed diffusion bridges simulate trajectories during training. We introduce Elysium, a simulation-free solver that jointly learns state transition and mass change. Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, without simulating trajectories during training. We show that the minimizers of the expected training objectives recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge. Empirically, Elysium reconstructs state transitions, population size, and event distributions on simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, outperforming existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers. On single-cell time courses, it interpolates cell state distributions at unobserved time points, tracks population expansion and contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Elysium, a simulation-free solver for unbalanced Schrödinger bridges that jointly learns cellular state transitions and mass changes (proliferation and apoptosis). It outperforms deterministic and bridge-based solvers on simulated killed-diffusion benchmarks and reconstructs single-cell time courses.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing cellular dynamics from destructive single-cell snapshots requires modeling both stochastic state transitions and individual cell births/deaths, but existing neural solvers for unbalanced Schrödinger bridges must simulate trajectories during training.
AI.method: Using a killed Brownian reference and its time reversal, Elysium constructs direct regression objectives from an optimal endpoint coupling and conditional bridge distributions, proving that objective minimizers recover the optimal unbalanced Schrödinger bridge without trajectory simulation.
AI.result: On simulated benchmarks with known killed-diffusion ground truth, Elysium outperforms existing deterministic and bridge-based solvers in reconstructing state transitions, population size, and event distributions; on single-cell time courses, it interpolates unobserved time points, tracks population expansion/contraction, and captures biphasic drug-response dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Elysium enables scalable, simulation-free learning of stochastic, mass-changing cellular dynamics from single-cell snapshots.

title: Horizontal Flow Matching for Single-Cell Spatiotemporal Dynamics
comment: 38 pages, 7 figures
summary: Learning the spatiotemporal dynamics of cells from spatial transcriptomics requires connecting snapshots of different cells acquired in different coordinate frames. A rotation or translation of a section can appear as cell movement and distort the inferred correspondence. We introduce horizontal flow matching, which learns changes in tissue organization, molecular state, and cell abundance up to shared rigid motion. The dynamics follow a continuity--reaction equation whose action assigns no cost to shared rigid motion, and the resulting horizontal projector removes this component from spatial prediction errors during learning and from predicted velocities during generation. An equivalent endpoint problem jointly estimates correspondence and relative pose in Wasserstein--Fisher--Rao geometry and yields analytic paths whose velocity and growth serve as regression targets. Regressing these targets recovers the horizontal dynamics under ideal population conditions. Our model, HORIZON, uses an equivariant transformer to predict velocity and growth from the current tissue, so that a tissue can be generated continuously from a single initial snapshot. On a simulated tissue observed in perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. On four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods, and interpolates held-out developmental stages.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces horizontal flow matching and the HORIZON model to learn single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics from spatial transcriptomics up to shared rigid motion. HORIZON outperforms existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods across four spatial transcriptomics time courses.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics snapshots are acquired in different coordinate frames, so section rotations or translations can be mistaken for cell movement and distort inferred cellular dynamics.
AI.method: Horizontal flow matching models tissue, molecular state, and cell abundance dynamics via a continuity-reaction equation whose action assigns zero cost to shared rigid motion; a horizontal projector removes rigid-motion components from errors and velocities, while an equivalent Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao endpoint problem yields analytic regression targets for an equivariant transformer (HORIZON).
AI.result: On simulated tissues with perturbed coordinate frames, alignment improves reconstruction and projection reduces rigid drift. Across four spatial transcriptomics time courses, HORIZON reconstructs tissue geometry, gene expression, and cell abundance more accurately than existing spatial and unbalanced trajectory methods and interpolates held-out stages.
AI.conclusion: Factoring out shared rigid motion via horizontal flow matching enables accurate, continuous reconstruction of spatiotemporal tissue dynamics from unaligned spatial transcriptomics snapshots.

title: Reconstruction vs. Prediction Pre-Training of Discrete Video Representations for Continuous Control
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Accepted to the PTA Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Self-supervised video encoders are commonly trained to either reconstruct pixels or predict latent features, yet it remains unclear how these objectives shape representations for downstream dynamics. We present a capacity-matched study isolating this choice: two identical video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck are trained under autoencoding and V-JEPA objectives on a continuous control environment. We introduce a simple asymmetric discretization scheme to apply the same bottleneck to the predictive model. The resulting representations exhibit a clear trade-off: the autoencoder preserves substantially more physical state information and achieves slightly better one-step latent prediction, while the predictive encoder accumulates less error under autoregressive rollout. Structural probes suggest that this advantage is associated with greater robustness to low-level visual perturbations and stronger dependence on temporal context. These results indicate that predictive and reconstructive objectives induce distinct representations of dynamics, trading state fidelity for properties that may benefit long-horizon prediction.

AI.tldr: This capacity-matched study compares pixel reconstruction (autoencoding) and latent prediction (V-JEPA) pre-training of discrete video representations (FSQ bottleneck) for continuous control. It reveals a trade-off: autoencoding preserves more physical state and one-step accuracy, while predictive pre-training reduces autoregressive rollout error.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised video encoders typically use either pixel reconstruction or latent feature prediction, but how these objectives shape representations for downstream dynamics remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors train two identical video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck on a continuous control environment under autoencoding and V-JEPA objectives, introducing an asymmetric discretization scheme for the predictive model and evaluating with dynamics and structural probes.
AI.result: The autoencoder preserves substantially more physical state information and achieves slightly better one-step latent prediction, whereas the predictive encoder accumulates less error during autoregressive rollouts and exhibits greater robustness to low-level visual perturbations and stronger temporal-context dependence.
AI.conclusion: Reconstructive and predictive objectives induce distinct dynamical representations, trading off fine-grained state fidelity for robustness and stability in long-horizon rollouts.

title: Learning Trajectories Leave Decodable Traces in Neural Network Weight Space and Internal Representations
summary: Neural networks trained on the same task develop related weight-space structures, yet remain distinguishable after learning. Do these differences merely reflect alternative solutions, or do they preserve information about individual learning histories? We tested whether final weights reveal initialization, task order, and earlier trajectory states. Training reorganized the ensemble: initial pairwise distances did not consistently predict final distances. Nevertheless, all 30 trained networks were correctly matched to their initial weights among ten candidates per dataset. Networks sharing an initialization also developed recognizable final hidden representations across different batch schedules, although direct comparisons with initial activity did not recover identity. Learning order remained readable as well. A linear probe decoded the order of two earlier tasks with 100% accuracy on 80 held-out networks after ten epochs of a common final task. Earlier intermediate weight states were partly predictable, but individual initial weights could not be reliably reconstructed. Final weights thus retain selective historical information rather than a complete trajectory record. Perturbed networks recovered classification performance without returning to their unperturbed training paths. This separation persisted across datasets, intervention times, and network layers. Moreover, 2,157 of 2,160 aligned endpoint pairs showed no positive loss barrier at sampled interpolation points, indicating low-loss connections between distinct solutions rather than convergence to one weight vector. Together, these findings show that a shared task constrains networks to related successful solutions without erasing their individual histories. Final weights reflect not only what a network has learned, but also where learning began and how it unfolded.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether neural network weights and hidden representations retain traces of their individual training histories. Across experiments, final weights reliably decode initialization identity and earlier task order, even though aligned solutions lie in low-loss connected basins.
AI.motivation: Networks trained on the same task develop similar weight-space structures yet remain distinct, raising the question of whether these differences reflect arbitrary equivalent solutions or preserved learning histories.
AI.method: The authors train ensembles of networks with varied initializations, batch schedules, task orders, and perturbations, testing initialization matching, linear probing of earlier task order, intermediate-state prediction, and linear mode connectivity across 2,160 aligned endpoint pairs.
AI.result: All 30 trained networks were matched to their initial weights among ten candidates per dataset, and a linear probe decoded earlier two-task order with 100% accuracy on 80 held-out networks after ten epochs of a common final task. Perturbed networks recovered accuracy without returning to unperturbed paths, and 2,157 of 2,160 aligned endpoint pairs showed no positive loss barrier.
AI.conclusion: Shared task training constrains networks to low-loss connected solutions without erasing selective historical traces of initialization and learning trajectory.

title: Bias-Only Training Dynamics in ReLU Networks
summary: Neural networks with randomly initialized, fixed weights and trainable biases are universal approximators, yet the dynamics of bias-only training remain largely unexplored. We study these dynamics in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks through activation codes, the binary patterns of active neurons that partition the input space into convex polyhedral regions. We show that the gradients with respect to the biases depend on each input only through its activation code, and hence the training dynamics can be characterized with these codes. In particular, as long as the activation codes remain fixed, training reduces to a linear least-squares problem with the codes as features. Training can then be understood as a sequence of least-squares problems, with transitions occurring when neurons change their activation states. We show that the fraction of switching neurons vanishes as the network widens, and the training dynamics approach those of linear least squares on the initial activation codes in the infinite-width limit. Our experiments support these theoretical findings, showing that while activation switches can noticeably affect training in narrower networks, their relative frequency and the associated changes in the dynamics diminish as the width increases.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes bias-only training dynamics in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks with fixed random weights through activation codes. It proves that training acts as a sequence of linear least-squares problems that converges to fixed-code linear least squares in the infinite-width limit.
AI.motivation: While ReLU networks with fixed random weights and trainable biases are universal approximators, their training dynamics are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors characterize bias gradients via binary activation codes (patterns of active neurons partitioning input space into convex polyhedra), showing that training reduces to linear least squares while codes remain fixed, and analyze neuron-switching rates as network width grows.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis and experiments show that the fraction of switching neurons vanishes as width increases; while switches noticeably affect narrower networks, infinite-width bias-only training converges to linear least squares on the initial activation codes.
AI.conclusion: Activation-code decomposition explains bias-only ReLU training as piecewise linear least squares that simplifies to a single linear solve at large widths.

title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
comment: Code available at: this https URL
summary: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM), an unsupervised geometric framework for survival analysis that models disease progression as geodesic flows on a curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian. On a 184-patient renal carcinoma cohort, SOSM achieves a 0.768 mean C-index and significant risk stratification (p < 0.001).
AI.motivation: Supervised survival models struggle with sparse, noisy, or censored endpoints in high-dimensional multi-omics data.
AI.method: SOSM decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels by projecting multi-omics arrays into a latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows.
AI.result: On a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort under 5-fold cross-validation, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of 0.768 +/- 0.068, significant out-of-fold survival divergence (log-rank p < 0.001), a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation for high-risk patients, and autonomous recovery of canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers.
AI.conclusion: Modeling systemic failure as an emergent geometric phase transition enables accurate, label-free prognostic representation learning from high-dimensional multi-omics data.

title: Synthesizing hyperspectral Data using generative Models to train spectral Unmixing Methods for low-cost Crop Residue Cover Mapping
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures. Published in the XXV ISPRS Congress 2026
summary: The spectral range of the Field Imaging Nanosatellite for Crop residue Hyperspectral Mapping (FINCH), developed by the University of Toronto Aerospace Team's Space System Division, poses significant challenges for hyperspectral unmixing to determine crop residue cover fractional abundances. The severe lack of standard indices necessitates the use of complex, data-driven unmixing models. Complex unmixing models require dense, well-distributed manifolds, whereas ground-truth datasets are sparse and expensive. To better leverage the information content in existing ground-truth datasets, this study presents a framework that decouples interpolation and abundance-mapping estimation via an intermediary conditional data generator, contrasting with traditional single-model unmixing pipelines. This decoupling enables the inclusion of physical prior knowledge about spectra, which is not natively accessible to unmixing models, thereby artificially expanding the dataset to serve as a Monte Carlo approximation of the population risk. To test this hypothesis, we have proposed two generator models: a 1D Conditional U-Net with Conformer Layers (GD-Streamline) and a Dual-Path Transformer Conditional Variational AutoEncoder (TCVAE), and two unmixing models: Multi-Layered Perceptrons (MLP) and Fourier Neural Operators (FNO). The results of the study indicate a need for rigorous integration and introduction of spectral priors within the scope of the proposed decoupling framework to prevent domain and mode collapse and hallucination by the generator models; otherwise, this leads to falsely approximated data manifolds, ultimately resulting in unsatisfactory and out-of-distribution unmixing performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a decoupled hyperspectral unmixing framework for crop residue cover mapping that uses conditional generative models (GD-Streamline and TCVAE) to expand sparse ground-truth datasets before training MLP and FNO unmixing models. It finds that without rigorous spectral priors, generators hallucinate and degrade out-of-distribution unmixing.
AI.motivation: Hyperspectral unmixing for the FINCH nanosatellite lacks standard indices and requires data-driven models, but ground-truth datasets are too sparse and expensive for complex unmixing models.
AI.method: The authors decouple interpolation from abundance estimation using two conditional data generators—a 1D Conditional U-Net with Conformer Layers (GD-Streamline) and a Dual-Path Transformer Conditional VAE (TCVAE)—to augment data for MLP and Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) unmixing models.
AI.result: Experiments show that without rigorous integration of physical spectral priors, generative models suffer from domain/mode collapse and hallucination, producing falsely approximated manifolds that lead to unsatisfactory out-of-distribution unmixing performance.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling data generation from spectral unmixing requires strong physical spectral priors to prevent manifold hallucination and achieve reliable crop residue cover mapping.

title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
comment: Accepted for publication in the Journal of Intelligent Information Systems (Springer Nature)
summary: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that prototypical parts—cohesive groups of related features—should be integrated alongside feature attribution in tabular XAI to reduce cognitive load and validate the data manifold. It introduces a Geometric Validity Triad and outlines open challenges for composite explanation pipelines.
AI.motivation: Tabular XAI relies heavily on feature attribution methods that force non-expert users to evaluate dozens of isolated features, imposing excessive cognitive load and neglecting data-manifold validity.
AI.method: The authors ground prototypical parts in Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to explain cognitive load reduction, and introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize how prototypes validate the underlying data manifold.
AI.result: The paper synthesizes cognitive and geometric arguments for pairing similarity-based prototypical-part explanations with feature-level auditing in composite pipelines, and identifies open research challenges and potential solutions.
AI.conclusion: Integrating prototypical parts with feature attribution offers a more comprehensible, manifold-valid paradigm for high-stakes tabular XAI.

title: What Survival Benchmarks Don't Tell You: Impact of Model Selection and Dataset Regimes
summary: Despite the proliferation of survival analysis methods, current benchmarks often operate under narrow conditions: they heavily rely on the concordance index (C-index) for evaluation and model selection, and frequently either exclude deep learning (DL) methods or underrepresent challenging dataset regimes. To address these limitations, we conduct a large-scale, neutral benchmark comparing 10 classical, tree-based, and DL methods across 49 diverse datasets. Crucially, we treat the model selection criterion (optimizing for C-index, Integrated Brier Score (IBS), or Mean Absolute Error (MAE-PO)) as an independent experimental variable. Using Bayesian mixed-effects modeling, we demonstrate that evaluation design heavily dictates conclusions. For complex DL and tree-based architectures, selecting hyperparameters to optimize for IBS instead of C-index yields substantial improvements in probabilistic accuracy and calibration at a negligible cost to discriminative ranking. Furthermore, method performance (C-index, IBS, MAE-PO, and X-CAL) is fundamentally governed by dataset characteristics. While DL models scale exceptionally well with larger sample sizes, they suffer notable performance drops in high-dimensional feature spaces. Additionally, we expose a structural vulnerability where heavy censoring artificially inflates absolute calibration metrics, creating overly conservative tests. Ultimately, our findings challenge the utility of global single-number performance summaries and advocate for survival analysis results that transparently report the evaluation setup. Our code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a large-scale neutral benchmark of 10 survival analysis methods across 49 datasets, showing that model selection criteria and dataset characteristics strongly govern evaluation conclusions.
AI.motivation: Existing survival analysis benchmarks often rely narrowly on the concordance index (C-index) for evaluation and model selection, while excluding deep learning (DL) methods or underrepresenting challenging dataset regimes.
AI.method: The authors compare 10 classical, tree-based, and DL methods across 49 datasets, treating the model selection criterion (C-index, Integrated Brier Score (IBS), or Mean Absolute Error (MAE-PO)) as an independent experimental variable analyzed via Bayesian mixed-effects modeling.
AI.result: Selecting hyperparameters for IBS instead of C-index substantially improves probabilistic accuracy and calibration in complex DL and tree-based models at negligible cost to ranking; DL scales well with sample size but drops in high-dimensional feature spaces, and heavy censoring artificially inflates absolute calibration metrics.
AI.conclusion: Global single-number performance summaries are insufficient, and survival analysis studies should transparently report their full evaluation setup.

title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables
summary: Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics are fast alternatives to physics-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Their foundational limitation is a lack of zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, which results in an expensive, custom training campaign for each new vehicle design. Similar to pretrained models in other fields, a pretrained surrogate should adapt to a new vehicle class using only a few simulations and stay accurate on its pretraining domain. No prior study has systematically tested this transfer behavior.
