We conduct a large-scale, controlled benchmarking study on five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets. These datasets differ from the source in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions. We find that fine-tuning these surrogates outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of the comparisons and lowers the accuracy of the surrogate on its source dataset. We introduce GeoReplay, a geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay that keeps source simulations resembling the target in training and applies their updates only when they agree with the target gradient. A risk bound separates geometric coverage from differences in the simulated physics, and we prove that every sufficiently small GeoReplay step decreases the target training objective. GeoReplay lowers the source error of fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings and matches its target accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks transfer learning for neural aerodynamic surrogates across vehicle classes and introduces GeoReplay, a source replay method that preserves source accuracy while matching fine-tuning target accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics lack zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, and no prior study has systematically tested whether pretrained surrogates can adapt to new classes with few simulations without forgetting their pretraining domain.
AI.method: The authors benchmark five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets and propose GeoReplay, which retains source simulations resembling the target and applies their updates only when aligned with the target gradient, backed by a risk bound and convergence proof.
AI.result: Standard fine-tuning outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of comparisons and degrades source-dataset accuracy, whereas GeoReplay lowers fine-tuning source error in 77 of 80 settings while matching target accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay enables pretrained aerodynamic surrogates to adapt to new vehicle classes without sacrificing performance on their original domain.

title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
summary: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework that composes specialized atomic reasoning LoRA experts via a distilled lightweight router to improve mathematical reasoning in LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches treat mathematical reasoning in LLMs as a monolithic capability, and even recent atomic-skill decomposition methods lack effective ways to compose these specialized abilities per problem.
AI.method: AMR trains capability-specific LoRA experts, uses gradient-free optimization on validation subsets to find low-loss composition prototypes, filters prototype preferences by token-level negative log-likelihood confidence margins, and distills pseudo-labels into a lightweight router for inference.
AI.result: On the AtomicMath benchmark with Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, and improves logical reasoning from 39.4% to 46.8%.
AI.conclusion: Instance-level composition of specialized atomic skills via a distilled router is an effective way to strengthen mathematical reasoning in LLMs without costly online optimization.

title: TangentPDE: Learning Local Operator Responses with Sparse Finite-Difference Supervision
summary: Neural PDE operators are often optimized through state reconstruction, which largely constrains operator values at observed inputs but does not fully characterize their sensitivity to local perturbations. A more faithful approximation of operator behavior requires not only accurate state predictions, but also correct variations along local perturbation directions. We present TangentPDE, which uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives and constructs task-relevant finite-step responses from the state outputs of a reference solver at sparse paired inputs. Its objective jointly constrains state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and response-magnitude calibration, thereby learning both operator values and their local variations. Because the response labels are constructed solely from state outputs at paired inputs, the method requires neither explicit derivative labels, linearized or adjoint PDE solves, nor full Jacobians, and remains applicable to nonlinear solvers without derivative interfaces. Building on this, we additionally propose a selectively executed adaptation mechanism to strengthen local operator representations under finite-difference supervision. Budget-matched and correspondence-perturbed controls isolate the effect of relational supervision from improvements attributable to additional state observations or increased data volume. Designed as a plug-and-play training framework, TangentPDE integrates with diverse neural-operator backbones. Across four PDE systems and 20 task-backbone settings, TangentPDE lowers the three-seed mean state error in 18 settings and the corresponding Rollout@20 error in 18, while intrinsic finite-step response gains are strongest on DiffReact and remain task- and backbone-dependent elsewhere.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TangentPDE, a plug-and-play training framework that uses sparse finite-difference supervision from paired solver states to teach neural PDE operators both state values and local perturbation responses.
AI.motivation: Neural PDE operators trained only on state reconstruction do not fully capture sensitivity to local perturbations, while obtaining exact derivatives requires linearized or adjoint PDE solves that are often unavailable for nonlinear solvers.
AI.method: TangentPDE constructs finite-step response labels from reference solver state outputs at sparse paired inputs, jointly optimizes state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and magnitude calibration, and adds a selectively executed adaptation mechanism.
AI.result: Across four PDE systems and 20 task-backbone settings, TangentPDE lowers three-seed mean state error in 18 settings and Rollout@20 error in 18 settings, with the strongest intrinsic finite-step response gains on DiffReact.
AI.conclusion: Sparse finite-difference relational supervision improves neural PDE operator accuracy and local sensitivity without requiring derivative interfaces or adjoint solvers.

title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Models, prompts, replies with tool calls, and code: this https URL
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a blinded test of GPT-6 Astra auditing clinical prediction models via query access alone, finding it accurately describes models and detects 96% of planted flaws, though many reported issues require verification.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to explain clinical prediction models and detect faults, but their ability to faithfully describe models, find flaws, and discover valid relationships has not been rigorously tested against ground truth.
AI.method: Using International Stroke Trial data, the authors train four model types, plant one flaw in each of 24 copies mixed with 8 clean models, and have GPT-6 Astra audit each blindly three times via a prediction-only query tool under pre-committed judging rules.
AI.result: Surrogate models (median 128 terms) reproduced log-odds with mean R^2 of 0.976, detected the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%), and 11% of 601 unexpected relationships held in later patients (33% after training-data checks); however, 60% of 1,089 checkable problem reports failed pre-specified checks and 15% were not found in the model.
AI.conclusion: With query access alone, an LLM can faithfully describe black-box clinical models and find nearly all planted flaws, but its problem reports must be verified against the model and its discoveries checked on data.

title: Monoculture Robust Learning
summary: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $\rho$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $\rho$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $\gamma$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = \Omega(\log(1/\gamma))$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces monoculture robustness in PAC learning to bound the joint failure of multiple hypotheses trained on a single dataset, connecting it to algorithmic replicability and establishing a sample-size lower bound.
AI.motivation: Algorithmic monoculture causes models trained on shared data or components to fail on the same inputs, raising the question of whether a single dataset can yield k hypotheses whose joint failure matches training on k independent datasets.
AI.method: The authors formalize individual monoculture robustness by bounding the conjunctive error of k hypotheses and prove that running a rho-replicable base learner independently k times on the same sample yields exponential error decay in k.
AI.result: The proposed replicability-based procedure achieves individual monoculture error shrinking exponentially with k (controlled by single-run error and rho), complemented by a worst-case lower bound showing that driving conjunctive error to gamma can require a sample-size multiplier of Omega(log(1/gamma)).
AI.conclusion: Algorithmic replicability provides a principled mechanism for achieving monoculture robustness in PAC learning, with matching theoretical limits on sample complexity.

title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Includes appendices
summary: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Cap-and-Track, an asynchronous LLM inference dispatch system deployed at Meta that uses fail-fast backend refusals to dynamically track serving capacity without output-length prediction.
AI.motivation: Fixed dispatch rates for LLM inference become stale as serving fleets resize, request sizes vary, and generative output lengths remain unknown at admission, causing either underutilization or long queue waits.
AI.method: Cap-and-Track combines durable external priority queues, a fail-fast admission check (Cap) at saturated resources, and a stateful dispatcher (Track) that probes upward and backs off using only refusal signals.
AI.result: In a production A/B test at Meta, Cap-and-Track served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than a queued fixed-rate precursor, ran within 1% of tuned fixed-rate goodput in replay with about a quarter of the refusal share, and handles over 300 million daily requests (peaking at 1.1 billion in 24 hours).
AI.conclusion: Steering stateful dispatch solely by capacity refusals while keeping in-engine queues short enables efficient, adaptive LLM inference across shifting capacity.

title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
summary: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Motivated by these gaps, we propose a new evaluation suite that combines utility of user simulators for evaluating agents and two measures of fidelity to real users: population-level fidelity assesses collective interaction patterns, while trace-level fidelity assesses the preservation of individual users' goals, constraints, and persona. Under the same detection criterion, our evaluation suite detects all 10 perturbations. Evaluating six user simulators on 351 real multi-turn sessions in which 348 distinct users across 23 languages and agents work together to create and refine artifacts such as full-stack web apps, games, design assets, and automated workflows, we find that population-level measures can miss when a simulated user pursues the wrong goal, ignores a constraint, or behaves out of character, highlighting the need to assess fidelity at comprehensive granularities.

AI.tldr: This paper meta-evaluates user simulator metrics for interactive agents, shows prior metrics miss half of induced failures, and proposes a new evaluation suite combining utility with population- and trace-level fidelity.
AI.motivation: Although user simulators are widely used to evaluate interactive agents, it is unclear whether existing simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, or premature stopping.
AI.method: The authors perturb simulated replays to induce 10 failure types, test three prior evaluation frameworks against them, and propose a new suite measuring agent-evaluation utility alongside population-level and trace-level fidelity across 351 real multi-turn sessions.
AI.result: Prior evaluation methods detected only 5-6 of 10 perturbations and even favored populations accepting broken work, whereas the proposed suite detected all 10 perturbations and revealed that population-level measures miss individual goal, constraint, and persona failures.
AI.conclusion: Assessing user simulators requires both population-level and trace-level fidelity alongside utility to ensure simulated users faithfully preserve individual user goals and constraints.

title: What Moves the Ceiling on Automated Audit: from General Code to Scientific Code, Results and Data
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: Models increasingly check what other models write. We study one shipped arrangement, in which an auditor from a different vendor reads the work and deterministic checks verify what code can verify, and measure its limits against ground truth no model supplies. On general-purpose code with hidden tests, eight readings of the auditor reach 30.0% recall [20.0, 40.7] at 16.0% [10.1, 22.3] flags on correct code, with diminishing returns and no plateau. The reading model (confounded with its sampling), one rulebook sentence and the decision rule each move that figure, and much of what is missed is, on a post hoc rating, behaviour the specification never determined. In three preregistered science studies, checking that reported numbers trace to their sources flagged all 49 inconsistent reports and none of 25 consistent fabrications, of which the model auditor flagged 23 (21 with a sound finding, post hoc); on data, a documentation-derived validator and the auditor flagged overlapping but different faulty items, together 112 of 140 at a 2.9% [0.7, 5.7] flag rate on clean data; and on scientific code, reframing the task around one step cut flags on correct code from 68.7% to 36.0%. Where both tiers ran, the deterministic one flagged no clean item and could not see consistent error; the model saw some and erred itself. Studies making model calls were preregistered, the two unregistered analyses are named, and every quoted report passed independent cross-vendor review.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the limits of cross-vendor LLM auditing paired with deterministic checks across general code, scientific code, results, and data, showing complementary strengths and persistent error rates.
AI.motivation: Models increasingly audit other models' outputs, yet the ceiling of automated auditing against ground truth across code, scientific results, and data remains unquantified.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a cross-vendor LLM auditor combined with deterministic checks against ground truth on general-purpose code with hidden tests and three preregistered science studies covering results, data, and scientific code.
AI.result: On general code, eight auditor readings reached 30.0% recall at 16.0% false flags on correct code; on science results, deterministic checks flagged all 49 inconsistent reports but 0 of 25 consistent fabrications (23 flagged by the auditor); on data, both tiers together caught 112 of 140 faults at a 2.9% clean flag rate; and task reframing cut clean scientific code flags from 68.7% to 36.0%.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic checks and LLM auditors catch different failure modes, and while task framing improves precision, automated auditing still faces a substantial ceiling on specification-dependent and consistent errors.

title: Measuring What Matters in the Age of AI: The Research Software Metrics Landscape
summary: Research software now serves as a primary instrument of science, but the methods the community uses to judge its quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact remain scattered across software engineering, open science, FAIR software, citation, and research-assessment literature. AI-assisted development sharpens the problem: code can be produced at rates that outpace human review capacity, provenance and attribution are harder to track, scholarly credit systems cannot keep pace, and existing metrics inherit assumptions about how research software gets developed that may no longer apply. To aid in navigating these challenges, we present a focused landscape synthesis of research software metrics based on 49 substantive references, organizing the recurring metrics into eight families described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to misuse. Many widely cited research software metrics serve as partial signals but make weak standalone measures of scientific impact. The AI era opens or widens gaps around provenance, maintainability of generated code, reviewer effort, model and data dependencies, reuse and community-health signal inflation, and credit for human labor that AI does not perform. We argue for responsible, contextual, mixed-method use of research software metrics, and offer decision guidance for Research Software Engineers (RSEs), principal investigators, institutions, and funders selecting metrics that support better software, fairer credit, and more trustworthy science. All findings rest on the 49-reference focused review; a reproducible search-and-triage protocol and a 727-record triaged corpus accompany the paper as a transparency artifact for a future full systematic mapping study.

AI.tldr: This paper synthesizes the research software metrics landscape from 49 references into eight metric families and identifies gaps widened by AI-assisted software development.
AI.motivation: Methods for judging research software quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact are scattered across disciplines, and AI-assisted coding strains existing assumptions around review capacity, provenance, and scholarly credit.
AI.method: The authors conduct a focused landscape synthesis of 49 substantive references (accompanied by a 727-record triaged corpus), organizing recurring metrics into eight families by data source, construct, validity, automation potential, and misuse risk.
AI.result: Many widely cited metrics are weak standalone measures of scientific impact, and AI-assisted development widens gaps in provenance, generated-code maintainability, reviewer effort, model/data dependencies, signal inflation, and credit for non-AI human labor.
AI.conclusion: Research software evaluation requires responsible, contextual, mixed-method metric selection tailored to Research Software Engineers, PIs, institutions, and funders.

title: Error Analysis of Deep Learning
comment: Mathematical survey of error analysis for neural network methods, with nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz method for elliptic PDEs as running examples. Covers function and Sobolev approximation, statistical estimation, and optimization error, together with stability estimates, convergence rates, and selected proofs
summary: This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.

AI.tldr: This review examines deep learning theory through error decomposition into approximation, statistical, and optimization errors across diverse problem domains.
AI.motivation: Understanding theoretical guarantees for trained neural networks requires tracing how individual error bounds combine across different loss structures and learning paradigms.
AI.method: The authors use nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples to illustrate error decomposition, then review representative analyses in scientific ML, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and LLMs.
AI.result: The review clarifies which error components are controlled in each domain, how they are combined, and what assumptions are required to obtain end-to-end guarantees for trained networks.
AI.conclusion: Error decomposition provides a unifying lens for analyzing and comparing theoretical guarantees across modern deep learning applications.

title: HydroMind: A Checkable Agent for Autonomous Hydrological Research
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 1 table
summary: General-purpose coding agents have written code for hydrological and Earth-system models. In these studies the researchers decided in advance how the model would be evaluated, for example the test period, the scoring function, and the standard the model had to meet. No study has tested what happens when the agent makes these decisions itself: how many of its claims are supported by its own data, code, and results, and whether readers can check them. Both may depend on the agent's harness, that is, the tools it can call and the written instructions it follows. We compared three harnesses: the agent's own harness; this harness plus the modeling tools of HydroMind, a hydrological modeling system we developed for general-purpose agents, which run every model through fixed commands and store its settings, trained model, and predictions; and both plus HydroMind's research procedure, under which the agent writes a research design before running any model and records every change to it. Under each harness, the same agent studied four open questions in hydrological model development and was given only the data. Under the three harnesses, the experiments submitted 23, 20, and 41 claims, each stating that one model or approach is better than, worse than, or similar to another. A claim does not hold if the difference recomputed from the experiment's own code and predictions disagrees with it, or if the code did not compare the two models or approaches the claim names. Under the three harnesses, 30%, 20%, and 5% of the claims did not hold. A statistical test, confidence interval, or decision rule that lets readers judge the stated difference was reported for 48%, 53%, and 83% of the claims. With the language model unchanged, changing only the harness reduced the share of claims that do not hold and increased the share that readers can check.

AI.tldr: This paper tests how agent harnesses affect autonomous hydrological research, showing that structured modeling tools and a pre-execution research procedure sharply reduce unsupported claims and improve checkability.
AI.motivation: While coding agents have written hydrological models under researcher-defined evaluation rules, no study has tested how many claims hold or can be checked when an agent makes evaluation decisions itself.
AI.method: The authors compare three harnesses on four open hydrological questions using the same LLM: the agent's own harness, adding HydroMind's fixed modeling and logging tools, and adding HydroMind's research procedure requiring a recorded design before execution.
AI.result: Across the three harnesses, the agent submitted 23, 20, and 41 claims, of which 30%, 20%, and 5% did not hold against the experiment's own code and predictions, while checkable statistical support rose from 48% to 53% to 83%.
AI.conclusion: Without changing the underlying language model, constraining the agent's harness with reproducible tools and a structured research procedure substantially improves claim validity and checkability.

title: SIGMA: speaker-isolated, symptom-structured multimodal estimation of depression severity from clinical interviews
summary: Clinical interviews are central to depression assessment but time-consuming and rater-dependent. Automated severity estimation offers scalable screening, yet existing methods often retain interviewer speech (confounding participant cues), fuse modalities late (losing fine-grained cross-modal dynamics), or score symptoms independently (ignoring inter-symptom correlations). We present SIGMA, a speaker-aware, symptom-structured framework for depression-severity estimation from semi-clinical interviews. SIGMA uses speaker diarization to restrict input to participant speech, cross-attention so that text, audio and video condition one another during encoding, and a graded-response head that predicts the eight questionnaire items jointly through a shared latent severity trait with item-specific ordered thresholds. On the Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, SIGMA achieves state-of-the-art performance (CCC 0.762, RMSE 4.13, MAE 3.30 over five seeds). Ablations confirm that isolating participant speech and joint, structured symptom prediction each substantially improve concordance and estimation accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SIGMA, a speaker-isolated, cross-modal, symptom-structured framework for estimating depression severity from clinical interviews, achieving state-of-the-art results on E-DAIC.
AI.motivation: Existing automated depression severity estimators often retain interviewer speech, fuse modalities too late, or score symptoms independently without modeling inter-symptom correlations.
AI.method: SIGMA applies speaker diarization to isolate participant speech, uses cross-attention across text, audio, and video during encoding, and employs a graded-response head to jointly predict eight questionnaire items via a shared latent severity trait.
AI.result: On the Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, SIGMA achieves state-of-the-art performance (CCC 0.762, RMSE 4.13, MAE 3.30 over five seeds), with ablations confirming gains from both speaker isolation and structured symptom prediction.
AI.conclusion: Isolating participant cues and jointly modeling structured symptom relationships substantially improves automated depression severity estimation.

title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
comment: 31 pages
summary: This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations. We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.

AI.tldr: This systematic literature review surveys the use of machine learning to optimize computer algebra algorithms and perform direct symbolic computation, identifying key benchmarks and explainability gaps.
AI.motivation: Traditional symbolic computation methods in computer algebra are mathematically rigorous but computationally expensive, motivating data-driven approaches to guide heuristics, select algorithms, or compute symbolically.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic literature review covering applications such as cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Groebner basis computation, and symbolic integration, comparing ML models from decision trees to transformers.
AI.result: ML techniques effectively guide heuristics and predict algebraic properties, but the field lacks standardized benchmark datasets, limiting cross-method comparison and model generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Establishing shared benchmarks and leveraging explainable AI tools will be essential to build trust and advance machine learning within computer algebra.

title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Rat Locomotion
comment: NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages main text, 41 pages total, 7 figures in main text. Code and videos: this https URL
summary: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Rat v2, Rat NCAP (a spinal-circuit-inspired neural architecture), and GPU-accelerated training infrastructure to simulate rat locomotion and study neural circuit mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Embodied simulations of animal behavior require coordinated advances in biomechanical bodies, biologically grounded neural architectures, and fast training infrastructure to study complex neural-body-environment interactions.
AI.method: The authors develop the Rat v2 biomechanical body, the Rat NCAP architecture incorporating mammalian spinal circuit connectivity and a flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface, and GPU-accelerated simulation and training tools.
AI.result: Without imitation learning, the model learns multi-speed locomotion and gait transitions matching experimental kinematics and cell-type-specific neural activity, while in silico ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict perturbation responses.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate-abstraction embodied simulations can simultaneously reproduce complex locomotion and provide mechanistic insights into underlying neural circuits.

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
comment: 29 pages, 4 figures. Code: this https URL . Data: this https URL
summary: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RFBench, a simulator-grounded multimodal benchmark of 10,000 passive RF layouts, revealing systematic weaknesses in current multimodal LLMs and showing substantial gains from domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Multimodal language models have not been systematically tested on connecting passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior.
AI.method: The authors build RFBench using 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated in ADS Momentum with paired geometric primitives, raster images, occupancy grids, S-parameters, and labels across seven tasks, and benchmark seven multimodal LLMs plus RF-specific fine-tuning.
AI.result: Baseline multimodal LLMs struggle to generate valid layouts and faithful electromagnetic responses, whereas RF-specific fine-tuning raises T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and T3 within-2-dB response prediction from 17.7% to 62.8%.
AI.conclusion: RFBench provides a grounded testbed for multimodal RF design, showing that domain adaptation yields large gains while leaving room for further progress.

title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables
summary: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes why sub-4-bit quantized vision CNNs collapse on ImageNet-1k, shows that keeping under 5% of critical activations in 8-bit recovers up to 92% of lost accuracy, and exposes CPU bit-unpacking slowdowns.
AI.motivation: Compressing vision CNN weights below 4 bits causes catastrophic accuracy collapse, yet where collapse occurs, how much mixed-precision recovery can rescue, and what runtime costs arise on CPUs remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors evaluate ResNet and EfficientNet backbones on the 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set, map layer-wise degradation, test a multi-step mixed-precision recovery waterfall, and benchmark runtime on ARM and x86 CPUs.
AI.result: Collapse is non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers; keeping under 5% of critical layer activations at 8-bit recovers up to 92% of lost accuracy, while software bit-unpacking on CPUs causes a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown.
AI.conclusion: Navigating sub-4-bit deployment requires balancing selective 8-bit activation retention against software bit-unpacking overhead on edge CPUs.

title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures
summary: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

AI.tldr: This paper investigates global self-attention placement and recurrent weight sharing in EfficientNet-B0 on ImageNet-1k, finding that zero-gated residual attention adapters boost accuracy and alternating two shared templates cuts parameters with minimal loss.
AI.motivation: Hybridizing compact convolutional backbones raises two open design questions: where global self-attention improves over pure convolution, and whether repeated blocks can share weights without losing capacity.
AI.method: Using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments on ImageNet-1k, the authors compare BiFPN wrappers against zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3-P5 and evaluate recurrent weight sharing with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics.
AI.result: Residual self-attention adapters reach 74.02% standalone (+0.954 percentage points over matched plain B0 at 73.88% vs. 72.92%), with attention amplitude rising from 27.2% (P3) to 66.3% (P5); alternating two shared templates in Stage 6 cuts parameters by 10.9% and recovers to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared).
AI.conclusion: Lightweight residual attention adapters at deeper semantic stages and alternating two-template weight sharing offer effective parameter-accuracy trade-offs in compact vision backbones.

title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
comment: Equal contribution: Minghe Zhang and Xuetao Kang. 38 pages, 8 figures, 13 tables
summary: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GUARD, a grader-free framework for stabilizing recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses using pre-execution self-checks, directional regret, and a Soft-HURT promotion gate.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement of agent harnesses without external graders often backfires because reflection and scalar scores conflate newly broken behaviors with unsolved tasks, causing regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat.
AI.method: GUARD decomposes tasks into pre-execution self-checks, grades trajectories against them to pin mastered rules and prioritize newly broken ones via directional regret, selects candidate edits by group-relative fitness, and promotes edits only when a Soft-HURT gate confirms gains outweigh regressions.
AI.result: Across memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning benchmarks, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially reducing deployment token usage.
AI.conclusion: Directional regret and gated promotion enable stable, reference-free continual harness evolution for autonomous agents.

title: JEPA for astronomy: multi-survey spectral alignment puts stellar parameters on the leading principal axes
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to AAS journals. Comments welcome
summary: Spectra from different surveys carry different systematics and are not calibrated against one another. Multi-survey foundation models for stellar spectra are then built by aligning embeddings of the same star observed across surveys. Most in astronomy follow the recipes established for language and vision, aligning with a contrastive loss that separates every star from the others. However, this does not ensure that the stellar physics is encoded in a form that a simple read-out can recover. Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed and varying only the alignment loss, we measure what an objective encodes from the principal-component geometry of the Gaia BP/RP (XP) spectra and from a linear probe of the stellar parameters. In a properly aligned embedding, the leading two principal components form a plane that recovers an analog of the Kiel diagram, the third component tracks [Fe/H], and [alpha/Fe] varies coherently across the plane, such that the chemically defined Galactic disks and accreted populations occupy distinct loci. We show that legibility, the ease of reading the information out, is highest for a training objective that never pushes stars apart, and instead constrains only the overall distribution of each survey's embeddings (JEPA). JEPA also exceeds the contrastive alternative at the same architecture, and the performance improves further as more surveys (Gaia XP+LAMOST LRS+DESI+APOGEE) are included. Predicted abundances for 8.0 million XP giants reproduce the main [alpha/Fe]-[Fe/H] structure of the Milky Way. These results indicate that the choice of alignment objective, not alignment alone, determines whether stellar labels are linearly recoverable.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that aligning multi-survey stellar spectra with a JEPA objective rather than contrastive learning produces embeddings whose leading principal components linearly recover stellar parameters and Galactic populations.
AI.motivation: Multi-survey stellar foundation models typically use contrastive losses that push stars apart, which does not guarantee that physical stellar parameters are encoded in a linearly readable geometry.
AI.method: Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed, the authors vary only the alignment loss—comparing contrastive learning against JEPA, which constrains each survey's overall embedding distribution—and evaluate principal-component geometry and linear probes on Gaia XP, LAMOST LRS, DESI, and APOGEE spectra.
AI.result: JEPA yields higher linear legibility and outperforms contrastive alignment at the same architecture, with leading principal components recovering a Kiel-diagram analog, [Fe/H], and [alpha/Fe] loci, and predicted abundances for 8.0 million XP giants reproducing Milky Way structure.
AI.conclusion: The choice of alignment objective, rather than alignment alone, determines whether stellar physics is linearly recoverable in multi-survey spectral embeddings.

title: Optimal Control of RKHS Diffeomorphic Flows for Classification and Generative Modeling
comment: 55 pages, 21 figures, 16 tables, 6 algorithms
summary: We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. Because the objective and gradient are deterministic, matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and related second-order solvers are practical for both tasks, which we benchmark against a range of first- and second-order optimizers; the learned map is a diffeomorphism with explicitly controlled regularity. In experiments from dimension 2 to 256, the reduced GN solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested and, together with joint L-BFGS, the least work; a multiscale kernel improves the density fit, and a trainable GMM reference reduces the deformation needed for multimodal transport at comparable likelihood while lowering the likelihood on real data. The full-model solve is quadratic in the particle count and sub-linear in dimension; a control-point reduction makes the particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified optimal-control framework using RKHS diffeomorphic flows for both classification and density estimation, enabling exact divergence and fast second-order Gauss-Newton optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing continuous normalizing flows rely on stochastic trace estimators or potential-flow restrictions, making deterministic second-order optimization impractical.
AI.method: The authors parameterize flow velocities in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) for exact deterministic divergence, eliminate the terminal classifier or Gaussian-mixture reference via variable projection, compute gradients with an analytic discrete adjoint, and solve with matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and control-point reductions.
AI.result: Across dimensions 2 to 256, reduced GN uses the fewest iterations and, with joint L-BFGS, the least work among tested optimizers; multiscale kernels improve density fit, and control-point reduction achieves linear particle-count scaling at near-lossless accuracy.
AI.conclusion: RKHS-parameterized diffeomorphic flows unify classification and generative modeling while making deterministic second-order optimization practical.

title: Balancing Partition Forest for Causal Weighting
summary: Balancing weights are used in observational causal inference to construct a population in which the treatment is independent of observed pretreatment covariates. The ideal weight is the ratio between the product of the covariate and treatment marginals and their joint distribution, for binary and continuous treatments alike. We propose Balancing Partition Tree (BPT) and Balancing Partition Forest (BPF), which estimate this ratio on a learned rectangular partition of covariate--treatment space. Each split maximizes the gain in a Bregman divergence computed from joint and marginal counts. Two choices of divergence yield criteria that maximize the mutual information captured by the partition or reduce the squared error of the weights. We show that the population residual of either criterion bounds the bias of inverse-probability-weighted and doubly robust response estimators that use the population partition weights. Across 17 synthetic and semi-synthetic settings and three response estimators, BPF obtains the lowest mean RMSE rank among seven weight estimators, and a single tree fits in 0.14 seconds on 16,512 observations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Balancing Partition Tree (BPT) and Balancing Partition Forest (BPF) to estimate causal balancing weights for binary and continuous treatments using Bregman-divergence-based rectangular partitions.
AI.motivation: Observational causal inference requires estimating balancing weights—the ratio of marginal products to the joint covariate-treatment distribution—for both binary and continuous treatments.
AI.method: BPT and BPF learn rectangular partitions of covariate-treatment space by maximizing Bregman divergence gain from joint and marginal counts, yielding criteria that either maximize mutual information or minimize weight squared error, with proved bias bounds for IPW and doubly robust estimators.
AI.result: Across 17 synthetic and semi-synthetic settings and three response estimators, BPF achieves the lowest mean RMSE rank among seven weight estimators, and a single tree fits in 0.14 seconds on 16,512 observations.
AI.conclusion: Balancing Partition Forest provides a fast, theoretically grounded, and accurate method for estimating causal balancing weights across treatment types.

title: GRAFT: Graph-Regularized Prototype Fields for Realistic Test-Time Adaptation of VLMs
summary: Unlabeled test data can improve the zero-shot classifier of a vision-language model, yet transductive and test-time adaptation methods often fall below the zero-shot baseline when only a few vocabulary classes are present in a batch or when streams are correlated. We trace this failure to a shared design: every class owns independent parameters estimated from its own samples, so absent or rare classes are left at biased text anchors or fitted to foreign samples. We propose Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (GRAFT), which models the adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field that is partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, together with an explicit class-presence model. Inference is closed-form and gradient-free on cached features. Anchor-only shrinkage and a single global shift are the two extreme settings of the prior; absent classes are provably harmonic extensions of the present ones, and the pooling strength can be chosen by empirical Bayes. Under the realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, GRAFT improves over the zero-shot model in every setting and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GRAFT, a closed-form test-time adaptation method for vision-language models that models prototype displacements over a semantic class graph to handle batches with few or correlated classes.
AI.motivation: Existing transductive and test-time adaptation methods for VLMs estimate class parameters independently, causing performance to drop below zero-shot baselines when batches contain few classes or correlated streams.
AI.method: GRAFT models adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field partially pooled over a semantic class graph via a Gaussian Markov random field prior and an explicit class-presence model, with closed-form, gradient-free inference on cached features.
AI.result: Across eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts under realistic batch and online protocols, GRAFT consistently outperforms the zero-shot baseline in every setting and beats anchor-based transduction when few classes are present.
AI.conclusion: Graph-regularized partial pooling of prototype displacements prevents degradation on sparse or correlated test streams and enables reliable gradient-free VLM adaptation.

title: Optical Neural Networks Should Be Evaluated by Function, Not Only Physics
comment: 28 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables
summary: Optical neural networks (ONNs) are attracting significant attention as alternative platforms for machine learning (ML). In an ONN, an optical module often takes over part of the computation inside a digital ML pipeline. How much of the task does the optical module itself perform, and how much does it contribute to any claimed system-level advantages, such as throughput or energy? This paper offers a simple, function-oriented evaluation methodology. Whatever its internal physics, the optical module appears to the surrounding digital pipeline as a mapping between real-valued tensors. We therefore evaluate it in three steps: (i) define its boundary in the pipeline, as real-valued tensors in and out; (ii) replace it with standard digital modules to identify those that match the optical system's performance on the same task and metric; and (iii) state system-level claims, such as speed or energy, per inference against the performance-matched digital module. We summarize steps (i) and (ii) in an Expressivity Card and demonstrate its use on published ONN systems. This helps isolate the optical module's contribution and provides a concrete digital reference for assessing its claimed system-level advantages, without the need to understand the physics. While we focus on optical systems as the most prominent example, the same approach applies to any physical analog computing platform used in ML, wherever a physical module takes over part of a digital pipeline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-step, function-oriented evaluation methodology and Expressivity Card to benchmark optical neural networks (ONNs) and other physical analog modules against performance-matched digital modules.
AI.motivation: Claims of system-level speed or energy advantages for ONNs often lack a concrete digital reference that isolates how much of the task the optical module actually performs.
AI.method: The authors propose defining the physical module's tensor boundary in the digital pipeline, replacing it with standard digital modules to find those matching its task performance, and comparing system-level claims per inference against that performance-matched digital reference, summarized in an Expressivity Card.
AI.result: Demonstrating the Expressivity Card on published ONN systems isolates the optical module's functional contribution and establishes a fair digital baseline without requiring analysis of internal physics.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating physical analog computing platforms by their functional mapping against performance-matched digital equivalents provides a rigorous, standardized basis for system-level claims.

title: Isthmus: Bridging Supervision Islands Restores Uncertainty and Stability in One-Step Flows
summary: One-step flow maps are increasingly used as posterior samplers, where the point of sampling is the uncertainty that the samples carry. We find that the one-step sampler loses this uncertainty and becomes less stable. Compared with multi-step samples of the same network, its samples lose variance and decorrelate. Supervising the one-step jump directly makes this worse; the samples collapse further toward the conditional mean and break down when training is extended. We trace both failures to the locations where training places its pairs of start and end times. Only pairs on the diagonal of the time triangle receive targets from data, and the pair used for one-step sampling is either left unsupervised or supervised on an island, a set of pairs that the self-consistency identity does not connect to the diagonal, where the objective neither determines the one-step map nor anchors its training. We bridge the island with an isthmus, which places 5% of the training pairs along the whole edge of the triangle that joins the one-step pair to the diagonal. The error of the one-step map is then bounded by the self-consistency residual along this edge. With the network, the loss and the inference code unchanged and at no added cost, the isthmus improves one-step sampling across several flow-map objectives, in MRI reconstruction, face inpainting, and unconditional generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32. On brain MRI, it restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and the correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93; both vary far less across seeds, and the agreement holds when training is extended to three times its length.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses why one-step flow-map posterior samplers lose uncertainty and stability, and introduces Isthmus—placing 5% of training pairs along the edge connecting the one-step pair to the diagonal—to restore calibration and correlation.
AI.motivation: One-step flow maps used as posterior samplers suffer from variance collapse, decorrelation from multi-step samples, and instability under extended training, which direct one-step supervision worsens.
AI.method: The authors identify that one-step pairs sit on an unsupervised or disconnected "island" in the time triangle and bridge it with an "isthmus" by placing 5% of training pairs along the triangle edge linking the one-step pair to the supervised diagonal, without changing the network, loss, or inference code.
AI.result: Isthmus improves one-step sampling across MRI reconstruction, face inpainting, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet 32x32; on brain MRI, it restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93, remaining stable even when training is tripled.
AI.conclusion: Bridging supervision islands in the time triangle is a zero-cost, general fix that restores uncertainty and training stability in one-step flow-map samplers.

title: How Uncertain Is My Action? Self-Correcting Visual Planning with Frozen World Models
summary: A frozen latent world model combined with sampling-based model predictive control is a visual planner. At deployment, the executed action can depart from the commanded one, and the frozen model has no way to notice. We show that the model can be run in reverse: for any hypothesized actuation shift, it predicts what it should have observed under that shift, and comparing this prediction with what was actually observed quantifies the shift and lets the planner correct itself. Unlike the residual energy, which mixes the shift with the model's own error, the score keeps only the part of the residual that a shift can produce. This shift score detects the shift with a locally optimal test, estimates it with Cramer-Rao error bars, names the dominant generator, and compensates the planner once an alarm fires. On PushT, TwoRoom and OGBench-Cube with a frozen latent world model, measured detection follows the prediction to within 0.05 AUROC. Self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and from 0.378 to 0.432 on the harder Cube task, levels with an oracle that is told the true shift at the same block, better than five common test-time adaptation methods. On a real robotic arm, the score identifies a base-joint offset that no joint encoder registers and reduces the reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm, and under shifts drawn at random and sealed before the session, estimates recover 92-94% of the error reduction achieved with the true shift. The broader implication is that a frozen world model can act as a filter by predicting the future, testing action-interface uncertainty and validity, and finally correcting failures.

AI.tldr: This paper enables frozen latent world models to detect, estimate, and self-correct actuation shifts at deployment by running the model in reverse to compute a locally optimal shift score.
AI.motivation: Visual planners using frozen latent world models cannot detect when executed actions depart from commanded ones at deployment, and raw residual energy mixes actuation shifts with model error.
AI.method: The authors run the frozen world model in reverse to predict observations under hypothesized actuation shifts, isolating a shift score that detects shifts via a locally optimal test, estimates them with Cramer-Rao error bars, and compensates the planner.
AI.result: On PushT, TwoRoom, and OGBench-Cube, detection matches predictions within 0.05 AUROC, and self-correction raises success from 0.650 to 0.862 on PushT and 0.378 to 0.432 on Cube (matching an oracle and beating five test-time adaptation methods); on a real robotic arm, it cuts reach error from 36 mm to 3-5 mm.
AI.conclusion: Frozen world models can serve as self-correcting filters that diagnose and compensate for action-interface shifts without retraining.

title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms
comment: 32 pages
summary: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically shows that using multiple, evenly spaced—and especially adaptive—binary rating scales significantly improves item ranking over a single rating scale on online platforms.
AI.motivation: Online platforms often suffer from inflated, uninformative user ratings, and prior work has focused on optimizing only a single binary rating scale.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze splitting a single binary rating scale into multiple 0-1 step-function scales for different users, characterizing optimal threshold spacing and extending the model to adaptive sequential scales.
AI.result: Splitting a single scale into two always improves item rankings, optimal multiple scales use evenly spaced thresholds, and adaptive scales conditioned on prior user responses yield exponentially greater distinguishing power.
AI.conclusion: Deploying multiple or adaptive binary rating scales is a principled mechanism to overcome rating inflation and improve item ranking accuracy.

title: When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
summary: Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates how well 11 LLMs formulate high-stakes prediction problems under decision dependency, finding they fail without explicit methodological guidance in prompts and proposing validity-centered guidelines.
AI.motivation: While generative AI is increasingly used for data science, its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems—specifically handling decision dependency where past decisions affect observed outcomes—remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors evaluate code and explanations generated by 11 OpenAI and Anthropic models across seven prompt conditions in child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, checking whether implementations and explanations properly account for decision dependency.
AI.result: LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency unprompted (sometimes acknowledging it in text without fixing the code), but specifying the target, assumptions, and estimation procedure in prompts raises target-aligned implementation to 99-100%, with frontier models responding to simple descriptions of decision effects.
AI.conclusion: Analysts should not rely on LLMs to formulate high-stakes prediction problems autonomously and should follow validity-centered prompting and verification guidelines.

title: Same Model, Different People: Numerical Execution Contracts and the Reproducibility of Fairness Audits
comment: 47 pages, 2 figures, 35 tables. Under review
summary: Fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, but the arithmetic that evaluates it is part of that function. This study holds the model, records, threshold and audit code fixed and varies the numerical execution contract in two tiers. Tier 1 changes only how products and sums are computed, with the serialized weights byte-identical, and is the causal test of arithmetic. Tier 2 runs reduced-precision deployment configurations (BF16 compute, FP8 and 8-bit weights), which can also round weights and change engines and kernels, so its effects belong to the configuration. It audits three tabular model families and two open-weight language models (4B and 24B parameters) on four public tasks, including hospital readmission, on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple. Tier 1 changed decisions near the threshold, and which ones depended on the GPU and its software stack, but no verdict under the prespecified, unweighted tests. Tier 2 configurations changed more decisions and some diagnostic verdicts, but no four-fifths verdict. Serving the 24B model with vLLM FP8 selected 54% of people rather than 45% and passed an employment-status audit by sex that its strict FP32 reference failed: its demographic-parity and equalized-odds gaps fell from 0.0567 and 0.0515 to 0.0417 and 0.0394, against a diagnostic tolerance of 0.05. At the reference's selection count FP8 failed demographic parity, and no reading gave its equalized-odds change a paired interval excluding zero. The declared audit depends on the configuration; FP8 is not shown to be fairer. At the frozen thresholds, every pass-fail verdict a configuration changed had a sampling interval containing its criterion. It proposes an audit stability protocol in which the auditor declares contracts, groups, weights and tests before scoring and records each verdict's range over them apart from its sampling uncertainty.

AI.tldr: This paper tests how numerical execution contracts (Tier 1 arithmetic order and Tier 2 reduced-precision deployment) affect fairness audits, showing that reduced precision can alter pass-fail verdicts and proposing an audit stability protocol.
AI.motivation: Fairness audits treat trained models as fixed functions, overlooking that hardware, software stacks, and reduced-precision formats alter the arithmetic that evaluates them.
AI.method: Holding models, records, thresholds, and audit code fixed, the authors audit three tabular families and two open-weight LLMs (4B and 24B) across four tasks on NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple hardware under Tier 1 (arithmetic-only changes) and Tier 2 (BF16, FP8, 8-bit) execution contracts.
AI.result: Tier 1 changed borderline decisions depending on the GPU stack without altering prespecified unweighted verdicts, whereas Tier 2 changed more decisions and diagnostic verdicts; notably, vLLM FP8 on the 24B model selected 54% vs. 45% in FP32 and passed an employment-status audit by sex that FP32 failed, though failing demographic parity at matched selection counts.
AI.conclusion: Declared fairness verdicts depend on numerical execution contracts, so auditors should pre-specify contracts and report verdict ranges across them separately from sampling uncertainty.

title: CratesBump: A Version-Bump Dataset for the Rust Ecosystem
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Dataset and tool: this https URL
summary: We release CratesBump, the first public dataset for predicting version bumps in the Rust ecosystem, together with semver-extract, the tool that builds it.
