CratesBump is built from every crate on this http URL with at least two releases before 14 September 2026 (about 220,000 crates), giving over two million consecutive release pairs. Each pair has 41 features (code changes from AST diffs, dependency changes, complexity, release cadence, GitHub commit and issue activity), its source repository where listed, and two labels: the literal reading of this http URL, and Cargo's rule, under which a 0.y bump is a breaking change. semver-extract regenerates the dataset from public this http URL data and the GitHub API. To illustrate its use we (i) benchmark bump predictors on held-out repositories, finding the task learnable but far from solved, with lower scores on later releases; (ii) measure which feature groups carry the signal; (iii) check, against declared dependency ranges, how often Cargo's rule shields dependents from pre-1.0 breaking releases; and (iv) audit a sample of releases with cargo-semver-checks, finding minor and patch releases that break the public API despite their version number. Dataset and tool are released under open licenses.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CratesBump, a dataset of over two million Rust crate release pairs with 41 features and two semantic-versioning labels, alongside the semver-extract tool.
AI.motivation: Predicting semantic version bumps in software ecosystems lacks large-scale public datasets capturing code, dependency, and repository signals.
AI.method: The authors build semver-extract to collect ~220,000 Rust crates with at least two releases, extracting 41 features (AST diffs, dependencies, complexity, release cadence, GitHub activity) and labeling pairs under both literal SemVer and Cargo's pre-1.0 breaking-change rule.
AI.result: Benchmarking bump predictors on held-out repositories shows the task is learnable but unsolved (with lower scores on later releases), and auditing with cargo-semver-checks reveals minor and patch releases that break the public API.
AI.conclusion: CratesBump and semver-extract provide an open benchmark for studying version-bump prediction and semantic versioning compliance in the Rust ecosystem.

title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
comment: Accepted to the Workshop on Dexterous Manipulation at CoRL 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $\pi_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to adapt Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to dexterous multi-finger hands using SFT and diffusion-steering RL, finding that freezing the VLM and training only the action expert works best while SFT rollout success poorly predicts post-RL performance.
AI.motivation: Most VLA datasets use parallel-jaw grippers, making adaptation to dexterous multi-finger hands difficult, especially when teleoperation demonstrations are scarce.
AI.method: Using pi_0.5 and a LEAP hand across two simulation tasks with few demonstrations, the authors evaluate five fine-tuning recipes combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL).
AI.result: SFT success correlates poorly with post-DSRL success, freezing the VLM while fully training the action expert yields the most steerable policy for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution placements, and LoRA is the least steerable recipe.
AI.conclusion: Adapting VLAs to dexterous manipulation is best achieved by freezing the VLM, fully tuning the action expert, and avoiding SFT rollout success for checkpoint selection.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
comment: 22 pages. Presented at the KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI (ETAAI; non-archival). Code and trial ledgers: this https URL (DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24174991)
summary: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes evaluating autonomous ML experimentation agents on process governance alongside task scores, introducing a control-plane ledger that exposes hidden failures across 1,445 trials.
AI.motivation: Autonomous ML experiment agents are typically judged only by best achieved score, hiding whether they respected edit scopes, silently dropped failed trials, or made traceable keep/discard decisions.
AI.method: The authors build a governed harness where a control plane—not the LLM—manages trial lifecycles, enforces edit scopes, decides keep/discard, and logs every trial to an append-only ledger to compute governance metrics (invalid-action rate, repeated-bad rate, provenance completeness).
AI.result: Across six ML tasks and 1,445 trials, the ledger exposed failures hidden by task scores (including a 120-trial all-failure arm and a reset failure), whereas a success-only logger missed 43 of 50 trials in a matched counterfactual.
AI.conclusion: Process-level governance ledgers are essential for auditing, reproducing, and diagnosing autonomous LLM-driven ML experimentation.

title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
summary: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "overlap" metric to measure the minimum conservatism forced by a world model's latent representation on conformal safety filters, showing a separate safety encoder minimizes unnecessary refusals.
AI.motivation: Conformal calibration ensures latent safety filters rarely accept unsafe actions, but a poor latent representation can force the filter to be overly conservative and refuse many safe actions.
AI.method: The authors group similar latents and actions into cells, define "overlap" as the share of safe transitions in cells containing unsafe transitions, prove it bounds minimum safe-action refusals, and compare three safety-filter designs on visual navigation.
AI.result: In visual navigation, training a separate encoder beside the world model achieves the lowest overlap, refuses the fewest safe actions at the same conformal level, and enables the planner to reach the most goals compared to world-model or classifier-on-top designs.
AI.conclusion: The overlap metric provides a general, representation-level diagnostic for comparing and designing less conservative latent safety filters.

title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, Accepted at WSDM 2027 Findings
summary: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MoMoVL, a modality-aware mixed-precision quantization framework for MoE-based vision-language models that reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% while improving the accuracy-compression trade-off.
AI.motivation: Deploying Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) VLMs on edge devices is constrained by high memory demands, and existing MoE quantization methods overlook how visual and text tokens induce different expert quantization sensitivities.
AI.method: MoMoVL jointly uses per-expert activation profiles and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide mixed-precision bit-width assignment across experts.
AI.result: MoMoVL outperforms state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines in accuracy-compression trade-off and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with only a modest accuracy drop relative to a uniform-precision baseline.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for modality-specific expert sensitivity enables more effective mixed-precision compression for on-device MoE VLMs.

title: Do 3D Point Representations Encode Architectural Functions? Probing Supervised and Pretrained Models on Urban Facades
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Physical World AI: Geometry, Characteristics, and Multimodal Sensing
summary: Semantic labels say what a building element is, not what it does: two identical-looking windows on one facade may be operable or fixed, a column may carry load or only decorate. We ask whether 3D point representations encode such architectural function. On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes per element, we hold out entire buildings and compare hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch and frozen self-supervised point transformers. Descriptors and frozen features are read by the same linear layer. No network trained from scratch, from PointNet to a 108M-parameter PTv3, clearly exceeds the descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732. Random-weight controls of the same architectures (0.649 and 0.652) attribute the gain to pretraining (Utonia: +0.080, 95% building interval [+0.035, +0.124]). Pretrained features improve at every tested number of labelled buildings while descriptors and random features plateau, and, in the configurations we tested, fine-tuning erodes the benefit: at today's data scale, function is better read from pretrained representations than learned from scratch.

AI.tldr: This paper probes whether 3D point representations encode architectural functions on urban facades, finding that frozen self-supervised point transformers outperform networks trained from scratch and hand-crafted descriptors.
AI.motivation: Semantic labels identify what a building element is (e.g., window or column) rather than its architectural function (e.g., operable vs. fixed, load-bearing vs. decorative), and it is unknown whether 3D point models capture such function.
AI.method: On 22 mobile-LiDAR buildings with 15 functional attributes and held-out building splits, the authors compare linear probes on hand-crafted descriptors, networks trained from scratch (PointNet to 108M-parameter PTv3), random-weight controls, and frozen self-supervised point transformers (Utonia).
AI.result: Networks trained from scratch do not clearly beat descriptors (0.610 mAP on functionally ambiguous elements), whereas frozen Utonia reaches 0.732 mAP (+0.080 over random-weight controls), improves with more labeled buildings, and outperforms fine-tuned variants.
AI.conclusion: At current data scales, architectural function is better read out from frozen self-supervised 3D representations than learned from scratch or fine-tuned.

title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures
summary: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces STORM, a lightweight, structure-free machine learning ensemble for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction that matches or exceeds Boltz-2 accuracy while running over five orders of magnitude faster.
AI.motivation: Physics-based free-energy perturbation (FEP) and ML cofolding models like Boltz-2 are too computationally expensive for large-scale virtual screening and rapid retraining on new experimental data.
AI.method: STORM ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and small-molecule representations trained on historical experimental affinity data without requiring 3D structure prediction.
AI.result: Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds Boltz-2 accuracy across multiple evaluation datasets while achieving over five orders of magnitude speedup in both training and inference.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight structure-free ensembles offer a practical, high-throughput alternative to cofolding models for binding affinity prediction.

title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
summary: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes COTEX, a continual tool-space extension framework that adds specialist vision tools to multimodal agents via orthogonally constrained adapters without degrading existing tool use.
AI.motivation: Multimodal agents rely mostly on generic tools, and adding specialist vision models to an already trained agent risks disrupting its ability to select and use existing tools.
AI.method: COTEX identifies parameter directions for triggering tool calls versus selecting specific tools, constrains new tool adapters to calling directions orthogonal to existing tool choices, and converts specialist annotations into verified tool-use trajectories.
AI.result: Evaluated on two agents and three specialist tools across ten vision-language benchmarks, COTEX improves task performance while limiting performance drops on existing tools to at most 0.3 points.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal adapter constraints enable efficient, continual integration of specialist vision tools into multimodal agents without catastrophic forgetting.

title: RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: Apoorva Vashisth and Manav Kulshrestha contributed equally to this work. Prof. Zachary Kingston and Prof. Aniket Bera jointly advised this work
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation, yet their performance often degrades on long-horizon tasks that require multiple interdependent manipulations. Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. To this end, we introduce \textnormal{\textbf{RePlan-VLA}}, a VLA-agnostic framework that translates a VLA's short-horizon capabilities into reliable long-horizon execution. RePlan-VLA explicitly monitors the robot's motion for progress evaluation, and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. We also validate our approach for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RePlan-VLA, a training-free, VLA-agnostic framework that monitors robot motion progress and adaptively replans long-horizon manipulation tasks, boosting success rates on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN.
AI.motivation: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models degrade on long-horizon tasks with interdependent steps when burdened with long-horizon reasoning, memory, and error recovery inside the policy itself.
AI.method: RePlan-VLA wraps an unmodified, frozen short-horizon VLA policy in an execution-aware framework that explicitly monitors robot motion for progress evaluation and adaptively revises future plans based on observed outcomes.
AI.result: Without additional fine-tuning, RePlan-VLA improves success rates by 21.9% on RoboCasa365 and 10.4% on CALVIN over the next strongest baseline, and is validated on a real Franka Research 3 robot.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling progress-aware replanning from frozen short-horizon VLA policies provides a reliable, plug-and-play path to long-horizon robotic manipulation.

title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary: Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations. We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents KIWI, a programmable GPU-to-CPU reverse-offload framework for GPU-initiated communication that outperforms GPUDirect Async and cuts vLLM time per output token by up to 29%.
AI.motivation: Existing GPU-initiated communication libraries favor GPU-side transport control (GPUDirect Async) and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slow fallback.
AI.method: KIWI provides a programmable reverse-offload interface addressing queue contention, polling overhead, and proxy load imbalance, supporting a SHMEM-like library (KIWI-P2P) and redesigned mixture-of-experts kernels (KIWI-EP).
AI.result: KIWI achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of ops/sec; KIWI-P2P beats GDA in latency and bandwidth, and KIWI-EP cuts expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x on AMD GPUs and vLLM time per output token by up to 29%.
AI.conclusion: Programmable reverse offload can serve as a first-class, high-performance communication path for modern GPU workloads.

title: Neural Memory Orchestration
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures
summary: Modern HPC workloads increasingly stall on the memory hierarchy rather than on compute, and page faults from mmap'd files, swap, and tiered memory are a growing fraction of wall time. Heuristic prefetchers in the kernel handle stride-like and temporally clustered patterns well but degrade sharply on the irregular, data-dependent access streams typical of these workloads. Learned prefetchers have been shown to capture such patterns in simulation but have not been taken to a deployed pipeline running against live workloads on real hardware. We present Overseer, an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system. An eBPF collector observes page faults on the target host, a transformer predictor (OverNet) runs on network-attached inference hardware and emits future page addresses, and a kernel-resident enforcer materializes those pages into the target's address space before they are demanded. OverNet encodes fault sequences through per-instance ordinal ranks over deltas, which lets a single trained model serve any target process without retraining. On two page-fault-heavy workloads, Overseer reduces runtime by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication, with corresponding reductions in major-fault counts.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Overseer, an end-to-end learned page-prefetching system using eBPF, a network-attached transformer (OverNet), and a kernel enforcer, cutting runtime by ~35% to ~10x on page-fault-heavy workloads.
AI.motivation: Modern HPC workloads stall on irregular, data-dependent page faults from mmap'd files, swap, and tiered memory, where kernel heuristic prefetchers fail and prior learned prefetchers have only been tested in simulation.
AI.method: Overseer uses an eBPF collector to observe page faults, runs a transformer predictor (OverNet) encoding fault sequences via per-instance ordinal delta ranks on network-attached inference hardware, and materializes predicted pages via a kernel-resident enforcer without per-process retraining.
AI.result: On live hardware running page-fault-heavy workloads, Overseer reduces runtime by roughly 35% on Hilbert-curve traversal and by roughly an order of magnitude on dense matrix multiplication, with corresponding drops in major-fault counts.
AI.conclusion: Rank-encoded learned page prefetching can be deployed end-to-end on real hardware to substantially accelerate irregular memory-bound workloads.
